The *Śataratnasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Śrī Umāpati Śivācārya.
I pay homage to the elephant-faced one, whose inner obstacles are shattered by teeth white as jasmine and the moon,
and who is accompanied by the song of bees falling upon the stream of his ichor.
I worship Śiva, who performs the eternal dance of bliss in the midst of his glorious assembly, and who is served by the goddess Umā.

May this Supreme Lord liberate us from the bonds that cause the manifestation of the bindu, which is capable of generating the pure path (śuddhādhvan), and who is the foremost bearer of the infinite command flashing forth to agitate Māyā— the mistress of the transformation of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Time.
In Cidambaram, there was a teacher named Śivaśrī Umāpati who had established a monastery and was a knower of the Śiva Āgamas;
he [expounded] the Svayambhuva, Niśvāsa, Mataṅga, Devyāmata, Mṛgendra, Kiraṇa, and Parākhya [Tantras].
Having examined the *Śrīdevīkālottara*, the *Viśvasāra*, the *Jñānottara*, and the ten [other] scriptures, as well as the one,
he extracted a hundred essential aphorisms (*sūtra*).
He fashioned a bond consisting of a hundred jewels.
I shall now provide a description of these one hundred jewels, who are worthy of ear-ornaments and endowed with knowledge of the scriptures.

And the quality of being a "jewel" (*ratna*) belonging to these sūtras, O King, is due to their producing passion for enjoyment and liberation, as well as from their providing what is desired. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*: "Because they reign over all principles (*tattva*), and because they produce passion and so forth in those who possess [spiritual] authority."
"And because the jewels are produced by the desired ritual, [the letters] Bindu and the others exist in the teaching of Śiva. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the Three Jewels, it is said as follows:
"O King, among all the principles (tattvas), [the deities] are the goddesses of passion (rāga) within the spheres of authority;
they are to be held in the mind by the lords and the Śivas. (4)
And for men, by means of a mass of vast, unimpeded rays,

and through the bestowal of desired jewels, the [principles] beginning with the *bindu* exist within the teaching of Śiva— the Three Jewels. (5) Here in this world, due to the onset of the Kali age, when the meaning of the Āgamas has been lost and heretical doctrines have increased—

While the lineage of teacher and disciple was still extant, the supremely compassionate Śivācārya, desiring to bestow grace upon his own disciples, [composed this work] which is the essence of the entire scriptural knowledge-section (*jñānakāṇḍa*) and serves as the cause for the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) and the manifestation of the nature of Śiva for those bound by the snares of transmigratory existence.

He compiled a hundred jewel-like aphorisms (*sūtra-ratna-śata*) that determine the established tenets (*siddhānta-nirṇaya*) analyzing the nature of the initiation of knowledge (*jñāna-dīkṣā*). According to the commentaries on that compilation by Sadyojyotiḥ, Rāmakaṇṭha,
Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, Aghoraśiva, and others, [it is as follows:]
And the commentary is being composed according to our own guru’s tradition. What is that commentary?
"Word-division, statement of word-meanings, analysis, syntactical connection, and the resolution of objections—this is the fivefold definition of a commentary. Thus it is said.

In this regard, since it is necessary at the beginning of a work to offer salutation to the chosen deity and to state the subject matter, the author of this compendium first cites the *Svāyambhuva-sūtra* for that purpose:
Having prostrated before Śiva, the supreme Lord of Death, I shall hereafter proclaim the initiation of knowledge; listen with concentrated minds.
Here, by the word "Śiva," is meant the one who removes inauspiciousness, the cause for the destruction of obstacles, characterized by the agency of knowing all things.
And for the sake of bestowing grace upon all beings, the Supreme Lord, who is beyond the state of quiescence (*śāntyatīta*) and whose nature is immeasurability and so forth, is set forth.
As it is said in that very same [text]:
"Immeasurable, indefinable, incomparable, and free from affliction."
Subtle, omnipresent, eternal, constant, imperishable, and sovereign.
It is immeasurable because it is infinite; it is indescribable because it lacks defining characteristics;
it is incomparable because it has no likeness; and it is free from affliction because it is stainless.
It is subtle because it is imperceptible and because it is all-pervasive;
it is eternal because it is devoid of a cause, and it is stable because it is immovable.
"By virtue of having the nature of the syllable Oṃ, the supreme Śiva shines as that which transcends tranquility.

Just as jewels in this world shine with great value, manifest themselves, and produce passion in those nearby; and as they are worn by men upon their limbs, they are radiant and fulfill one's desires.

And likewise, all categories beginning with the *bindu* manifest as both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) within all the principles (*tattva*s) beginning with *śakti*, by virtue of these causes which are the selves of the Lords (*īśvara*s) such as Ananta and the Śivas established in the states of Sadāśiva and so forth.
In accordance with their respective offices, characterized by the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary, passion (rāga) is ever-present.

Furthermore, these [qualities] are sustained by the intellect (dhī) of persons as objects of meditation. Possessing unimpeded and extraordinary splendor, they bestow the desired fruits known as enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti). Therefore, these too are included in the Śiva-śāstra.

The word "jewels" (*ratnāni*) is stated; the ellipsis [to complete the sense] is "are proclaimed. Furthermore, by means of your unimpeded and extraordinary splendor, their excellence has been demonstrated. Since even those who have attained liberation (*muktātman*) are characterized by these very marks—which delineate the Three Jewels—they too would become objects of salutation.

Lest that [objection] should arise, he has stated "the supreme state" (*paramapada*) as its qualification. "Supreme" (*parama*) means established from beginningless time. However, there is a distinction between liberated souls (*muktātman*), for they possess the state of Śiva obtained through His grace.
As it was said by the Teacher (Sureśvara):
"Though they are liberated souls and auspicious, these are liberated by his grace;
he alone is to be known as eternally liberated from the beginningless. [Tattvaprakāśa 6] Having paid homage to such a Śiva, thereafter, by the grace of Śiva, which has shaken off...

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: having prostrated before one's own Guru, named Nidhaneśa, who has manifested the power of knowledge and action regarding all objects, who bestows grace upon all, and who is Rudra, the introducer of the Tantra;
this is what is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Measured by half of three crores, it was self-manifested from the Lord of Destruction;
the Lotus-born heard this self-manifested [teaching] from the Lord of Destruction.
(1.59). Here, by the word *svayambhūta*, the *Svāyambhuva Āgama* is meant. [This concerns] knowledge and initiation.
"I shall explain" (*pravakṣyāmi*). "Knowledge and initiation" (*jñānadīkṣe*) is a copulative compound (*dvandvasamāsa*).
"I shall explain" means "I shall explain thoroughly"; this is the statement of the formal promise (*pratijñā*).
By this promise regarding knowledge, it follows by implication that the categories beginning with the Lord (*pati*), which are to be known, [are also included].
The thesis is established. Furthermore, the use of a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is for the purpose of indicating the primary importance of both;

for some, knowledge is primary, while for others, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is primary—this is the explanation of initiation. Between these two, knowledge is primary for the teacher who performs them, whereas initiation is primary for the seeker of liberation. [Thus it is said] regarding knowledge and initiation.

Having made the formal promise, "I shall proclaim [this] as the essence of the meaning of the Tantra by including it within the subject matter of the path," he then [taught] the sixty thousand sages known as the Bālakhilyas— who were purified by the initiation of Śiva through the descent of Śiva’s power, who sought knowledge, and who were fit for the authority [of practice].

"Having composed yourselves, remain steady; listen with concentrated minds"—this is the meaning of "listen with concentrated minds" regarding the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) under discussion. By this summary of the first sūtra, the author [of the compendium] has also performed the salutation to the deity and the teacher (*devagurunamaskriyā*), as well as the formal promise (*pratijñā*).

It should be understood that [these] were composed to establish his own disciples in a state of attentiveness. The relationship of the teacher is fivefold, characterized by the relation between the one to be known and the knower, beginning with the *para* (supreme). Among these, the relationship between Śiva and Sadāśiva is *para*; that between Sadāśiva and Nidhanēśa is *mahat* (great); [that between] Nidhanēśa and...

The fivefold relationship, beginning with "parādi" (the supreme and so forth), should be understood as follows: for the two self-born ones (*svayambhū*), it is divine; for the self-born ones and the *bālakhilyas*, it is both divine and non-divine; and for the *bālakhilyas* who are human, it is non-divine.
Thus it has been said:
The "other" (para), the "great" (mahat), the "divine" (divya), the "both divine and non-divine" (divyādivya),
and the "non-divine" (adivya)— these five are proclaimed as the relations (sambandhas).

The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this compendium consists of knowledge and so forth; its fruit (*phala*) is that very knowledge. The relationship (*sambandha*) between this [work], knowledge, and initiation (*dīkṣā*) is that of the expounded and the expounder.
Those who have been initiated are the qualified recipients (*adhikārin*); thus, the subject matter, purpose, relationship, and qualified recipient are to be understood. || 1 ||

Now, he presents the first aphorism of the *Raurava* and *Svāyambhuva* [Tantras], which indicates the relationship between the subject and the object of instruction, as well as the purpose, regarding the two topics of knowledge (*jñāna*) and initiation (*dīkṣā*) that have been proposed:
"Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma known as impurity (*mala*), illusion (*māyā*), and the self (*ātman*)."

And for the manifestation of the state of Śiva, knowledge proceeds from Śiva. Now, immediately after the state of being oriented toward the exhaustion of the agency that causes the obstruction of the power of consciousness,
for the sake of liberation from the bonds of karma known as the impurity of the self and Māyā— for the individual souls (aṇus)— the [impurity] in the form of *mala*...

For the sake of liberation from that threefold bondage which consists of the forms of *māyā* and *karman*, and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva—that is, for the revelation of the nature of Śiva—knowledge proceeds, meaning it arises, from Śiva, that is, Paramaśiva. And this is the root aphorism (*mūlasūtra*), because it defines the meaning of the Tantra. Thus...
And because it is adorned with words and so forth. Thus, in the *Mṛgendra*:
"That in which the tree of the meaning of the Great Tantra is present, as if planted like a seed—that is the *mūlasūtra*, which is further adorned with words and so forth. So it is said.

In this context, *mala* is that which obstructs the state of Śiva-nature inherent in the all-pervading Self. With its Śiva-nature thus bound by it, the Self is unable—without a means (*upāya*)—to know the object of knowledge or to perform the action to be done.
For one who requires the means for experience, the bondage called *māyā*, consisting of *kalā* and the other categories, is taught. *Māyā*.

The source of the world; that which is called by that name is the bondage so designated. For one who is endowed with the means of experience and intends for experience, the object of experience is karma, known as dharma and adharma. This is the threefold bondage of the self, beginning with impurity (mala) and the rest. For indeed, when one is joined with this [bondage], one's state of Śiva-nature is not manifested everywhere simultaneously.

It shines forth. For the sake of liberation from this threefold bondage of that Self and for the manifestation of its Śiva-nature, knowledge proceeds from Śiva, who desires to uplift [the soul]. That knowledge which proceeds from the bound souls (paśu) and from the bonds (pāśa), because it manifests the form of the bound and possesses the nature of the bonds, on the contrary [serves] the bonds.
It generates firmness.

In treatises such as the *Tattvaprakāśa*, it is stated that "the fivefold object is the bond" (*pāśa*), and so forth; [this refers to] the impurity (*mala*), karma, the gross and subtle *māyā*-bonds, and the powers of Śiva that govern these bonds.

One should not raise the objection: "The five objects have been described as being bonds, yet here a threefold [classification] is mentioned; how is there no contradiction? For, since the insentient entities known as *mala*, *karman*, and *māyā* lack the capacity to produce their own effects, they are accepted as being dependent upon that which favors them [the sentient subject].

Since the power of the Supreme Lord (parameśvaraśakti) constitutes a secondary bond (gauṇapāśa), and since Māyā—though divided into gross and subtle forms—is intended here as a unity, the threefold nature of bondage is logically established. [Note:
This verse is not found in the printed edition of the Mṛgendra.]

Śiva, however, is distinct from both the bound soul (*paśu*) and its fetters (*pāśa*); he is the adversary of the fetters and is augmented by every capacity. Therefore, the knowledge that proceeds from him is sufficient and firm for the cessation of the fetters. For that which possesses obstructed power must be of the same class as that which possesses unobstructed power.

It is the manifestor of power (*śakti*). Śiva is of the same genus as the self; for that [self] whose state of Śiva-hood is obstructed, this [Śiva] initiates true knowledge in order to manifest that state of Śiva-hood which is unobstructed—this is logical. And here, by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), which denotes the power of Śiva, that which consists of awakening (*avabodha*) is meant.
Both forms of initiation (*dīkṣā*) are thus subsumed.

Now, if it is asked how initiation can have the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), it is said in reply: just as the ray of the sun, while illuminating objects and also burning them, does not abandon its nature as light.
Even though it possesses both forms, it is called "light" (*prakāśa*); even in that state, it does not abandon its nature as knowledge (*jñāna*).
Therefore, it is said that knowledge consists of both forms.
Being bound by the fetters of impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and karma is the characteristic of those who are to be graced (*anugrāhya*). This [characteristic] is distinct [from the nature of light].
And both the individual and the collective are intended [to be included]. For some, there is grace for those joined with impurity (*mala*);
for some, for those joined with impurity and karma; for some, for those joined with impurity and what is called *māyā*;
and for some, for those joined with impurity, *māyā*, and karma. Why is this both individual and collective?

Regarding the phrase "intended to be spoken": for he will later state that even those who are *akalās* (devoid of *kalās*) are both objects of purification (*śodhya*) and objects of cognition (*bodhya*). These *akalās* are of two kinds: *vijñānākalas* and *pralayākalas*. For both of these groups, there is first of all no [connection with] that which is called *māyā*. As for the *vijñānākalas*, their *karmas* have been exhausted; as for those among them...

Those who are favored by grace that is without further office (*niradhikāra*) become equal to Śiva. Those who are favored by grace that involves an office (*sādhikāra*) become Lords of Knowledge (*Vidyā-Īśvara*) who have transcended *māyā*.
Even for those joined with what is called impurity (*mala*) and *māyā*, grace will occur when [the impurities] have been diminished through some means.

The bondage known as *māyā* within the sphere of action (*karma*) undergoes dissolution into its own cause. And it is precisely at the time when that [bondage] is about to dissolve that, sometimes, there occurs the grace of the Supreme Lord’s power, because the time of its manifestation is not fixed; this applies to the self as well.

Because the time for the cessation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), the agency of the agent, and the onset of the exhaustion [of karma] is fixed, grace (*anugraha*) indeed occurs. For those such as ourselves, for those situated in the spheres of *māyā* and so forth,
and for the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s), grace consists in the abandonment of the bonds of impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and karma.

Since there is also grace bestowed upon those Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras who reside in the maṇḍalas of Māyā and the rest, who are endowed with the *kalās* and so forth, and who are enjoyers of worldly experience; therefore, the definition of the means of grace as "knowledge proceeding from Śiva" is too narrow (*avyāpaka*), for [grace] occurs even by His mere will.

If it is argued that grace is intended for some, and that such a desire is not pervasive within knowledge, we say no. Desire, too, is simply the power (*śakti*) of Śiva. And because it is characterized by bestowing and destroying [impurities], it falls within initiation (*dīkṣā*);
furthermore, because it consists of consciousness and involves relinquishment, it is indeed pervaded by this [category of] "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
"Separately and collectively. Thus it has been stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:

"The bound souls (paśus) are to be known as threefold: the Vijñānākala, the Pralayākala, and the Sakala. Among these, the first is joined with impurity (mala), and the second is joined with both impurity and karma. (1.8)
"Endowed with impurity (mala), māyā, and karma, [he is] sakala... Thus it is said.

Now, if it is argued that since knowledge alone is the cause for the manifestation of the principle of withdrawal (nivṛtti-tattva), it follows that ritual action (kriyā), yoga, and conduct (caryā) are rendered useless—this is certainly true. Nevertheless, regarding conduct, ritual action, ...

Because there is no futility [of the yogas], as they serve as the cause of the knowledge that bestows *śivasāyujya* (union with Śiva) by means of accomplishing *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sārūpya* through the sequence of the *vidyātattva* and so forth;
as it is said in the *Devīkālottara*:
However, ritual actions and conduct are proclaimed as the means for the arising of gnosis.
Thus it is said in the *Suprabheda*: "Having first practiced yoga, one should then practice gnosis therein;
at that time, one should destroy the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of gnosis."
In the *Śivajñānabodhasaṃgraha*:
"Furthermore, the Carya-pāda, Kriyā-pāda, likewise the Yoga-pāda,
and the Jñāna-pāda, have been expounded by Śiva in their proper sequence."
This fourfold path bestows the fruits beginning with *sālokya*.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*: "Namely, *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and likewise *sāyujya*."

In this context, although initiation is equal in all four— conduct and the rest— insofar as it establishes one's qualification (*adhikāra*), its primary importance is stated here alongside knowledge because it accomplishes the upward movement (*ūrdhvagati*) in the form of union (*sāyujya*), which is the fruit of knowledge. As the author of the *Saṃgraha* will say:
"Because initiation alone liberates one from the extensive bondage that obstructs the state of the Supreme, and leads [the soul] upward even to the abode of Śiva.
And here, the classification of initiations is demonstrated in the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍana*:

But that which is performed without distinction by one established in the office of a teacher (*ācārya*) through the procedure of the *tuṣādhikaraṇa* is common to all; it is fourfold, occurring both with and without the sequence of the initiation into the seed (*bījādhikāra*).
The first of these is twofold, arising from devotion to the world of Śiva or to *dharma*; among those, the first is the material (*bhautikī*).
But another is the lifelong [vow], which, though characterized by birth, is made through the performance of renunciation and consecration.

The seedless [initiation] for men is of two kinds, bestowing immortality either immediately or after a long time; it is that which, through the abandonment of the constant and other [levels of] support, is freed from the authority of the [lower] offices.
Furthermore, this is fourfold as "with support" (sādhārā), and it is again twofold by way of knowledge and action.
"The wise man [acts] through knowledge, while the action of the ignorant is preceded by the eyes.
(1) Now, he summarizes the twofold nature of knowledge— distinct from the initiation (*dīkṣā*) denoted by the word "knowledge"— by means of the *Devīmata-sūtra*:

Knowledge is declared to be of two kinds: it is remembered as the higher (para) and the lower (apara). The higher is called awakening (avabodha), while the lower is the supreme scripture (śāstra). || 3 ||

In this regard, knowledge is twofold according to the distinction between the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). The higher is the nature of supreme awakening; the lower means that which consists of the *Kāmika* and other Tantras. Thus it is said in the *Sātvatasaṃhitā*:
"Knowledge is auspicious; the higher is awakening, while the lower is designated as Tantra."

Knowledge, which is of the nature of awakening, is indeed the power (*śakti*) of Śiva. That [power] is twofold: residing in inherence (*samavāya-vartinī*) and residing in appropriation (*parigraha-vartinī*). Among these, that which resides in inherence is also twofold: consisting of consciousness (*bodha-rūpā*) and consisting of action (*kriyā-rūpā*). Therein, that which consists of consciousness is the discerning agent of all objects. That which consists of action is also twofold.
It consists of the form of grace (*anugraha*) and the form of concealment (*tirobhāva*). Thus it has been said: "Grace and concealment are indeed the two attributes of Sadāśiva.
Here, [the nature of the Lord] is of the form of supreme awakening (*parāvabodha*).
Knowledge proceeds toward objects precisely by being mounted upon the form of words, which are themselves of the nature of non-supreme knowledge (*aparajñāna*). Now, one might object:

"This knowledge is the fruit of initiation (*dīkṣā*); therefore, how can it be said that knowledge and initiation are equal as means of grace? This is true; however, knowledge [depends] on the teacher...

It makes known both the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). And because he has thus understood the goal and the means, he is able to employ the means for the sake of establishing the goal for those who are to be assisted.
Furthermore, in all cases, the proponent of liberation (*muktivādin*) asserts that knowledge alone is the means for the attainment of liberation. Not [other things].

Furthermore, even where it is said "only through knowledge," there too the performance of the means (sādhana) is necessarily present. Therefore, it is logical that the previous sūtra stated that both knowledge and initiation (jñāna-dīkṣā) are equally means of grace. || 3 ||
Now, by means of the *Mṛgendra-sūtra*, he demonstrates the sequence for attaining the nature of vision for supreme knowledge, which consists of awakening:
"At the time of emanation, Maheśāna [acts] for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human beings."
It bestows pure knowledge characterized by the five streams. || 4 ||

At the time of creation, at the commencement of the world-emanation, the Great Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, acts for the sake of the accomplishment of the goals of human existence—that is, for the attainment of the goals of man consisting of both supreme liberation (*mokṣa*) and worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*). Regarding the term "pure":
because it first emanates in the form of *nāda* from the nature of pure consciousness, it has not yet assumed the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

"Characterized by five streams": those five streams are the "five-streams," namely those facing upward, east, south, north, and west; it is characterized by them on all sides, that is, marked by their spreading forth.
This means that, in the form of Sadāśiva, it has attained the nature of various systems of philosophy (darśana) such as the *Kāmika* and others. Such [is the deity].

It ordains—that is, it brings forth—knowledge in the form of scripture. From the partless Śiva, knowledge itself, whose nature is pure consciousness, first issued forth in the form of sound (*nāda*). Subsequently, from the form of Sadāśiva, it attained the form of the *tantra*. As it is said in the *Pauṣkara*:
From the unmanifest, quiescent, and auspicious supreme cause, the scripture has emerged in the form of sound. Thus it is said.
In that very place it is said:
"Even the Lord Sadāśiva has arrived in the form of sound;
that knowledge consisting of the six categories is indeed manifold in its meters."

If it is asked, "How can the partless Śiva, who is devoid of the organ of speech and other such faculties, be a producer of the *nāda*?"— the answer is no. For just as a magnet, though devoid of organs and the like, possesses the power to attract iron, so too is the capacity of Śiva logically established.
As it has been stated in the *Parākhyatantra*: "By whose presence the accomplishment of every task occurs,
even when [the body] is devoid of senses, that capacity is seen in the Self who performs the drawing-in [of the senses]."
"In the same way, the Lord's capacity for all actions is innate.
And in the Pauṣkara:
"The power of Him who is independent of the organ of speech has issued forth everywhere."
"What wonder does she express by means of that [speech], given its absolute purity?
Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Is this [Supreme Lord] not omnipotent (*akalya*) because he is partless (*niṣkala*), or how could the world exist if he were not omnipotent?"
"Just as one acts here according to one's capacity, so too is the scripture not the master [in this regard].

Here is the etymological definition of the word *śāstra*: "The scripture (*śāstra*) is that which protects (*trāyate*) the pure souls (*śuddhātmanām*) by providing their welfare (*hitam*) from the ocean of worldly existence (*bhavārṇavāt*)."
Because it protects that teaching, it is called a "śāstra" (treatise).

In that regard, there are twenty-five streams (*srotas*) of Sadāśiva, each distinct according to five divisions: worldly (*laukika*), Vedic (*vaidika*), spiritual (*adhyātmika*), super-pathway (*atimārgika*), and mantra-based (*māntrika*).
Within these alone is contained the entire body of speech, the entire web of scriptures (*śāstrajāla*). Thus, it is said in the *Kāmika*:
The worldly, the Vedic, and likewise the spiritual,
as well as that which transcends the paths and is called Mantra— thus the division of Tantra is manifold.
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Mahāghora, and Puruṣeśāna are each five-faced; by them, the worldly [rituals] and so forth were taught.
The division of the stream is proclaimed to consist of twenty-five parts;
within these alone is contained the entire body of literature, both that which expresses reality and the reality itself.
Likewise, in the Somasiddhānta: "The worldly tantra is fivefold, as is the Vedic tantra;
likewise the ādhyātmika tantra, and similarly the atimārga."
"In the same way, that which is called Mantra and Tantra among them has been extensively proclaimed.
Thus, this nature of the worldly [systems] and so forth has been elaborated upon in the *Siddhāntadīpikā* composed by Sarvātmaśambhu;
it is not written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. Let it be understood from that very source. Therein—
The fivefold mantra-system is, in order, associated with the directions of the zenith, the east, Kubera (the north), Varuṇa (the west), and Yama (the south);

it is known by the names Muktiprada (Bestower of Liberation), Siddhānta, Sarvaviṣaharaṇa (Remover of All Poisons), Gāruḍa, Sarvavaśīkaraṇa (All-Subjugating), Vāma, Bhūtagrahanivāraka (Averter of Spirits and Planets), Bhūtatantra, and Śatrukṣayakara (Destroyer of Enemies) Bhairava. Likewise:
In the Kāmika:
"Likewise, that which is called Mantra-tantra, born from the mouth of Sadāśiva;
the Siddhānta, Gāruḍa, Vāma, Bhūta-tantra, and Bhairava."
From the faces facing upward, east, Kubera (north), water (west), and Yama (south),
these [scriptures] beginning with the Siddhānta appear respectively; as stated in the Kāmika,
there is the Śaiva speech which is both general and specific, and the Vaiśiṣṭika speech.
And here, regarding the knowledge of the form of the scripture (*śāstra*), the knowledge of the Vedas and so forth is secondary; the knowledge of the established tenets (*siddhānta*) is primary.

Even within the knowledge of the established tenets, the knowledge of Śiva is primary, while the knowledge of Rudra is secondary. Furthermore, even within the knowledge of Śiva, the status of being primary or secondary is determined by the sequence of the speakers and the sequence of the original progenitors. Thus...

The knowledge of Rudra is also [to be understood in this way]. Likewise, the higher and lower nature of the sub-divisions (upabheda) should be understood as the distinctions between the higher and the lower. Thus, just as with the knowledge of sound-form, so too for the knowledge of the form of consciousness (avabodha), there are the pure path, the impure path, Śiva, Sadāśiva, Paśu, Māyā—

The distinctions between the higher (para) and the lower (apara) are to be understood through [the categories of] illumination and so forth. Likewise, for knowledge in the form of initiation (dīkṣā), the higher and lower distinctions are to be inferred through such classifications as the final (naiṣṭhika), the elemental (bhautika), the seedless (nirbīja), the seeded (sabīja), the state of Śiva’s nature (śivadharmi), and the worldly state (lokadharmy). This has been stated in the Svāyambhuva:
Although that [consciousness] is one, it assumes multiplicity arising from the lotus-like mouth of Śiva;
through the distinction between the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā), it proceeds toward the attainment of its objects.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:

"In the beginning, knowledge was twofold according to the distinction of those qualified for it; through the division of the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā), it reveals the meaning of the Lord (pati) and the bound soul (paśu)."
The knowledge that reveals Śiva is remembered as the supreme Śivajñāna;
it is the higher realization beyond the Vedas and other sciences, which reveals the true nature of both the bound soul (paśu) and its fetters (pāśa).
"Just as the eye is of a different character for a dog and a cat at night,
so too is this knowledge of the higher and the lower of a different character.
Thus, the knowledge of the Siddhānta— beginning with the *Kāmika* and others, and extending from the syllable *praṇava* up to the *aṃśu*— has been set forth.
Those which are designated as the Śiva-bheda are the knowledge whose locus is Śiva; thus, the Śiva-bheda is so called.

The eighteen tantras, beginning with the Vijaya, which are declared to belong to the primordial Rudras and other Rudras—those are designated as the Rudra-bheda, and the knowledge whose locus is the Rudras is the Rudra-bheda.
Thus, because it is distinct from the self of Rudra, the Tantra consisting of Śiva and Rudra is twenty-eight-fold, being eighteen-fold [in its divisions] plus the one consisting of Rudra himself.
In the Svāyambhuva [Tantra], it is said:
"Like a wish-fulfilling gem, this alone— the single knowledge of Śiva— stands here as the cause of all, yet it is further divided tenfold."
Thus, divided eighteenfold and spreading through further subdivisions,
the variety of recipients is described in the *Mukuṭatantra*:
"The recipients of the divisions of Śiva consist of three lineages each."
But for each pair of divisions of Rudra, sixty-six [subdivisions] have been stated.
The differentiation of that [knowledge] is elaborated in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Immediately after creation, the Lord, having created the ten Śivas as his sons,
divided this single knowledge and taught it to them according to that same number."

The fruit of the one called Praṇava is the fulfillment of desires; that of the one called Sudhā is born of yoga; that of the one called Dīpta is to be meditated upon; and that of the one called Kāraṇa is the very cause.
The Ajita belongs to the Lord known as Suśiva; the Sudīptaka belongs to Sūkṣma; and the Sahasraka belongs to the one named Kāla.
Suprabheda belongs to Gaṇeśa, while Aṃśumān belongs to the one known as Aṃśu;
thus has the first [lineage] been declared, and now follows another sequence of gurus.
From Praṇava, Trikala was obtained; from Trikala, Hara received the Kāmika;
from the one named Sudhā, the Yogaja Tantra [was received]; and from that, the Lord known as Bhasma.
From Dīptādrudra, Cintya was born; from him, Gopati; from him, Ambikā;
from Kāraṇa, Śarva; and from him, Prajāpati was obtained.
Ajita received it from Suśiva; Umēśa and Acyuta received it from him; Dīpta received it from Īśa; and then Hutāśana received it from Trimūrti.
From Sūkṣma, Sūkṣmabhava was obtained; from him, Prabhañjana was obtained;
from Kālasaṃjña, Sahasrākṣa; from him, Bhīma; and from him, Dharma; and from him, Khaga.
From Gaṇeśa, [the scripture] named Suprabheda was obtained; from Avighneśa, Śaśin;
from Aṃśujña, Aṃśumat; and from him, Ravi received the foremost [scripture].
Thus, these ten Śiva-bhedas beginning with Śiva are proclaimed;
furthermore, another supreme Rudra-bheda is considered to consist of eighteen in number.
Having first produced the Rudras by the number eighteen,
the wise Śiva, O bird, then awakened them here again by that very same number.
This supreme *Vijaya-tantra*, the great *Pārameśvara-mahātantra* of the one whose form is Śrī, was proclaimed by Rudra, who is known as Anādi.
The exhalation of Daśārṇa is the name "Prodgīta" of the Wielder of the Trident;
therefore, the tranquil orb of the Bindu is considered to be the perfected state.
The lineage of one devoted to Śiva is the Lion;
that of Sauma is said to be the Candrahāsa; and that of Ananta is considered auspicious as it consists of all souls.
The self-existent,
stainless crown of the radiant one is known as Kauravya, belonging to Brahmā, Īśa, and the one named Śiva.
The ray of the Father of the Gods (Brahmā) is known as Lalita, while that of Cālaya is Āgneya;
that of Vyoman is likewise, and furthermore, the supreme [ray] belongs to Śiva.
These have arisen within innate knowledge (sahajñāna); now hear again [of those] from the body of Śiva.
The Supreme Lord attained victory from that which is known as beginningless;
and from Him, in the form of Śrī, the sage Uśanas received the Pārameśvara [tantra].
From the ten-syllable [mantra], Niśvāsa was obtained by Śailasambhavā;
from that which is known as Rudra, the excellent sage named Kaca received the Prodgīta.
The tranquil sage named Dadhīci,
from whom the [mantra] known as Bindu was perfected, attained the status of the Gaṇa Caṇḍeśvara.
From Śivaniṣṭha, Haṃsavāhana obtained the lineage;
and from the gentle Nārasiṃha, the great Nṛsiṃha obtained it.
From Ananta, the priest of the gods (Bṛhaspati) obtained the Candrahāsa sword;
from Sarvātmadeva, the great attendant Vīrabhadra obtained the Bhadra sword.
Padmasambhava, being intent on protecting his subjects, attained the Svāyambhuva [state] from Nidhana and reached Viraja through his splendor.
From Brahmā, Nandikeśvara obtained Kauravya;
from Īśāna, Mahādeva, who has the banner as his support, obtained the crown.
The sage Saṃvartaka received the *kiraṇa* from the divine ancestors;
Rudra, assuming the form of Bhairava, received the *lalita* from Ālaya.
The Fire-god, having returned once more from that which is known as the Sky, [reappeared];
thus, the division of the Tantras has been declared by me here with its concise characteristics.

Among those divisions, whatever division is a sub-division is called a "sub-division" (upabheda). Since that [sub-division] is conceived through metaphorical designation (upacāra), it is therefore considered a "division" (bheda) by figurative usage.
No distinction in the fruit is to be imagined here; rather, a distinction in the knowledge is postulated.
This knowledge proceeds sequentially upon the earth through the lineage of Sadāśiva, Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, and the assembly of sages.
Likewise,
it was previously composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter by the Lord Sadāśiva, and thereafter by the wise Ananta in many millions of verses.
In the Pauṣkara,
it is said that the Supreme Lord spoke this to the great-souled Śrīkaṇṭha;
from Śrīkaṇṭha the Ṛṣis received it, and from them it was received by the excellent humans.
This Great Tantra consists of four parts. Thus, it is said in the Mṛgendra:
"The Lord of the World [taught] the Great Tantra, which has four parts and three categories. (4)

To demonstrate that knowledge of the nature of other words is to be accepted— despite its initial distaste when it first dawns— because it results in happiness upon its full development, like medicine, he establishes its medicinal quality by means of the *Parākhya-sūtra*:
Accept this knowledge arising from the earth of Śiva as a medicine for the self;
it is sweet, its bliss ripens in the end, and it reveals extraordinary qualities.

"Take this knowledge, which is the medicine for the self"—the meaning is "let it be grasped. Since all medicinal herbs arise from the earth, he shows the birthplace of this medicine in the form of knowledge by saying "arisen from the auspicious earth" (*śivakṣmottham*). Śiva himself is the earth; [knowledge] arises from that.
The meaning is that it was produced from that.
In the *Mātaṅgapārameśvara*, however, it is stated thus:
"Formerly, it was composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter to the number of ten million."
Then [it was received] by the god Sadāśiva and by the wise Ananta.
—the *Mātaṅgapārameśvara*.

"Consisting of three categories" (*tripadārtha*) means that it expounds the three categories (*padārtha*) consisting of the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*), since all other categories are included within these very ones. "Consisting of four quarters" (*catuṣpāda*) refers to [the quarters of] ritual action (*kriyā*), conduct (*caryā*), yoga (*yoga*), and...
The meaning is that it is divided into the sections on knowledge (vidyāpāda).
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "blissful in its transformation" (pariṇāmasukha). What is "transformation" (pariṇāma)? It is the future result; that which produces happiness at a later time.
It is "palatable" because it is equal to nectar. It is "a revealer of specific qualities."

It is the manifestor of qualities such as omniscience; in the case of the medicinal plant, it is the indicator of the specific quality of health. By these three qualifiers, even the suspicion that this knowledge is ungraspable is dispelled. [It is] like those things in the world which, being of the nature of nectar, bring about happiness in the future.
This is because all things that produce specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) are perceivable by everyone.

The intended meaning of the phrase "the medicine for the self" is as follows: just as the eye’s power of illumination, though present, is obstructed by the impurity of animality (paśutva), it is [restored] by the supreme Śiva-physician in the form of the Guru.

By the one of supreme compassion, through the application of the knowledge of its medicine, it is manifested once again by means of the removal of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva). As it is said in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Just as the medicine for diseases is, by its very nature, their opposite..."
In the same way, Śiva is remembered as the antidote to the defects of saṃsāra.
Just as one may eliminate a disorder through the efficacy of medicine,
so too is a disorder turned back by the medicine of self-knowledge.
Therefore, that wise man—tranquil, ascetic, and having conquered his senses—is liberated by contemplating the true nature [of reality] through connection with the knowledge of Śiva. || 5 ||

By this extensive treatise, having first proposed that the knowledge [of Śiva] is to be explained, having described its purpose, having stated its twofold nature, and having established that it takes the form of many distinct systems,
its necessity as something to be accepted by all has been demonstrated. Now, by means of this knowledge of Śiva...

In order to establish inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by making known the existence of the three categories to be established— namely, the Lord (*pati*), the individual soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*)— he first sets forth the fourfold nature of inference according to the *Matanga-sūtra*:
In some cases, the subject is established by means of its property; in some cases, the cause is established by means of the effect;
and in some cases, the effect is established by means of the cause, as seen in the traditional scriptures.

Here, by the first quarter [of the verse], inference is described as that which possesses the two acquired designations of "the universal" (*sāmānya*) and "that which consists of neither" (*anubhayātmaka*). By means of the property (*dharma*), such as the form of odor and so forth—
which is the object to be supported— the property-possessor (*dharmin*), such as earth and so forth, which is the supporting object, [is established].

It is established and known. Because it is rooted in a connection consisting solely of the intrinsic natures of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), apart from the nature of cause and effect, this is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) that is neither of those two. Likewise, in the *Yogapāda*:
The "remainder" (*śeṣavat*) and the "prior" (*pūrvavat*) are other types of inference; the "common" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is also recorded as another.
According to Amarasimha, *udarka* means a future result.
By this inference, in certain contexts concerning the category of substance (*dravya*), [one infers] by means of the property consisting of power (*śakti*).

The possessor of the attribute (*dharmin*) is established by means of the attribute (*dharma*). For example, in the section concerning the category of the "bound soul" (*paśu*), the *dharmin* characterized as the bound soul is established by means of the *dharma* characterized by knowledge and action.

Or, for example, musk and the like [are established] by means of their scent and so forth. Likewise, by the second quarter [of the verse], it is shown that the effect is a logical mark (*liṅga*) and that it possesses specific characteristics.
Inference has been described as having two types of established notions (*saṃjñā*). In some cases, a cause is inferred from its effect;

likewise, within the context of categories (*padārtha*), the causes beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and ending with *māyā* are established by means of their effects, such as the form of earth and the other elements. For example, an intoxicated elephant is inferred from the scent of rut and other signs. Similarly—
In the section on yoga:
"With its back covered by a heap of dung from its coarse movements and smelling of ichor,
the intoxicated elephant was here [known] by signs such as its post and its bed."
"For the past is to be established by means of inference for the wise through the *śeṣavat* [type].

By this third quarter [of the verse], inference—having received the two designations "that which has a cause as its mark" (*kāraṇaliṅga*) and "that which is like the former" (*pūrvavat*)—is stated. In some places, within the section concerning the objects of experience (*bhoga*).

By means of the performance of good and evil deeds—which possess the status of causes established by scripture—the effect, namely the objects of enjoyment in the hereafter consisting of either pleasure or pain, is inferred. Furthermore, by means of the performance of the means to be attained (*upeya*), the fruit characterized as spiritual perfection (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*) is inferred. For example:
An effect such as rain is inferred from specific causes such as clouds; as it is said in this very *Yogapāda*:
"By means of dense, high-reaching clouds, resembling black collyrium and accompanied by lightning..."
Unimpeded, vast, and gentle, they were filled with the roar of thunder and lightning.

"When rain is observed during the onset of the rainy season, the occurrence of rain is inferred; likewise, the existence of rain is always [inferred] by means of inference based on what has occurred previously. By the fourth quarter [of the verse], inference based on scripture (*āgama*) is stated. "In some cases" refers to where even all three types [of evidence]...

In that regard, there is the removal of the obstruction concerning the essential nature of the relationship between cause and effect; this is established through inference based on scripture, as seen in the sacred tradition (āmnāya). For example, it is inferred that the mantra-deities, Mantreśvaras, and others possess bodies consisting of *bindu* and so forth.

But surely, a property such as whiteness, residing in multiple locations, deviates from a restricted locus; how then can a qualified subject be established on its basis? Likewise, an effect such as smoke is seen to arise from fire, from the top of a wheel, and so forth; and a cause such as wealth is also seen to be an effect.
Since rain and so forth sometimes occur and sometimes do not, they are inconclusive; how, then, can cause and effect be established by means of them?
To this it is replied: it is not intended that this mere property (*dharma*) alone constitutes the reason (*hetu*); rather—

Because it is ascertained that a certain qualified property of a qualified subject possesses such an intrinsic nature (*tathāsvabhāvatva*), its deviation is impossible. That which deviates, such as paleness (*pāṇḍutva*) and the like, does not possess the status of a logical reason (*hetu*). And through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) of that...
Because there is no deviation when one grasps the specific property residing in a determinate subject (*niyatadharmigata*), it is indeed a valid logical reason (*hetu*). As it has been said:
"That which has not been properly distinguished does not deviate from the subject.
Likewise, a cause such as a cloud and so forth—provided it possesses a nature that necessarily produces its effect—is [a valid reason]. It is not otherwise.
Even Brahmā would be unable to obstruct it; however, that which is non-productive by nature cannot be made productive even by Indra.
Thus, it has not been properly discerned that a cause deviates from its effect, as it was said:
"What is not to be will not be; what is to be will not be otherwise.
Why is this medicine, which destroys the poison of anxiety, not drunk?
Thus, there are six sūtras as an introduction to the definition of the categories (padārthas) such as "husband" and so forth, which are to be discussed hereafter.
These have been taken up. For example:
"They declare that the *upodghāta* (introduction) is for the purpose of establishing the nature of the subject matter (*prakṛti*). (6)
Thus ends the introductory section (*upodghāta-prakaraṇa*).

Having thus presented four types of inference as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of the categories (*padārtha*), [the author] first seeks to establish the category of the Lord (*pati*) by means of an inference possessing specific characteristics (*viśeṣavattva*), following the *Viśvasāra*.
He grasps [the world]—as the Lord who impels the insentient [principles] such as Māyā;
he is established as the knower of all objects, the agent, the pervasive, and the eternally manifest. (7)

He is the knower of all objects, the omniscient one; the agent, the creator of all; the pervasive one, the all-pervading; eternally risen, perpetually liberated, the Lord of the insentient and inert—of Māyā and the rest, headed by Māyā and Mahāmāyā, as the originator of the world's activity, He is established and fully known. This is what is intended:

The activity of insentient things such as *māyā* is preceded by the superintendence of a sentient being, because it is the activity of an insentient thing, like the activity of a chariot and so forth; thus, through the inference based on the mark of the effect in the form of activity, the Lord (*pati*) is established as its cause. Likewise, the earth and other elements have an agent, because they are effects.

The proof of the existence of the Omniscient Lord (*sarvajñapati*)— characterized by being distinct from the bound soul (*paśu*), whose powers of cognition and action have been obstructed— should be inferred through such inferences as "like a jar," as stated in the *Vāyavīya*:
"There exists a certain substratum of qualities that are infinitely beautiful."
"The Lord is the creator of the universe, distinct from both the bound soul (paśu) and its fetters (pāśa). Thus it is said in the Pauṣkara:
"O Brahmins, the world is insentient; without the impulsion of a sentient being,"
Whether in engagement or in withdrawal, it is not independent, like a chariot and so forth.
"He who is the efficient cause here and is capable [of it] is declared to be the Lord" (1.5).

"The universe, which is the subject of dispute, is preceded by an omniscient creator, because it is an effect, just as jars and other such things are established for both of us to be effects" (1.6). Thus [it is said].
Mataṅga said:
"Since the activity of this entire world is indeed observed to be dependent [on another], therefore Maheśvara is the agent."

The Lord is Śivabhaṭṭāraka. How is this determined? By the word "Lord" (pati), derived from the root *pāti* ("he protects"), only the cause is understood; he is indeed qualified [by specific attributes]. || 7 ||

According to the principle that "the establishment of a thing occurs through its characteristic (lakṣaṇa) and its measure (pramāṇa)," he states the definition (*lakṣaṇa*)— in the form of the unique attributes (*asādhāraṇadharma*)— of the Lord established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in the *Parākhyasūtra*:
"That whose sovereignty consists of vision and action, preceded by the act of giving..."
He should be understood here as the Lord, the Sovereign endowed with two powers.

He whose sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which consists of the nature of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyāsvarūpa*) and is characterized by vision and activity (*dṛkkriyātmaka*), is not preceded by a giver—that is, it was not previously given by anyone; the meaning is that it is innate (*svābhāvika*). He is endowed with the two powers (*śaktidvayayuta*), namely knowledge and action.

He is endowed with power (*śakti*). The purpose of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) is the cognition of the world as its object, while the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is the cause of the world. As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
"By the power of knowledge he cognizes; by action he creates the world."
Thus: the Lord (prabhu) is to be understood and known here in this scripture as independent (svatantra) and as the Sovereign (īśvara), though not [limited by] a higher lord.
Here, it has been stated that the defining characteristic of the Lord (pati) is the possession of powers characterized by vision and action that are inherently pure.

[The definition] occurs as follows: if it were stated merely that "it is the possession of power" (*śaktimattva*), there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to impurity (*mala*). To exclude that, it says "characterized by vision and action" (*dṛkkriyālakṣaṇa*). Even with this much stated, there would be an over-extension to the bound self (*baddhātman*); to exclude that, it says "pure" (*nirmala*). Even with that much stated, there would be an over-extension to one liberated through grace (*prasādamukta*); to exclude that, it says "natural" (*svabhāva*). [This refers to] their purity of power (*śaktinairmalya*).
Because it depends upon the grace of Śiva, it lacks inherent existence. As it is stated in the *Parākhyatantra*:
"The nature of the Self is of the form of consciousness, characterized by the qualities of knowledge and action;
even for that which abides in the form of cognition, its essential nature consists of knowledge and action."
And it will be said:
"The power of the agent in the soul is eternal and all-pervasive, like the power of the Lord;
yet, being obscured by darkness, it does not shine upon objects unless it is accompanied by grace."
In the Pauṣkara it is said:
"Knowledge and action are declared to be Śiva, pure, supreme, and present in all objects. Thus [ends the verse]. || 8 ||

Now, it may be objected: "The Lord has been established as both omniscient and the creator of all through his defining characteristics and means of knowledge; yet, in that context, agency is untenable without a physical form. Anticipating this doubt, the following two and a half verses from the *Ataṅgasūtra* (3.1–3) are presented to demonstrate that even his physical form is nothing but his own power (*śakti*).
He grasps it— then the abode of the Lord, consisting of the rays of His own power,
[is grasped] in that heaven; [the Lord] whose self is brilliantly luminous, unwavering, and possessing an immovable form.

Now, the word "atha" (then/now) at the beginning of the chapter serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). The "abode" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign—who is subsumed under the category of the "Lord" (*pati*)—is that which is presided over (*adhiṣṭhīyate*) by Him through His pervasive presence in all effects; it is indeed a distinguished place.
The word "is declared" (*procyate*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. And that [nature] of His is not distinct from Him, as is the case with the Vidyās, Vidyeśvaras, and so forth;

rather, it consists of the rays of His own power (*svaśakti*). His essential nature (*svarūpa*) is composed of those rays, which are His very powers consisting of knowledge and action. Just like the light of the sun, these powers are indeed of the same nature [as Him], because they possess the capacity for functions such as burning and illuminating.

In that context, they are metaphorically designated as the objects to be presided over. Those who, even there, imagine a world consisting of *vidyā* or the *bindu*—based on the delusion produced by other scriptural passages such as "Śiva, whose form is the *bindu*, is to be meditated upon"—are refuted by this [text]. And just as in this heaven the sun possesses the nature of both burning and illuminating...

Thus, in that supreme heaven—the abode of play consisting of the rays of power—he is the Lord whose self (ātman), that is, whose very nature (svabhāva), is "well-illuminated" (suddipta) by the splendors of knowledge and sovereignty over all objects; the meaning is that he is of that very nature. However, it is not [as the Naiyāyikas and others claim] due to the conjunction with a mind (manaḥ-saṃyoga).

Is his consciousness (saṃjñāna) an illumination resulting from the union with the intellect, like that of Siddheśvara, or like that of a perfected being (siddha) according to the Pātañjala system? Furthermore, he is "unwavering" (niṣkampa), meaning that from him all wavering—namely, transformation (pariṇāma)—has departed;
or [he is unwavering] through the distinction between the Bindu and Sadāśiva, or through the distinction between the Mantra and Mantreśvara.

The meaning is that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), undergoing transformation through the differentiation from illusion (*māyā*) down to earth (*pṛthivī*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being insentient, like clay and other such materials.

Consequently, for those who are permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the *Kaula* and other scriptures, when either the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) or the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is accepted—
The non-dualistic doctrine (*advaitavāda*) of the Lord is superimposed [upon this], by which they are to be refuted; however, by others such as the Pāñcarātras and so forth, it is stated:
"For the presiding deity must be bodiless; the Self could not be like the liberated soul."
Out of fear of this defect, the Lord has been accepted as being indeed endowed with a body. To exclude that [view], he says:
"possessing an immovable form.
This opinion is not found at all in the established treatises such as the *Pracalita-nyāya* and others; in all of them, [it is otherwise].
This is because the Lord is admitted to possess eternal knowledge.
He whose form is immovable is "the one of immovable form" (*acalamūrtimān*). For the form of souls is twofold: movable and immovable.
Among these, the movable consists of the bodies of the *tattvas* and the *bhuvanas*, while the immovable has the nature of knowledge and action.

And this Lord possesses an immovable form; the meaning is that he is not endowed with a body made of the elements (bhauvana). That very same [reality] is the supreme limit (kāṣṭhā), subtle, omnipresent, consisting of nectar, with all veils destroyed, peaceful, the mere reality (vastumātra), and intensely longing for [that state]. (10)
The virtuous one, who is devoid of beginning and end, is figuratively designated as "form" (mūrtti).

The meaning of this is as follows: that very power (śakti), characterized by an immovable form, is the supreme (parā), the most excellent (prakṛṣṭā), the ultimate limit (kāṣṭhā), the final goal (niṣṭhā); that is to say, she is the highest of all.

By this it is shown that the presiding deity, possessing an immovable form, excels those such as ourselves who possess moving forms. Thus, those who claim that liberation is superior to the Supreme Lord are refuted;
for there is no excellence for Him other than the attainment of omniscience and omnipotence.

Regarding the phrase "the state of being more excellent" and so forth: because there would be a persistence of distinctions in liberation based on states established by notions such as "more" or "most," there would indeed be an infinite regress regarding liberation; however, this does not imply any superiority over the Supreme Lord.
For a distinction that is merely a conceptual designation never departs from its status as such, even in the subtlest sense.

It is subtler than even the atom and so forth; it pervades all directions and extends in every direction. This means that it encompasses all the effects of reality (tattva) which will be described hereafter. By the word "subtle" (*sūkṣma*), those who maintain the doctrine of an *Īśvara* who is a transformation (*vikāra*) of the form of Hiraṇyagarbha—possessing a gross physical body—are refuted. By the phrase "pervading all directions" (*sarvadikka*), [the same is further clarified].

The Pāñcarātra doctrine—which posits that the Lord is Pradyumna and others, who are produced from a material nature (*prakṛti*) that is not all-pervading—is also refuted. [The term] *amṛtātmikā* means that whose essence (*ātman*), or inherent nature (*svabhāva*), is immortal (*amṛta*), being free from death; by this—

The doctrine of a Supreme Person (Puruṣeśvara) established by the Mīmāṃsakas is also refuted; for that person’s form is of the nature of mortality. The point is that although he may possess the capacity merely to acquire merit and so forth, since no capacity is observed for the creation of bodies, rays, and worlds, he is indeed not the Lord (Īśvara).

*Pradhvastāvaraṇā*: that whose covering (*āvaraṇa*) has been destroyed; "destroyed" means the covering, which consists of all fetters (*bandhana*), has ceased to exist. By this, those who assert the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) for even Sadāśiva—on the grounds of demonstrating his connection with fetters in the form of grace (*anugraha*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*)—are refuted. [This concerns] Sadāśiva.

Because the status of being the creator of the world is untenable if there were a connection with bonds (*pāśa*). Nor can grace (*anugraha*) and concealment (*tirobhāva*) be considered bonds. This is because their bond-status is refuted by the following inference: "The two subjects under debate are not of the nature of bonds, because they consist of specific types of activity, like creation and so forth. For this very reason, he does not possess the state of a bound soul (*paśu*). [He is] *śāntā*.

"Free from attachment and aversion. By this, the claim that the Blessed One—despite being the Lord of all—possesses attachment and aversion like a king or similar authority, insofar as He bestows desired and undesired fruits based on whether He is propitiated or not, is refuted. This is because His propitiation is something enjoined [by scripture].

Because, like the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and others, it bestows a distinguished and desired fruit by virtue of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*), and because it lacks the common characteristics of kings and the like; for this very reason, she is "extremely longing" (*atilālasā*). *Lālasā* is an excess of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*); she in whom that exists excessively is *atilālasā*.

The meaning is that even in the absence of passion and aversion, [He] protects the entire world, like a father his sons and others, according to their respective capacities. *Vastumātrā*: she is the mere reality characterized as the Protector (*pati*); however, distinctions such as her dissolution (*laya*) or enjoyment (*bhoga*) are not intended here. Now, is she not related to the Vidyeśvaras, the liberated souls (*mukta*), and the Śivas?

To the objection that one should accept [the Lord] as eternally existing through a continuous stream (pravāha), as the proponents of an eternally streaming Lord do, he says: "lacking beginning and end.

This means it is devoid of both a first and a last. However, the form of the Vidyeśvaras is possessed of both a beginning and an end; the form of the liberated Śivas (muktaśiva) is possessed of a beginning. Thus, in both cases, the quality of being devoid of beginning and end is unestablished.

Nor is the position of an eternally streaming Lord possible; for since the state of being a Lord consists in the attainment of the manifestation of one's own essential nature, its destruction is impossible. Indeed, only if such destruction were possible could there be a position of an eternally streaming Lord.

If it is argued that even for the liberated Śivas (mukta-śivas), because they are equal to the Lord (pati) and thus there is a multiplicity of lords, all purposes cannot be accomplished due to their having unequal intellects— [we reply: no, because since they act with vision that accords with reality due to their omniscience, their having unequal intellects is not established.
Because faults are observed only in those humans who are possessed of attachment, aversion, unequal knowledge, and so forth;

if this were the case, then since there would be no purpose in attaining what has already been attained, the activity of creating or manifesting this form would not be logical. For it is said: "Not even a fool acts without aiming at a purpose."
To address the objection based on this logic, he says: "The virtuous woman. She is virtuous, meaning she is endowed with compassion;
for those possessed of compassion are seen to act for the sake of others even in the absence of their own personal interest. Thus, there is no fault here regarding the lack of a motive.
Now, one might ask: since the Lord has been described as having the nature of a brilliantly radiant Self, how can she be His form?
Since it is said everywhere that the form (mūrti) is indeed distinct [from the Lord], he says: "it is figuratively designated as a form.

It is figuratively designated as a form, that is, as a body; however, in the primary sense, that form is not distinct from the Lord—this is the meaning. And it has been stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Knowledge and action are declared to be auspicious, pure, and supreme with respect to all objects.

By the emphasis on the restriction "that very [consciousness] alone," it is excluded here that the form (mūrti) belongs to the mantras, the lords of mantras (mantreśvaras), or liberated souls who, even though joined to the state of Bindu and Sadāśiva through initiation, are merely designated by that term figuratively. And therefore—
It is stated that their primary form consists of pure *māyā* as its material cause (*upādāna*). As it is said in the *Ratnatraya*:
"Because they are produced from *bindu* as their material cause, they are called 'born of *bindu*' (*baindava*)."
The Vidyās and the Lords of the Vidyās are the non-dual deities known as Nāda.
"By virtue of their authority over [the worlds of] latency and enjoyment, they possess bodies, objects of enjoyment, and sense organs.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇatantra*: "His body is said to consist of pure *yoni* (wombs/sources), born of stainless merit (*akalmaṣa*).
In this regard, if Vidyās, Vidyeśvaras, and others were possessed of actual physical bodies, it would follow that they are not omniscient.
The refutation of such collections of fallacious inferences, by means of [pointing out their] inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) and other defects, must be established.
The method for that refutation, however, has been set forth in detail in the *Mataṅgavṛtti* composed by Rāmakaṇṭha.
This portion is not seen in the *Mudrita-ratnatraya*;
it should be consulted there. However, it is not written here for fear of increasing the bulk of the text.
For this very reason, even the conceptualization of forms such as Sadāśiva and others is intended solely for the purpose of meditation. As stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
However, this form is traditionally taught for the sake of the practitioner's goal. As it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:
"Having assumed these forms for the purpose of bestowing grace upon both the conscious and the unconscious, that Lord..."
"He bestows grace upon those whose powers are obstructed by the impurities of beginningless [karma]. (2.14). Thus [ends the verse]. 10.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the power (*śakti*) characterized by knowledge and action is the Lord's figurative body because it is non-different from him; nevertheless, how can there be causality in the performance of tasks through a primary body other than [that figurative one]? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies: even such a body of his is indeed the very body of the presiding officer for each respective task, and not [something else].
Regarding the ultimate reality, he cites the *Mṛgendra-sūtra*:
"Because no body exists [inherently], whatever action he performs, in each instance a body is assumed by him that conforms to his role as the agent. (11)
Since that Lord lacks— that is, is impossible without— a body consisting of hands, feet, and other limbs, whatever task such as creation he performs, in that very task,
a body for this Lord is fashioned or conceived as being "conformable" (anu), that is, similar to the body of the agent required for each specific task.

The meaning is that the body of the qualified authority (*adhikāri-śarīra*) itself is the primary body for those respective functions. Alternatively, it means it is "constructed" by means of the bodies of those performers—the fivefold bodies suitable for the five functions—which consist of the five Brahmans and the Śākta body. As it has been said:
In the venerable *Mṛgendra* itself it is said:

"That body [of Śiva] consists of five mantras suitable for the five acts; [the parts] beginning with the head are formed by the mantras Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta" (*Viṣṇusaṃhitā* 3.8).

In reality, however, the Lord’s possession of a physical form through his ultimate nature is established solely by the greatness of his own power. Nevertheless, since the accomplishment of an effect is never observed in one who is bodiless, whatever effect he brings about,
in each instance his body as its agent possesses a gracious form in cases such as bestowing grace.

The meaning is that seekers should contemplate [the deity] as wrathful during anger and so forth, and as having a nourished form during nourishment and so forth. As it is stated in the *Sarvasrotasaṃgrahasāra*:
"In whatever form the practitioner should always remember [the deity]," and so on.
"Lord becomes identical with that [object], like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).

Regarding the reading "the body does not perform the body," the meaning is as follows: whatever action that Lord performs, in that particular instance, that action is carried out by the body of the Lord as the agent; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

"In due order, those [five mantras] beginning with Īśāna, which necessarily have utility in the fivefold functions characterized by favoring, withdrawing, bestowing, protecting, and generating—that body [of the Lord], beginning with the head, is said to belong to the God. The word "is said" (*ucyate*) is to be supplied from the context. This is for the sake of favoring devotees.
Because the apprehension of those respective forms is taught in the Āgamas; and so it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"This form is remembered as the goal for the sake of the practitioner" (Rāmakaṇṭha-vṛtti).
One who acts is an agent (*kartṛ*); that form is the body, the physical form whose nature is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), by which everything [is accomplished].

The meaning is that the action (*kṛtya*) is accomplished. The sense is that there is no other "body" (*vapuh*) produced or brought into existence apart from the power of action belonging to the form of the agent; the reason for this is stated as "because of the non-existence of a body. Due to the absence of the three causes, [there is nothing] distinct from the power.
The meaning is that a body for the purpose of action is impossible for Śiva, just as it is for ourselves and others.

This is the intended sense: if one were to admit a body for the Lord (pati), since a material body is incompatible with his purity, a body composed of the *bindu* must be asserted. The material cause (*upādāna*) of that [body] is the *bindu*.
It must be stated that this is not possible here; for instance, in all cases, only the agitated *bindu* possesses the nature of being the material cause (*upādāna*).

Is its agitation (*kṣobha*) due to itself, or due to Śiva? Not the first, because it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). In the second case, does Śiva possess a body (*vapus*) for the sake of performing that act of agitation, or is it for the sake of agitating the *bindu* which serves as the means of realization (*sādhaka*) for that body?

Furthermore, if one were to postulate another body, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the agitation of the *bindu* occurs there by the mere presence of his immobile form alone, then what is the purpose of postulating another body for him in his activities such as creation? In this very way, the necessity of auxiliary factors dependent on a body—namely, the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and their instrumental causes—is refuted. Therefore, [this applies] to Śiva.

Just as the Self possesses agency over the movement of its own body even in the absence of a created body due to the absence of the three causes, so too is its agency over actions such as creation logically established. As it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Just as there is agency for one without a body in the impelling of its own body" (1.34). || 11 ||

Now, one might object: "The activities of the Lord, consisting of the creation, maintenance, and so forth of the world, cannot be without instruments, because they are actions, just like the action of cutting; therefore, He too must possess an instrument. Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates that instrument by means of the *Mṛgendra-sūtra*:

And the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not something other than power (*śakti*); power is not insentient, for it is consciousness (*cit*). Because there is no restriction regarding its objects, that [consciousness] is one and the same in both cognition and action. (Vi. 3.4) (12) No entity other than Śiva’s power, nor anything else distinct from power, can be an instrument. In this regard...

The positive injunction is stated by way of negation: the meaning is that power alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*), because it is precisely through that [power] that various actions are accomplished. "Of consciousness" (*citaḥ*) means of that which has the nature of consciousness; the genitive case is used in the sense of a relationship.
That power related to consciousness does not have an insentient nature, for it is of the very essence of consciousness.

The meaning is that it is impossible for power (*śakti*) to be of the nature of the insentient (*acit*). Since objects of knowledge and things to be accomplished are infinite, this [power] must therefore possess infinite instruments (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, the knowledge and activity of the Supreme Lord have unlimited objects. As it has been stated in that very same work:
"That single [consciousness], due to the infinity of objects, undergoes an infinity of divisions;
because it is non-different from that [consciousness], agency likewise [appears] through metaphorical designation. (5.17).
Therefore, because the object and the action to be performed are not fixed...

Because the cause is undivided (*anavacchinna*), that single instrument (*karaṇa*) consisting of power is likewise unrestricted, undivided, and indeed infinite, both in respect to cognition— namely the object of knowledge— and in respect to action— namely the object to be accomplished. Thus it is said in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:

The power (śakti) is the body of the Lord and the instrument for objects to be known and for effects to be accomplished; endowed with its various manifestations, it undergoes differentiation according to its qualities through action and knowledge.
That [power] is eternally established by the agents of all other things upon the pure and impure paths.
"She alone, following her husband and consisting of the power (śakti) of Vāmā and the others, performs the task. Thus [ends verse 12].
Now, since the Lord (Īśvara) has been described as having the form of the powers of knowledge and action, a doubt arises as to how He can be the cause.

In response to this, he cites the *Kiraṇasūtra* to demonstrate that it is the power of will (*icchāśakti*) alone that functions as the instrument, and that His status as an agent (*kartṛtva*) is not contradictory even though He is formless (*amūrttitva*).
Just as time, though formless, is seen to be the accomplisher of results,
so too Śiva, though formless, performs his work by his own will.
(2) Just as in the world time— consisting of moments, muhūrtas, and so forth, and taking the form of the six seasons— is the cause of results and effects.

Its accomplisher—time, though formless and bodiless—is seen and proclaimed as the achiever and agent of the moment-by-moment ripening of substances, such as flowers and fruits appropriate to their respective seasons, as well as of stages such as childhood and youth. In this same way, Śiva, though formless, indeed brings about the effect, the world consisting of earth and so forth. By this...
The absence of agency in Śiva, despite his lack of a physical body, has been resolved. He states the nature of his instrument:

"by will" (*icchayā*). The meaning is that he acts through the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). Thus, the intention is that, like a yogin, will alone is the instrument for all actions of Śiva. This has been stated in this very same work:
"Desire alone is its instrument, as is held by the Yogins.
Nor should it be argued that the status of being an agent is unestablished in the absence of instruments such as the senses;
for that is possible, just as even a magnet devoid of organs acts as an agent in attracting iron. As it is said:
In the venerable *Kiraṇa*:
"Indeed, even one who is devoid of senses is seen to be a puller [of the soul], like a ploughman who extracts the thorn.
And in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"The Blessed One, whose nature is beginningless, is the one who descends [into this world] by his own will. || 13 ||

Thus, by means of the *Mṛgendra-sūtra*, the threefold nature of the agent—the category of the Lord (*pati*)—who creates a body consisting of his own power and who is devoid of the creation of a physical body, is stated:
"The agent is held to be threefold: the capable, the striving, and the active."
The distinction of that [agent] is due to the difference in the activity of his power; this is a figurative designation.

(14) (6) Here, the agent is the Lord (*pati*), who is "capable, prepared, and active"—that is, capable (*śakta*), prepared (*udyukta*), and active (*pravṛtta*). This is a collective singular form of a *dvandva* compound.

The absence of the neuter gender is a Vedic (archaic) usage; or it may be a *tatpuruṣa* compound in apposition. That which is "capable" (*śakta*), "exerted" (*udyukta*), and "engaged" (*pravṛtta*) is held to be threefold, of three kinds. The distinction of that Lord (*pati*) is the distinction of the capable and so forth—that is, the distinction of the capacity (*śakti*), namely the conscious power (*cicchakti*), according to its different modes of engagement (*pravṛtti*), that is, according to its different functions (*vyāpāra*).

The meaning is: by means of activities consisting of indifference (*audāsinya*), exertion (*udyoga*), and engagement (*pravṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "figuratively" (*upacārataḥ*), the word "is" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied. Thus, the sense is this: here, that capacity which is fitness toward the effect is the state of being partless (*niṣkalāvasthā*); one who possesses that is called "quiescent" (*śānta*). That which is the state of being engaged (*udyuktatva*) is the state of being both with and without parts (*sakalaniṣkalāvasthā*).
Sadāśiva is so called because his activity is in motion, whereas he is called Īśvara because of his grossness.

This distinction of states pertains to the sphere of action; therefore, these three principles are said to be distinct only figuratively, not from the perspective of ultimate reality. Thus it is stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
He is declared to be the partless (niṣkala), the gross (sthūla), and likewise the part-and-whole (sakalaniṣkala);
