he abides here by the names Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta.
"Because he performs [the functions of] will and grace, he possesses the authority over dissolution and enjoyment;
thus he is described as threefold according to the distinction of his activities and according to the difference of his names.
Thus it is said in the *Mataṅga*.
The supreme reality beyond peace is imperishable and immutable, whose nature is Śiva;
by the power of [His] unfolding their true being, bound souls have attained the state of Śiva.
The dissolution of the body of Sadāśiva occurs within the principle (tattva) that is utterly partless (ati-niṣkala);
that which consists of the four forms and is pure is the "both-with-parts-and-partless" (sakala-niṣkala).
In Him, the enjoyment of the Lord of the universe is declared to exist eternally.
(3.32.1) Now, concerning the Supreme Abode of the Lord who sports as the qualified sovereign, it must be stated that even though He is independent, this is His primordial nature. (4.1)
"Likewise, though Śiva is of a single form, he appears in many forms, like an actor. Thus it is said.
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra] it is said: "In Śiva, there is no real distinction between dissolution (laya), enjoyment (bhoga), and authority (adhikāra);
however, those [distinctions] are considered to be real only in the case of the Bindu and individual souls (aṇus)."

In that context, the state consisting of the withdrawal of effects, the exertion toward effects, and the fulfillment of effects is characterized by dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*). The *bindu* is also threefold; namely, according to the distinctions of the real *bindu*, based on the substrata of the principles (*tattva*) of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority. This applies even to Śiva, by virtue of his dissolution, enjoyment, and authority.

There is a threefold nature. There is a threefold nature by way of the forms beginning with the partless (niṣkala); and there is a threefold nature by way of the names Parameśvara, Śiva, and Sadāśiva.
All of this is figurative. By the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "capable, striving, and engaged," [the other states] are included.

Now, if Sadāśiva is manifested from Śiva by Nāda and established by Sadāśiva according to the rules of words and so forth, then there would be a difference between these two principles; and if there were such a difference,
it would contradict the scriptures.
For that supreme reality is indeed one alone—pure and immutable;
Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śānta are established as its synonyms.

Thus it is said. This is true—that reality is indeed one; however, due to the difference in its functions (*kṛtyabheda*), it receives designations of diversity, just like a gem. For example, a gem-substance assumes various appearances depending on the objects placed near it. In the same way, the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*) assumes various designations because it bestows dissolution (*laya*), authority (*adhikāra*), and enjoyment (*bhoga*). Thus [it is called] *sakala*.

And there is a distinction [of Śiva] based on the difference between the "with parts" (*sakala*) and the "without parts" (*niṣkala*), just as in the case of the Self (*ātman*). Just as the Self is said to be "with parts" due to its connection with a body, "without parts" in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), and "supreme" (*para*) in the state of liberation (*kaivalya*), so too Śiva is metaphorically described as being distinct through the differentiation of the "with parts" and "without parts. || 14 ||

Some say that for the Lord, who is of such a nature as the agent (*kartṛ*), there exists both the status of being the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) and the material cause (*upādānatva*) with respect to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because they accept His non-difference as both efficient and material cause. To refute them,
[the author] establishes the existence of three distinct causes for every effect by means of the *Parākhyasūtra*:
He demonstrates this:
That which is observed as the instrumental cause called Īśvara, and that which is the subtle material cause inherent in all effects—[these two constitute his nature]. (15)

That which is called "Īśvara" is so named because its sovereignty consists of the powers of knowledge and action; that which is the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa), that which is the observed auxiliary cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa) such as the staff and the wheel, and that which is the subtle material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) such as clay.

That triad is also "combined" (*saṃhita*) and interconnected in all effects. Thus, by the subsequent statement that "the three causes are combined in all effects," and by demonstrating the pervasion of the three causes throughout each individual effect, it is shown that even the world (*prapañca*), as an effect, is likewise [pervaded] individually.

Because these three causes are necessary, the theory of a non-different efficient and material cause (*abhinnanimittopādānatva*) is refuted. If it is argued that the spider is seen to possess both the status of an efficient cause and a material cause with respect to its web, we say no; for even in that case, it is only the saliva located in its mouth that serves as the material cause there. Furthermore:

If God were the material cause (*upādāna*), it would follow that He is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and is of a non-conscious nature (*acid-rūpa*). Furthermore, it would entail that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), as His effect, would also possess the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpatva*). For this very reason, the power inherent in Him (*samavāyi-śakti*) cannot be the material cause either. If one were to accept that the world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Consciousness, it would result in the unreality (*asatyatā*) of the world.

Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it is impossible to deny the world that is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it is said in the Pauṣkara:
"There is no material cause (*upādāna*) possessing power, because its nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), just like Śiva."
It is taught that transformation is accumulated; it is not possible for a conscious entity.

"Consciousness alone is said to be the manifestation (*vivarta*); if that were the case, there would be an absence of effects. How can the world be a manifestation of consciousness, given that it is established by all means of valid cognition? (2.4–5).
And here, God (*īśvara*) is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), while the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
The *bindu* is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). As it is said in this very [text] (Pauṣkara 8.17):
"The Lord is their efficient cause (*nimitta*), while that sovereign *bindu* is the material cause. Elsewhere:
Just as radiance is inherent in the sun, moonlight in the moon, and heat in fire, so too is Śakti inherently united with Śiva; she is both the primary cause and the auxiliary cause.
One's own power (*svaśakti*) is the Lord (*īśvara*), which is *māyā*, like the clay, the wheel, and the potter.

In that regard, on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), Śiva is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and *bindu* is the material cause (*upādāna*). On the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), however, it should be understood that Ananteśa is the efficient cause and *māyā* is the material cause.
And so it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:

"In the pure path, Śiva is declared to be the agent; in the impure [path], the Lord Ananta [is the agent]. Regarding the phrase "in the pure path," this refers to the pure and impure [states] of Bindu and Māyā. In the pure-impure...
It has been stated that the causality consisting in the transposition of effects is appropriate. In the *Śrīpauṣkara* (2.6):
"Even Māyā is not the material cause here, because it deludes by its own power.
The meaning here is "in the pure path" (*śuddhe 'dhvani*). Nor [is it the case that] only Māyā, Time, Karma, and so forth [are the causes].

It must be stated that the world has [the Lord] as its cause, and not [any other]; for since it is impossible for those insentient things to produce effects without being impelled by a sentient being,
and since a sentient impeller must necessarily exist, and since beings such as ourselves lack the capacity to impel them due to our obstructed vision and action,
[it follows that the world has] only the omniscient and omnipotent Lord as its cause.
Because it is appropriate that He alone is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) with respect to the entire phenomenal world due to His existence therein;
in the reading "the efficient cause, called God, whose auxiliary cause is *adṛṣṭa*," the status of action— denoted by the word *adṛṣṭa*— as an auxiliary cause is stated.
As it is said here in this very *Āraṇeya-paṭala* (*Pauṣkara*, 8.18):
"The Lord is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) for them, while that Bindu is the material cause (*upādāna*).
Human action (*nṛ-karma*) serves as the auxiliary cause; thus, this effect has three causes."

Therefore, it must be accepted by all that the three causes—namely the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the others—of the effect that is phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) consist of the triad beginning with Īśvara. 15.
Now, regarding one who maintains the eternality of the phenomenal world according to the maxim: "The world was never otherwise than it is now."
To refute the view that the world is not an effect, he establishes its status as an effect by means of another aphorism from the *Parākhya*:
"Those objects which are corporeal, possess parts, and have various forms and coverings,
because they consist of gross components, must be preceded by an intelligent cause."
Therefore, there exists some intelligent Lord who is eternally established.

"Embodied" means possessing form. "With parts" means accompanied by constituent members. "Having various forms as their coverings" means those whose covering or enclosure consists of various—that is, manifold—forms and specific configurations; such are the objects.

Earth and the other elements are here taken as the subject (*pakṣa*). Attributes such as "having form" (*mūrttatva*) and so forth are employed as qualifiers of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) for the purpose of indicating, respectively, that each serves as a reason (*hetu*) for proving their being effects; they are not, however, intended to exclude sublation (*bādhā*) and other such fallacies. He states the proposition (*pratijñā*): "They are preceded by an intelligent cause. That which possesses intelligence is the "intelligent one" (*buddhimān*).
"Intelligent" (*buddhimān*): that which is both intelligent and a cause is an "intelligent cause" (*buddhimaddhetu*).

Those things for which this [cause] is the prior limit are "of such a kind. The meaning is: they have as their agent one who possesses direct knowledge of the material causes and so forth. This is stated merely to establish that these things are preceded by a cause.
Even though the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) has already been established, the term "intelligent" (*buddhimat*) is employed with the intention of establishing a specific kind of agent.
He states the reason for this: "because it is composed of gross constituent parts" (*sthūlāvayavaśiṣṭatvāt*).
This means because it is connected to, or composed of, gross parts that are perceivable by the external sense organs of beings such as ourselves. In this regard—

Furthermore, the word "gross" (*sthūla*) is employed solely to indicate the avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddhi*)—namely, that the parts are not perceived and thus the property of being composed of parts is not established—and not for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Here, the example "like a jar, etc. (*ghaṭādivat*) is to be supplied. He states the conclusion (*nigamana*): "Therefore..."

Precisely because they possess parts, there exists some intelligent Lord (*īśvara*) who is established as the agent of the earth and so forth—this is the ellipsis to be supplied—who is situated and proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, in the *Vāyavīya*:
"Whatever is insentient, such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so on..."
That [world] is not seen to have been produced by itself, without an intelligent cause.
The universe is dependent upon a creator because it is an effect and possesses constituent parts;
therefore, the agency over this effect belongs to the Lord (pati), and not to the bound soul (paśu) or the fetters (pāśa).
By this proof of having an agent (*sakartṛkatva*), the fact that the earth and other elements are effects (*kāryatva*) is established;

therefore, although the proof of their being effects is easily obtained, it is established by way of proving they have an agent for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of non-theism (*nirīśvaravāda*), as it is inseparable from the establishment of God (*īśvara*).

And this is an inference based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireki-anumāna*), because it possesses five formal characteristics. As it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara* (7.40):
"The property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) must exist in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and be excluded from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)."
Lack of awakening, which has no counter-position, consists of both negative and positive concomitance. || 16 ||
Now, by means of the *Mṛgendra-sūtra*, [the author] states the limitation of the Lord's activity in terms of its extent, as well as its possession of means and purpose:
"The creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and liberation of the world..."
Indeed, this alone is to be known as its function (*kṛtya*), along with its instruments and results (2.3).
"Birth, persistence, destruction, concealment, and liberation"—this is a *dvandva* compound. "The birth of the world," and so forth, is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound.

These are the five [acts], beginning with the creation of the world. This fivefold activity belongs to this very Supreme Lord alone. It should be known—that is, understood—as being accompanied by the instruments (kārakas), such as the powers (śaktis) and so forth, and by the fruit, which consists of enjoyment and liberation.

Here, by the word "world" (*jagat*), the cycle of living beings subject to birth is meant. Their birth is one of the five cosmic functions (*kṛtya*) of Śiva. The direct creation by Śiva pertains to the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*); it consists of the production of the pure principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth, preceded by the generation of those [beings] who dwell in those worlds from the material cause (*upādāna*) consisting of the *bindu*.

The production of sound occurs through the sequence beginning with *nāda* by means of the conjunction of the bodies of the *Vidyās* and *Vidyeśvaras* with the *bindu*. Regarding the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), creation proceeds through the gateway of Ananta and others;
first, there is the production of the impure principles (*tattvas*) and worlds (*bhuvanas*) from the material cause called *māyā*, which serves as the basis for experience.
Furthermore, the term "birth" (*janman*) refers to the repeated manifestation of [the soul] together with its adjuncts (*parikara*) within various specific wombs. It is stated in that very same work:
"In that regard, first, He creates an eightfold group of suitable, isolated atoms (*kevalāṇu*)."
Endowed with the powers beginning with Vāmā, and accompanied by a retinue of seventy million.
Among them are Ananta and Sūkṣma, as well as Śivottama,
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, and Amitadyuti.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin are the lords of the lords of the kings of kings. Here, "kings" refers to Indra and the other world-protectors; their "kings" are the hundred Rudras;
and these [two] are the lords and sovereigns even of those lords, such as Maṇḍalin and the rest.
This refers to those up to the Vidyāmaheśvaras. Furthermore, all of these are impelled by Śiva and are not independent. Thus it is said:
"Because they have not yet fully attained the state of a yogin, the Parameṣṭhins are subject to being commanded."
Even though they possess qualities such as omniscience, they remain subject to injunctions due to a portion of impurity;
thus, the mantras situated at lower levels are distinguished from one another.
"And impelled by the manifest Śiva-power of the lords of mantras, they bestow grace upon those men with whom [the power] is joined. (Mṛgendratantra 2.4–6).
And those mantras are set in motion by the manifest Śiva-power of the supreme and subordinate lords of mantras.

They bestow grace upon some at some time according to their capacity, but not independently of that capacity. Depending upon the body of the one who employs [the mantra], that [mantra] performs its function throughout the entire path; having fulfilled its office, it enters into Śiva along with the Lord at the end of its duration.

Except in the case of a *adhikaraṇa* (formal dispute), another [impurity] following a primary impurity departs after one has performed the desired *adhikāra* (observance) for the Lord, provided the removal of sin is virtuous.
Then, manifested through Ananta and the others from the principle of the *granthi* (the knot) of the lords (*patis*),
[Ananta] brings about one hundred and eighteen [deities] for those whose bodies are composed of *kalā* and the other [categories].
The Blessed One, having entered even those world-lords who possess eyes—
those from whom all this [universe] proceeds and whose power is bound by karma— [acted].

"The authors of the treatises on the bound (paśu), the bound beings who follow them, together with the instruments for their own goals, remain until the end of the abode of Time. (Mṛgendra-tantra 4.4–11). This is the state [of the world], which is perceived by Him and restrained by His will, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of all people.

The second function is *sthāpana* (establishment), which consists of the application [of the soul] for the sake of accomplishing its activity. As it is said in that very same [text]: "Having overwhelmed these [elements] along with their causal factors by means of his own splendor while they remain [in their state], he joins them to the accomplishment of his own purpose, unobserved by the beings. (Mṛgendra-tantra 4.12)

Dissolution (*dhvaṃsa*) occurs at the end of persistence (*sthiti*), through the process of merging the body, organs, worlds, and other means of experiencing the pure and impure paths— which consist of *bindu* and *māyā* and are endowed with their respective powers— into the substrate that presides over the multitude of individual souls (*aṇu*) contained within.

The third task is the establishment [of the world] for the rest of transmigrating beings who are exhausted by wandering through the paths of existence. As it is said in that very same work: "Having withdrawn the means of enjoyment and having caused them to take refuge in the cause..."
And that [consciousness], having relied upon and traversed that which possesses a self, remains for the sake of rest.
Because he is intent on the welfare of all beings for those who are destined for existence and weary of worldly life—Mṛcchakaṭikā 4.13–14.
This very dissolution is called *pralaya*. And that is of three kinds, distinguished as inferior, middling, and superior. Of Brahmā’s...

At the end of a day of Kālāgnirudra, during his sleep, the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar—are dissolved; this is the inferior dissolution (adhama-pralaya). At the end of a day of Śrīkaṇṭha, during his sleep, the dissolution of all principles from the Bhūta-tattva up to the Guṇa-tattva is the intermediate dissolution (madhyama-pralaya). [Furthermore,] the dissolution of the worlds beginning with Kālāgni up to the end of Nāda is [the superior dissolution].
This is the supreme dissolution (*uttama-pralaya*). All of this has been demonstrated in detail in the *Mataṅga*;

it is not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length. In this great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there is the withdrawal of everything except Māyā, Puruṣa, and Śiva. Thus, in the *Acintyaviśve*:
At the time of the withdrawal of the great purpose, all those whose nature is illusory (māyā) and Śiva himself remain through impure māyās, while others are dissolved.
"These remain everywhere for the sake of their own enjoyment.
Likewise, the Teachers have said:
"Māyā, Puruṣa, and Śiva—this triad [is present] at the dissolution of the Great Purpose."
"That which remains proceeds again as before in creation. (Tattvaprakāśa 69).

Concealment (*tirobhāva*) is the fourth task (*kṛtya*), consisting of the non-falling away from experience (*bhoga*) according to its suitability for bound souls (*paśu*) through the favoring of their fetters (*pāśa*). This very same [task] is described elsewhere by the name "protection" (*saṃrakṣaṇa*).
As the venerable author of the Vārttika said: "The non-falling away of embodied beings from their experience, which is appropriate to their own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),
is declared to be 'protection' (*saṃrakṣaṇa*) when maintained according to the rule."

Liberation (*vimukti*) consists of contemplation (*anudhyāna*), grace (*anugraha*), and the bestowing of both higher and lower liberation upon individual souls (*aṇu*) through the concealment of their bonds (*pāśa*). Among these, lower liberation is of six kinds, whereas higher liberation is of one kind. Thus it is stated in the *Mataṅga*:
This liberation has been described in its sevenfold division;
for among these, one is supreme and subtle, pertaining to the sphere of both cause and effect.
The past is complete, independent, and all-pervading;
it is one, without a lord, and self-abiding. The other six are considered to have a lord.
"And others, whose powers are obstructed, are proclaimed as the gross divisions. Thus it is said.
Śiva performs this act of grace (anugraha) both at the time of creation and at the time of withdrawal.
This has been stated in this very [text]:
Those whom he liberates during the sleep [of dissolution] immediately become auspicious;
whether they are the individual souls (*aṇu*) or the Lords (*pati*) who have arisen at the time of reabsorption or manifestation.

"Those who, having relied upon a Guru possessed of consciousness, do not seize [the opportunity] during the state of maintenance (sthitau), become partakers of the status of Rudra, Mantreśvara, and Īśāna. (Mṛgendratantra, Vidyāpāda 5.2–3).
In the Svāyambhuva, the purpose of the ritual action (kṛtya) has been stated:
For what reason is this rite called by such a name?
It is declared that the union of the bound souls (paśu) with the body is for the sake of both enjoyment and liberation.
"Nevertheless, they say that [Śiva] is the one who releases [the soul] from beginningless impurity along with [the world].

Here, by the use of the particle *eva* (only), he shows that these fivefold acts belong to Śiva alone, while for Vidyā, the Vidyeśvaras, and others, they exist through his instigation. Thus it is stated in the venerable Raurava:
"Empowered by the injunction of Śiva’s will, they exercise their authority.

Furthermore, this task cannot be accomplished by Māyā and the other principles, nor by karmas, because they are insentient; nor can it be accomplished by the individual soul (puruṣa), because his power is obstructed by impurity (mala). By the phrase "together with its instruments," [the text indicates...]
Furthermore, dependence upon a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for Śiva has been demonstrated;
otherwise, liberation would be causeless. Because it would not depend on anything else, it would either belong to everyone or to no one at all. As they have said:
"Existence or non-existence must be eternal, because they do not depend on anything else;
for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of things is possible. (16)
The Mṛgendra-tantra states in another aphorism that even during the sleep of the Supreme Lord, His powers of transformation and so forth remain intent upon accomplishing their respective effects:
"Even in sleep, He remains awakening those who are fit for awakening."
Obstructing those who are to be obstructed and ripening the fruits of karma,
manifesting the powers of illusion (*māyā-śakti*) so they become perceptible, he perceives everything— whatever collection of objects exists— exactly as it is.

Just as in the waking state, even in the state of sleep, He awakens those who are capable of awakening— those fit for enlightenment depending on the degree of ripening of their impurities— bringing them to realization; and He restrains with His power of obstruction those who are to be restrained— those fit for obstruction— of the *karmiṇaḥ*, those possessed of *karman*.

Karma is the cause of the body, the sense organs, birth, lifespan, and experience. It brings the subtle form of karma to maturity, rendering it ready to yield its fruit. As it will be stated [in the *Mṛgendra-vṛtti*]: "In that way, it matures the seed of the body and so forth until the final dissolution" (*Mṛgendra-vṛtti* 5.11).
This is the intended meaning. It has been stated in this very same work (*Mṛgendra*, Vidyāpāda 5.11):

"It does not immediately become a factor for [spiritual] fitness, like a medicinal herb and the like. Even that which is fit for ripening is not capable of ripening itself by its own self; for [this applies to] everything...

This is a common characteristic of any transforming substance, such as milk and the like: that its state of transformation depends upon something else and not otherwise. Therefore, because it is subject to transformation, even the maturation (*pāka*) of *karman* depends upon another factor. Likewise—
"Even though it is capable of being cooked, it cannot cook itself by itself;

this is the common nature of all that is subject to transformation. (Mṛgendra-vṛtti 5.12). "The powers of *māyā* (*māyāśaktīḥ*)" refers to the powers of both pure and impure *māyā*, namely, the powers that produce their respective effects.

"Making [them] ready for manifestation," that is, making them intensely inclined toward production. Here too, the sense is that it is not possible for even the powers of *māyā*—which possess transformative action (*pariṇāmikarma*)—to be brought to a state of inclination toward production by themselves alone. "The entire collection of things," consisting of consciousness (*cit*), the unconscious (*acit*), principles (*tattva*), states of being (*bhāva*), elements (*bhūta*), and worlds (*bhuvana*).

Having become one who sees and contemplates the collection of objects exactly as they exist, he remains; "Śiva" is the understood subject. By the phrase "seeing things as they truly are," the appearance of objects existing otherwise—as they do for those like us—is excluded from Śiva. By the phrases "awakening," "obstructing," "maturing," and "acting," [the nature] of Śiva...
By the phrase "seeing," both the state of being the creator of all (*sarvakartṛtva*) and omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) are indicated;

for without knowledge of all objects, the status of being the creator of all is untenable. For whoever knows the accomplishment of whatever action, as well as its constituent parts and its fruits, he alone [is the agent].

The status of being an agent of various specific actions is possible for one who possesses the intention to employ those respective diverse causal factors, just as a weaver and others are agents in the production of cloth and the like. Therefore, he who is ignorant in that regard is not capable of performing that effect, just as a fool is incapable of presenting the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*) and so forth. This has been stated in this very work (*Mṛgendra*, 5.13):
"He who knows and performs [an action] together with the means, the constituent parts, and the results, he alone is the deity; this is well-established.

By the word "exists" (*āste*), the existence of Śiva during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is indicated, as well as his being capable of being known by those who are fit for such knowledge, and so forth.

By the phrase "the existence of the Puruṣa and the powers of Māyā," the existence of both the Bindu and the nature of Māyā is demonstrated. Furthermore, the fivefold activities (pañcakṛtya) of Śiva even during the time of dissolution (pralaya) have been shown. As it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"Even during the dissolution, the Blessed Lord bestows grace, creates, protects, destroys, and conceals [the world], always and without dependence on time. Thus,
with these thirteen verses beginning with "the insentient," [the author establishes] the definition and the means of knowledge regarding the Lord (pati).

The fivefold cosmic functions have been established as being characterized by omniscience, which depends upon auxiliary causes and material substrates, and by agency, which is conditioned by the lack of dependence on a causal body such as the *adhiṣṭhāna-mūrti*. By knowing the nature of the Lord (*pati*) in this manner alone, beings become liberated from transmigratory existence; it is not, however, by way of the nature of the fetter (*pāśa*).

Regarding those who know the Lord, it is stated in the *Mṛgendra* (5.18): "Those who know the reality of the Lord through [the categories of] existence, essential nature, the purpose of the instruments, and the objects of action—though these are indicated only briefly—they liberate living beings submerged in the mire of worldly existence; they do not [need to explain] in detail the nature of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) and its bonds (*pāśa*)."
Thus [it is said].

Here too, by the phrase "of the insentient [nature] such as Māyā," the existence of the Lord (Īśvara) is established. Then, by the phrase "the presiding over [it] by the Master," His essential nature is described. By the phrase "and the instrument," the instrument is mentioned. And by the phrase "He remains even in deep sleep," His purpose—the objective consisting of enjoyment and liberation—is indicated.
It has been described. By the phrase "the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the world," the fivefold function (*pañcakṛtya*) which constitutes the object to be accomplished is stated.

By the phrase "perceiving everything, whatever the collection of objects may be as it is," it should be understood that the nature of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), denoted by the term "vision" (*dṛk*), is stated. Thus, those who assert the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman and its universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*)...

The Vedāntins [hold that] those who perceive the reality of the Lord through the perspectives of existence, essential nature, instrumentality, purpose, and the object of injunction— perspectives expressed in the passage beginning with "of the insentient Māyā, etc. and ending with "seeing everything, whatever the collection of objects may be"— [are the ones intended].

Only those men who know [this] are liberated from saṃsāra and deliver the transmigrating beings who are submerged in the mire of saṃsāra. However, those who consider the Lord—who is of the nature of both the bound soul (paśu) and the bond (pāśa)—to be "the Self alone is all this" or "the Person alone is all this," do not become liberated from saṃsāra; such is the meaning.
Those who maintain that Īśvara consists of the bound soul (paśu) and the bond (pāśa), as well as those who maintain that [Īśvara] consists of time (kāla), karma, and Īśvara,

declare that the nature of Īśvara is that of a bond. Having thus stated the definition of the Lord (pati), [the author] finally describes the true nature of the bound soul (paśu) by way of its distinction from consciousness (cit).
He establishes this through the Parākhyasūtra:

"The bound soul (paśu) is distinct from the body, imperishable, all-pervasive, separate [from matter], possessed of impurity, non-inert, the enjoyer of the fruits of its own karma, the agent, possessing limited knowledge, and dependent upon a Lord. (18)
The self (ātman) is other than the body; it is distinct from the physical frame. By this, the Cārvāka position is refuted.

For the Cārvākas indeed argue as follows: "I am thin," "I am fat"—since the notion of "I" is observed only with respect to the body, no self distinct from it is perceived. Furthermore, the eyes and other sense organs exist for the sake of another.

The self (ātman) is established by means of an inference such as "because it is an aggregate, like the parts of a bed," or "because instruments are employed by an agent. This is not tenable, because [such an argument] is unestablished for the Cārvākas, who deny the existence of the self; for they admit no means of knowledge other than perception (pratyakṣa).

There would be some means of valid cognition [for it]. Even if [the self] were established, the consequence would follow that the inferable self is "other" (paratva), just like Devadatta and others. For that which shines forth by itself is indeed the self; whereas that which is illuminated by it is "other.
If the states of being self and other were thus distinct yet appeared as mixed together, there would be confusion and an infinite regress.
As it has been said:
"If the self were an object of knowledge, its knower would have to be something other than itself.
In that case, the self would become 'other,' for it is that which is measured (known) which is other."

Thus it is said: "The one consciousness shines forth; everything else, however, is illumined by it. And that which is illumined must be an object (karman), so how could it exist without an agent (kartṛ)?"

Therefore, by means of inference, a self distinct from the body is not perceived. Nor should it be argued: "How can the body be the self, given that it lacks consciousness? For just as the power of intoxication arises from the transformation of substances such as *kiṇva*, so too does consciousness arise within the body, which is a transformation of the four elements.
Furthermore, that which increases when something else increases, or decreases when that other thing decreases, must be of the same nature as it.

For example, heat follows the increase and decrease of fire. Likewise, consciousness—which conforms to the two types of bodily growth related to the body, namely those caused by youth and old age, and by the presence or absence of food—[must be of the same nature].

[The opponent claims: "The body alone constitutes the self; therefore, the body itself is the conscious self. This is incorrect. For instance, the body is never conscious, because it is an object of experience (*bhogya*) and because it is subject to modification (*vikārin*). Whatever is subject to modification, subject to transformation, and is an object of experience is observed to be insentient (*acetana*), such as cloth and the like. That...
Therefore, the body as well is of such a nature and is not conscious.

[Objection: But is not its being an object of enjoyment (bhogyatva) rendered inconclusive by women and the like? [Response: No, because even though they are objects of enjoyment, consciousness is not absent in them. It is not [inconclusive].

[It is] beautiful (*kāntika*), because that very body is the object of enjoyment. If this is so, how is it that there is no enjoyment of a lifeless body? There is indeed enjoyment appropriate to that state for those such as carnivores (*kravyāda*), but not for lovers (*kānta*) and the like. This is because the state of being a beloved woman and so forth undergoes modification (*vikāritva*) through the transition into another state.
Because it is the cause of the sentiment of disgust (*vībhatsa-rasa*), its description occurs right here:
"Where is that face? Where is that nectar of the lower lip? Where are the sidelong glances of the long-eyed one?
and so forth.

The same should be understood regarding elephants, horses, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that because the body is subject to modification and is an object of enjoyment, it is insentient; and because it is insentient, it exists for the sake of another. Nor does the fact that the self is distinct from the body contradict such cognitions as "I am thin," for [that cognition] is sublated by the distinct cognition that grasps the difference, namely, "the body."
Because it would be contradicted [by perception]. Nor should it be argued that if the self were an object of inference, it would follow that it is "other" (paratva);
for the application of inference is solely for the purpose of demonstrating to those who hold contrary views that self, which is established through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).
Furthermore, it is not possible for that [inference] to refute the validity of inference itself; for the validity of that inference—

Because the very reasoning that attempts to refute [the soul] would result in self-contradiction by being itself an inference; furthermore, consciousness does not conform to the body, as this is contradicted in the case of a corpse. Therefore, since experience and memory must reside in the same substratum, the conscious Self is indeed other than the body.

And here, by the statement that [the body] is distinct from the self, the status of the self belonging to its correlates— the sense organs and so forth— is refuted. For instance, the manifold of sounds produced by the organ of speech, which is impelled by the mind that retains objects grasped externally,
serves as a medium like a mirror for revealing the intentions of the person engaged in worldly discourse.
It is only appropriate that the insentient sense organs function as instruments;
and so it is stated in the Mataṅga:
"By means of the distinct organ of speech, which is indeed filled within by the mind..."
That conceptual proliferation known as inference is common among those who engage in worldly discourse.
For by that [body], the self is inferred through the illustration of a mirror for vision.
Furthermore:
whatever is composite is for the sake of an enjoyer, just as a bed and so forth; and this [body] is composite.
Since there must also be an enjoyer for the group of faculties such as the eye, the existence of an enjoyer distinct from the faculties is established.
[This enjoyer] is imperishable and eternal; for if it were momentary or perishable, like that of the Buddhists and others, [there would be no continuity].

Or, if [momentariness] were accepted, the performance of ritual acts, the enjoyment of their fruits, and so forth, as well as the recollection of previous experiences, would not be possible. Thus, in this very context:
"If knowledge is subject to momentary destruction, the acquisition of karma could not occur."
When knowledge has been destroyed without remainder, that fruit of karma is no longer to be experienced.

And it is seen thus in the *Śāntiśataka* composed by Śilhaṇa (verse 27): "Where is that lotus-face, where is the nectar of those lips, where are those long side-glances? Where are those tender conversations, and where is the play of the eyebrows, curved like the bow of Love?"
"Stability is to be understood through its own movement; memory does not exist apart from experience.
Because the knower is both the rememberer and the experiencer due to stability, he is the stable one on earth. Thus it is said.

It is all-pervasive and omnipresent. If it were not all-pervasive—as in the case of the Jainas—then the experience of results in another location would be impossible, just as the enjoyment seen by a Kashmiri in the Deccan is not possible [for him]. This is because that formless entity cannot be led to another location by insentient *karma*, any more than a sky-flower can be moved by a body. [The same applies to] the body...

Furthermore, if it were limited, or possessed the nature of contraction and expansion, there would follow the defects of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and insentience (*acetanatva*), and so forth. Likewise, in that very same [text]:
"Even one who is not liberated would become a practitioner of yoga (*yogin*) [if he could attain] a fruit in another location."
If it were corporeal, there would be no fruit to be enjoyed, because a corporeal form is perishable.
"Since the [soul] is formless, how can that [karma], which is restricted and pervasive by some action, lead it [to a result]?
For that fruit resides in a different location; because of its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), it arises from a connection with the body. Thus.

"Distinct" means manifold; it is not, as for the Vedāntins, a single entity. For if that [Self] were ultimately one, there would result the emergence of duality through the distinction between bondage and liberation, and between knowledge and ignorance; furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the liberation of one would entail the cessation of existence for all, as well as defects such as the equality of experiences. Thus, in that very same [text]:
Because its nature is consciousness, there is unity; its differentiation arises from the diversity of experiences.
And that [differentiation] of it originates from its own karma; that is ignorance, characterized as bondage.
When duality exists for you, that knowledge which severs it would arise;
through the distinction between knowledge and ignorance, the grasping at duality comes into being.
If liberation were established as being omnipresent, it would follow that cyclic existence is already severed;
yet such a severance of cyclic existence does not exist, and for that reason, those [liberated ones] are considered to be many.
In the venerable Pauṣkara:
"If [the will] were non-different for all, then there would be a desire to enjoy at one and the same time;
yet when one has a desire to enjoy, another may have a desire to depart."
At that very moment, consciousness (caitanya) is considered to be of a different nature from that [state].

"Samala" means accompanied by impurity (*mala*). By the word *mala*, ignorance (*ajñāna*)—which is distinct from karma and is the cause of attachment (*rāga*) while obscuring knowledge—is denoted. Thus, it is said in that same [text]:
Therefore, that ignorance, distinct from karma, is the cause of attachment;
that formless ignorance envelops [the soul], like the potency of poison.
Therefore, this impure *paśu* (bound soul) is the locus of qualities that follow [it].

"Non-inert" (*ajaḍa*) means he does not become inert; the meaning is that his essential nature consists of knowledge and action, because in the absence of consciousness, the activity of an agent would be impossible. Thus, in the *Pauṣkara* (6.186):
The body and so forth, as they function, are always presided over by a conscious agent,
because, being insentient, they lack inherent activity, just like a jar or similar objects.
But that which is the initiator is traditionally taught as this "Self.
Likewise, in that very same work: "In every action, having observed the existence of the agent residing in the object..."
Since activity is observed, that entity is denoted by the word "existent."
"Therefore, why do you not consider that state [of the self] prior to consciousness to be like that of an agent?
Thus, it is the enjoyer of the fruits of its own actions. Its own action is 'svakarma,' consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);

it enjoys the fruit of that, hence it is 'the enjoyer of the fruits of its own actions' (*svakarmaphalabhuk*). [This applies] to two people engaged simultaneously in service, agriculture, and so forth."
Because the attainment of the result occurs for one of two men and not for the other;
likewise,
between two who have engaged in service and possess equal qualities and character.
The perfection of the fruit belongs to one [person]; therefore, that is the stage of its cause.
The unseen [force], because it is a subtle cause, is understood through its connection with its effects;
that cause, known by the name "karma," exists in the nature of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).
In the Pauṣkara (3/40):
"O twice-born ones, even though the labor of both is equal in agriculture, one person acquires grain while the other acquires nothing; [this difference arises from] his past actions as the cause."

The "agent" (kartā) is the accomplisher of the aforementioned action; for since an insentient entity such as the body cannot logically possess agency, and because even though an action requires an instrument—just as an axe does—the person alone is primary due to the instrument's lack of excellence. Thus, in that very same [text]:
The person (puruṣa) is declared to be its agent; the body does not possess agency because it is insentient.
Therefore, agency exists only in that which is immortal.
Although agency resides in the instrument, it nevertheless possesses primacy;
just as in the world, when a tree is being cut, people do not praise the axe.

"He is the agent; for that reason, because of his preeminence, he is remembered as Puruṣa. One who knows only a little is "kiñcijjña," meaning one who knows only a small amount. The author himself will explain this state of being "kiñcijjña" later in the text with the words "being all-pervasive (vibhu)," and so forth. He is "seśvara," [meaning] together with Īśvara.
"Accompanied by the Impeller" means not independent as the Sāṃkhyas claim; this he will state later with the words "by action, the body," and so forth.
"The bound soul" (*paśu*) is one joined with the impurity of boundness (*paśutva-mala*), because boundness is impossible for one who is liberated. Thus, in the Pauṣkara (4.1):
A bound soul (paśu) is called "bound" because of its connection with the state of being a bound soul; it is not liberated.
And this bound soul is threefold, distinguished as the Vijñānakala, the Pralayākala, and the Sakala. These, respectively, possess one, two, or three impurities (mala).

"Because, although devoid of the *kalās* that possess his own power of vision and action, he is not the Supreme Lord; yet he remains established like Śiva—as all-pervasive, consisting of consciousness, and subtle. (Pauṣkara 4.2).
Furthermore, the state of being a knower of only a little (*kiñcijjñatva*) will be demonstrated by the author of the Sūtras later on. (18)

Having thus described the characteristics of the bound soul (paśu), he now defines the individual (māṇava) impurity, which is distinct from the five fetters (pāśa) that possess different characteristics, by means of the *Svāyambhuvasūtra*: "Now, the beginningless impurity of persons is proclaimed to be their state of bondage (paśutva)."
That [ignorance] should be known as being like the husk and the shell for the sprout of the seed-vessel of māyā. (19)
Now, following the characteristics of the bound souls (*paśu*), the impurities (*mala*) and so forth are explained—this is the remainder [of the sentence].

It is "beginningless impurity" (*anādimala*) because it is both beginningless and an impurity. It is called "impurity" (*mala*) because it makes [the soul] turbid, that is, it obscures the light whose nature is vision and action. The word *mala* is a synonym for "obscuring agent" and ends in a *kṛt* suffix. Not... [text continues]

That which has a beginning is *ādi*; that which does not have a beginning is *anādi*. Here, just as in the case of the word "beautiful" (*śobhana*) functioning as an adjective for "cook," the term *anādi*—acting as an adjective for the obscuring ignorance (*ajñāna*)—establishes through the demonstration of the beginninglessness of its connection with the act of obscuration the beginninglessness of that which is connected to it.

The beginninglessness of impurity (*mala*) has also been stated. This impurity is proclaimed to be the state of bondage (*paśutva*) for *puṃs* (souls) or *puruṣas*. Regarding the nature of that impurity, he provides an illustration: "like the husk and the chaff," and so forth.
That which is the form of impurity is like mud; it is both the sowing and the sprout of the seed of *māyā*.

"Sprout of the sowing" (*āvāpāṅkura*) is a compound in the singular form. "Sprout of the sowing of illusion" (*māyāvāpāṅkura*) means [the sprout] of that which is the sowing of illusion; it should be understood as being like the husk and the inner shell (*tuṣa-kambuka*). For just as the husk and the inner shell are the cause of the swelling of the rice grains during their sowing, [so too is this].

The state of being oriented toward procreation is the cause for the arising of the sprout; likewise, by the power of Śiva’s will, Māyā is the cause for the descent (āvāpa) that is oriented toward procreation, as well as for its effects such as *kalā* and the rest.
This is what is meant: for one who possesses this [descent], Māyā becomes oriented toward procreation.
"It exists and produces *kalā* and the rest.

Now, an objection may be raised: "The impurity (*mala*) resides in the Self (*ātman*), like the husk and the chaff, whereas the sprouting of *kalā* and the rest occurs in *māyā*. Since these have different loci, how can there be a single-locus analogy? To this, [the author replies]:
True. This is not a complete analogy; rather, there is no fault because it refers merely to the relationship between cause and effect.

Here, by means of the example of the husk and the kernel, the example of copper and its blackness mentioned in other scriptures should also be understood as an illustration. As it is said in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
(From the *Puṃpradhāneśvarasādhanapaṭala*, verse 80):
"The innate [nature] is proclaimed to arise from union, like copper and its impurity.
Here too, just as the impurity (*kālikā*) of copper is removed by the power of mercury (*rasa*), so too is the impurity [removed].

It should be understood that the status of this as an illustration lies merely in the fact that [the world] is brought about by Śiva’s power (śivaśakti), and not in every respect through complete similarity. Furthermore, its synonyms are shown in the *Mṛgendra*:
"By means of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), the veil of the bound soul (paśunīhāra), death, fainting, and the collyrium of impurity (mala)."
The covering of ignorance (avidyāvṛti) is destroyed by the eradication of the root of evil and other means. As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Impurity is ignorance; darkness is the state of being ignorant, and it likewise acts as an obscuration."
"The Lord is the fettered soul (paśu), which is ignorance"—this is a synonym for impurity (mala). || 19 ||

Here, by the use of the plural "of men" (*puṃsām*) and the singular "impurity" (*mala*), it is implied that a single impurity possesses a variety of powers to obstruct the activities of many individuals; this meaning is explicitly demonstrated by the *Mṛgendra-sūtra* (1.7.8): "The Lord, having first established the individual soul (*pudgala*) as distinct from the body and so forth, then [establishes] its state of bondage through the power of karma, which is itself a manifestation of the power of Māyā. This indicates that while the soul is fundamentally one, its association with the power of Māyā results in the diversity of karmic forces that obscure its true nature for many persons. Thus, although the impurity (*mala*) is essentially one, it manifests a manifold capacity to veil the various functions of numerous souls.
That is one, the beginningless, dense, and great essence of all beings,
abiding within each individual soul and possessing a multitude of powers that persist until the end of its own time.

That obscuration is one and the same for all fourteen kinds of living beings. Why is this? To provide the reason, he states it by way of a qualification: "beginningless" (*anādi*). It is beginningless, meaning it is not adventitious like the bondage of *māyā*. For that very reason, it is one; for were it manifold, being insentient (*acetana*), it could not [function as a single cause].

Because it would be impossible for [bondage] to be beginningless if it were preceded by another cause. Nor should it be argued that even if it is preceded by another cause, it is nonetheless beginningless because it acts as a binder through a succession starting from *kalā* and so forth; for such a continuous succession (*pravāha*) is not admitted to be beginningless. If, however, that were admitted, then for souls—

Because the state of being free from impurity is necessary, there would follow the undesirable consequence that, like Śiva, there could be no further bondage at that time. Therefore, impurity does not possess beginninglessness through a continuous stream (*pravāha-anāditva*) like karma;
rather, its beginninglessness is due solely to the absence of a cause, just like *māyā*.

"Dense" (*nibiḍa*) means compact, that is to say, indivisible. It is "great" (*mahat*) because it obscures the all-pervading selves. Now, if impurity (*mala*) were one, then upon the liberation of one, there would be the undesirable consequence of the liberation of all; to this he replies: "Abiding in each individual self, not departing from its own time, like a collection of powers. Abiding in each individual self (*pratyātmasthāḥ*)... [text continues]

That which possesses a collection of those powers— powers that abide in the *puruṣa*, which bring about their own respective ends in time, and which recede at the time of their own particular transformations— is "endowed with them. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvatrayanirṇaya*:
"The powers of impurity (*mala-śaktayaḥ*) are distinct for each individual soul, and they are the obscurers of its qualities.

This being the case, even though impurity is one, because its obscuring powers are infinite and the objects to be obscured by them are likewise diverse, there is no contingency of universal liberation upon the liberation of a single soul.

By this sūtra, which establishes the oneness and other attributes of impurity (mala), its essential definition (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa) has been stated. Regarding that, the proof should be understood as a *śeṣavat* inference based on the mark of its effects, characterized by delusion (moha) and so forth. For example: the effect consisting of delusion and the rest must have a cause, because it is an effect, like a jar.

And here, since illusion (*māyā*) and the rest are established as causes of delusion only by virtue of being manifestors [of objects], it follows by process of elimination that impurity (*mala*) is established as the cause of delusion. Thus, in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"Light is denoted by the word 'manifestation' (*vyakti*), and obscuration by the word 'impurity' (*mala*)."
"The manifestation which is the stainless [state] of the individual soul (aṇu) is clearly said to be like a lamp and darkness.
And in the Mataṅga:
"Therefore, the pair—impurity (mala) and Māyā—is always like a lamp and darkness."

"And the difference in nature between the two has been declared by you, O Sage. Thus, there are seven kinds of effects of impurity, beginning with delusion (*moha*). As it is said in that very same [text], the *Mātaṅgapārameśvara* (6.103):
Delusion, intoxication, passion, despondency,
emaciation, mental distraction, and that which is called exhilaration— these seven are the innate impurities.
The essential nature of these should be examined in the Mataṅga and other [scriptures]. || 20 ||
These powers of impurity do not obstruct or withdraw independently;

rather, they are dependent upon the Supreme Lord’s power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*). That very power of obstruction is also designated as "fetter" (*pāśa*) by way of metaphor, as established by the two *Mṛgendra* sūtras [7.11].
Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā, who bestows grace upon all;
she is metaphorically designated as a "bond" (pāśa) solely because she follows the course of dharma.

The *māheśvarī* is the power of Śiva; it is so called because it follows after—that is, conforms to and pursues—the nature of those impure powers (*mala-śakti*). This is a causal ablative (*hetu-pañcamī*). It is metaphorically designated as a "fetter" (*pāśa*) by virtue of its being a fetter.
And here, the status of being a "fetter" (pāśa) is not primary. To specify the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*) as the cause for that [status], he says:

"Śivā, who is the benefactress of all. Since she is the benefactress of all—meaning her very nature is the grace toward the entire world—and since she is Śivā because she accomplishes that supreme good (*śreyas*), the meaning is that [obstruction] does not possess the primary status [of being a fetter]. || 21 ||
Now, having raised the objection— "How can this power of obstruction, whose sole nature is to obstruct, exercise grace?"— he says:
"And she transforms these [energies] up to the limit of obstruction by means of her intensely piercing splendor."

When it brings about its unfolding (*unmīlana*), then it is called "gracious" (*anugrāhikā*). (Mṛgendra-tantra 7.12) And these [powers], residing in all beings and connected with impurity (*mala*), cause the power of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) to undergo transformation until the end of its obstruction—
that is, for as long as its period of authority lasts— by means of such transformation they join it to that state.

From the nominal stem *pariṇāma*, by applying the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of a verbal root according to the rule "after a nominal stem, [the suffix *ṇic* is added] in the sense of the action of the root," the form *pariṇāmayati* ("she causes to transform") is produced.

Here, the absence of shortening (*hrasva*) before the suffix *ṇi* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). That power of the Lord (*pati-śakti*) is the "sparkle of the sun of consciousness" (*kārka-cittviṣā*). What is "arka"? It is *kārka*; "with the sparkle of consciousness" means with the radiance whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa-tviṣā*), by that "sparkle of the sun of consciousness. By the word *ka*, the head (*mūrdhan*) is meant.
The Lord (Īśāna) is said to have the sole activity of constant grace, according to the indicative mark of the mantra "Īśāna is the head.

Because He is eternally engaged in bestowing grace upon the entire world, He is compared to the Sun (Arka). Then, when—at which time—by means of the light of consciousness (cittviṣā), that is, the radiance of knowledge (jñānabhāsā) which has proceeded therefrom and serves as the cause for illuminating the supreme good (paraśreyaḥ)— [The rest of the sentence continues: ... [the yogin] beholds the Self... [as described in the following verse]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.)
It brings about the "unfolding" (*unmīlanam*), which effects the expansion of the latent dispositions (*āśaya*) of the group of individual souls whose true nature has not yet been unfolded;

at that time, it is called or spoken of as "gracious" (*anugrāhikā*), meaning it bestows grace. Although the obstructive power (*rodha-śakti*) possesses a nature characterized primarily by obstruction until the very end of the ripening of impurity (*mala-paripāka*), nevertheless—

The meaning is that immediately thereafter, it possesses the quality of being "gracious" (*anugrāhaka*) because it causes the expansion of the inner disposition (*āśaya*) of the classes of individual souls (*aṇuvarga*).

And thus, this very power of *Īti* favors the insentient forms— the impurity (*mala*), karma, *māyā*, and their effects— until the ripening of the impurity, while simultaneously concealing the conscious nature of the self.

Immediately after maturation, She bestows grace upon the Self; She veils the fetter (pāśa). Because She effects grace for all—both conscious and unconscious beings—it is established that She is the "Bestower of Grace upon All. For example:
"The Power of Śiva is the eternal bestower of grace upon all."
Through the cessation of the nature of the fetters, by means of the cause of the fetters, [the fetters are destroyed].
Because it renders them capable of cessation,
and because it obstructs the attributes of the fetters (pāśa), it bestows grace upon the bound souls (paśu).
It is metaphorically designated as "the obstructer" because it obstructs by means of its identity with that [object]. || 22 ||

Having thus described the two bonds (pāśa) consisting of the power of impurity (mala) and concealment (tirodhāna), [the author] now demonstrates the form of Mahāmāyā— which is more venerable than Māyā and the others— by means of the subsequent sūtra of the *Viśvasāra*, since it is stated that "Mahāmāyā is above Māyā" among the remaining bonds.
And Vāgīśvarī is the material cause of the pure path;
for an effect is never observed to exist without a material cause. (23)

She is the fundamental material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the pure path (*śuddha-adhvan*). The word "ca" (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). She alone is Vāgīśvarī, the Great Māyā. As it is said in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"The supreme knowledge is Vāgīśvarī; Māyā is remembered as the lower ignorance (*avidyā*)."
Mahāmāyā has many synonymous names, such as Nāda and others. Thus, it is said in the *Nādakārikā*:
"The perfected Nāda is the supreme Maṅgalā, Mālinī, and Mahāmāyā."
The unstruck sound (*anāhata*), the drop (*bindu*), the lower breath (*adhoṣā*), speech, and the reality of the Brahma-kuṇḍalinī.
Thus it has been stated in their respective scriptures by various such terms as "Vidyā" (Knowledge).

By this, the definition of Mahāmāyā as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) is demonstrated. And by that, there is an inference based on the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgaka*) which establishes its existence.

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been implied. For instance: this pure [consciousness] possesses a material cause (*sopādāna*), because it is an effect, like a jar. Nor should it be argued that the inhering power (*samaveta-śakti*) itself is established as the material cause; for if that were the material cause, it would follow that it is insentient, and thus its inherence in the sentient Śiva would be impossible. Just as...
It is heard in the Pauṣkara (2.11):
"When Śiva is the agent, this Kuṇḍalinī does not exist [as separate] due to identity, for the reason that she is subordinate to him, just as clay is to a potter. Thus it is said.

In this context, since *māyā* and *prakṛti* are delusive by nature, they cannot logically serve as the cause for the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) consisting of the bodies and instruments of awakened persons; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the existence of *mahāmāyā* is established as the cause that conforms to those [awakened beings]. Thus, it is stated in the *Pauṣkara* (2.6–7/10):
Even *māyā* is not the material cause here because it causes delusion by its own power;
for that reason, it is not the cause of the bodies and organs of awakened persons.
All those who abide on the pure path are awakened by the splendor of Śiva;
therefore, for that pure path, the cause is indeed its own reflection.
"O best of the twice-born, let this pure [reality] called Kuṇḍalinī be accepted.

Now, one might object that the fact that an effect possesses a material cause (*sopādānatva*) is unestablished, because it is contradicted in the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). Anticipating this, he says "upādānam," etc. "Upādāna" means the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
An effect is never found or observed without an interval [of cause].
The intention is that the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) must be avoided by providing the qualification "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) for the reason "being an effect.
Furthermore, because these [bonds] act as obstacles to the supreme liberation of those dwelling on the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), they are indeed fetters (*pāśa*).
As it is stated in the venerable Pauṣkara (2.2–3):
"Furthermore, that by which the rudrāṇavas are bound, wherein they abide,
or from which they are liberated— that should be understood as the Bindu."
Now, by means of another [Svatantra-tantra] Sūtra, he demonstrates his activity within the pure path (*śuddhādhva*), which serves as the cause for the arising of the entire world:
"Furthermore, that power *Kuṇḍalinī*, which follows after *māyā* and karma..."
The world exists as her effect, consisting of sound, the bindu, and so forth. || 24 ||

Here, the word *atha* (now/thereupon) refers to the power inherent in Śiva (*śivasamavāya-śakti*), because it establishes that Śiva, as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), exists above *māyā*. Thus it is heard in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The supreme power is partless (*niṣkalā*), inconceivable, and facing in all directions."
She is subtle, stainless, eternal, blissful, and the bestower of liberation.
She who unfolds within the principles (tattvas) and indeed [pervades] everything—
by her alone, though she possesses manifold forms, the entire universe is sustained.

"Above this [Prakṛti] is that which is without support, without substratum, free from affliction, inconceivable, all-pervasive, peaceful, and devoid of creation and dissolution. Thus, below the inherent power (samavāyi-śakti) exists Māyā, which follows the influence of karma.
*Karma* and *māyākarma*; *māyākarmānusāra* means following after *māyākarma*.

That which possesses this [following] is called *māyākarmānusāriṇī*. In the form of the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and the rest, she is the support for the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth, which are the effects of *māyā*, and she exists in the form of the power of speech (*vākśakti*) corresponding to the actions of those who abide therein.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, she is favorable to *māyā* because she produces the body of the god Ananta, who causes the agitation of *māyā*. She is favorable to *karman* because she produces sound through the penetration of the suffixes denoting states (*bhāvapratyaya*) born of *karman*. Kuṇḍalinī is the power (*śakti*) of Śiva known as Kuṇḍalinī.
The power of grasping (*parigraha-śakti*). As it is said in the *Ratnatraya* (166):
"Mahāmāyā, who is the source of mantras, abides as the power of grasping.
And as stated in the commentary on the *Sarvajñānottara*: "In this context, she who is denoted by the word Kuṇḍalinī..."

The meaning is that she exists with a distinction for each individual person through her own function in the form of *nāda*, which is coiled like a serpent, but not by means of her essential nature (*svarūpa*) as existing separately for each individual person.
This is stated in the venerable *Trayodaśaśaktikā*: "coiled like a serpent. This refers to that *Mahāmāyā*.

The effect consists of *nāda*, *bindu*, and so forth; *nāda* and *bindu* are "nādabindu," and that which has these as its beginning is "nādabindvādika"—namely, the cosmic manifestation (*jagat-prapañca*), the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [are included] the principles (*tattva*) known as *nāda* and Īśvara, which reside within the five principles beginning with *nāda*.
This includes the worlds, bodies, and organs, as well as the *tantras* such as the *Kāmika* and others.

Alternatively, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), even the pure and impure principles (*tattva*) are included, because Kuṇḍalinī is the cause of the entire phenomenal universe both directly and indirectly. As it is said in the *Kālottara*:
Indeed, the thirty-five principles have emerged from the Śiva-principle;
therein is their persistence, their growth, and therein alone does their dissolution occur.

In this context, from Mahāmāyā, who has been stirred by Śiva through his inherent power (*samavāyi-śakti*), the principle (*tattva*) named Nāda first arises. This very [principle], because it is supported by Śiva, is also called the Śiva-tattva. From that, the one known as Bindu [arises].

The *tattva* arises. And this *tattva*, by virtue of being the substratum of power (*śakti*), is the *śakti-tattva*. From that *śakti-tattva* arises the *tattva* called Sadāśiva; from that called Sadāśiva arises the *tattva* called Īśvara; and from that called Īśvara arises the *tattva* called Vidyeśvara. In this sequence, the five pure *tattvas* are produced.
Therein, within the *vidyātattva*, there is the Lord of the *vidyātattva* (*vidyātattvādhipati*), the seven Vidyārājñīs beginning with Bhṛguṇī,

the seventy million great mantras subordinate to them, the expressive words such as the *vyomavyāpin* syllables, and the twenty-eight [Tantras] beginning with the *Kāmika* and the *vaikharyādi* [speech levels].
And the tantras proceed as follows; for instance, in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Bhṛguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā, Rūpiṇī, Nandinī, and Jvālā—these seven are the lords of the seven *arvudas*. (13/156) || 19 ||
In the Śrīmataṅga it is said: "O observer of noble vows, these indeed exist primarily as Vidyās and Mantras;
that Goddess who consists of eighty-one words is the Power whose essence is Śiva."
Previously, when emerging from Śāntātīta, her locus was of that same nature;
at the time of dissolution it is called the Śiva-tattva, and at the time of manifestation it is the supreme pair consisting of the Bindu.
In the state of Sadāśiva, [the teaching] called Īśvara is the domain;
in the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva), there is authority, for the Yoni is always to be known as such.
"O Sage! Within that very [power] abide the mantras and various vidyās;
this, indeed, is the great power (mahāśakti) of Śiva, the Supreme Self. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 7.30–34).
Here, [it refers to] the Śiva who bestows dissolution, enjoyment, and authority upon the individual selves (ātmanām).

Although it bestows a body belonging to the realm of the Bhuvanas, the connection with dissolution, enjoyment, and authority is stated for the collection of imperishable syllables (*akṣara*) that pervade space, because they constitute the body as the locus of manifestation; however, this is not natural, since—
like the imperishable syllables that remain when the destruction of their substratum has occurred— they are insentient by nature.
Because that [connection] is not possible, its primary relationship is therefore with the *vidyātattva* itself, which is the source of the syllables (*akṣarayoni*).

In the *īśvaratattva*, there are the eight *vidyeśas*, beginning with Ananta; the eight presiding powers over them are the *śaktis* beginning with Vāmā; and the eight powers that are their playful manifestations (*vilāsinī*) are those beginning with Bhānumatī.
The five Rudras, beginning with Ucchuṣma, who are worshipped in the Siddhānta scriptures;
the eight lords of the Gaṇas, beginning with Nandin; the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, along with their weapons;
and the eight [qualities] beginning with Dharma, which constitute the seat of Śiva—these all abide there. As it is said in the Mṛgendra-tantra (13.158):
"The Ucchuṣmas, Śambaras, Caṇḍas, those of great heroism,
the Padadruhas, the Rudras, the Gaṇas along with the world-protectors (Dikpālas), the Śāstras, and then the Lords (Patayas).
Thus it is said in the venerable Mataṅga-tantra.
Vidyā is named Bhānumatī, and she indeed possesses a radiant form;
moreover, there is another highly fortunate one, Raudrī, by virtue of her connection with Rudra.
Viśvā, Kālī, Kāpālī, and another Vidyā of great prosperity;
another renowned as Sukhodayā, and likewise she celebrated as Vajrī.
"These eight illustrious ones are the playful consorts of the high-souled Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), who release the fetters of bound souls (paśus). (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 7.19–22).
However, within the Sadāśiva-tattva, there is Sadāśiva in his state of authority, as well as the ten [deities] beginning with Praṇava.

The *aṇavas*, Sadāśiva, and the five Brahmans, as well as the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the *nāda*—which consists of the forms of the syllable (*akṣara*), the point (*bindu*), the gross (*sthūla*), and resonance (*dhvani*)—all exist. As it is said in the *Svacchanda*:
"Oṃkāreśa, Śiva, Dīpta, Kāraṇeśa, and the lords of the ten directions."
"Suśiva and Kāla are of subtle form and possess a portion of [His] splendor.
Thus it is said in the Śrīmataṅga (Vidyātattvapaṭala, verse 25):
"Those which are the Brahmāṇi-mantras and the Aṅgas exist within the sphere of Sādākhya."
Nāda and Bindu are said to be dependent upon the principle (tattva) called Sadākhya.

All who have attained this Sadāśiva-tattva become equal to it. Just as in the Mataṅga [Tantra], grass, clods of earth, and so forth, once they have reached the summit of Mount Meru, become completely [one with it].
"In the same way, they attain the state of gold in the level of Sādāśiva.

However, within the *bindu-tattva*, there exists Śiva— whose nature is the cause of the imperishable *bindu* and the subtle *nāda*— in the form of the worlds known as Nivṛtti and the others, bearing names such as Sadyojāta and so forth, and designated as both *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts).
"In the *Mṛgendra* (13.161), it is stated: 'In the Bindu, there are the lords of the Kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti.
In the commentary on the *Tattvaprakāśa*, this is because the subtle *nāda* is included within the *Śakti-tattva*."
By the statement "because it has been so declared," the abiding of the subtle *nāda* within the principle of *bindu* is revealed.
This is the meaning in the *Siddhāntadīpikā* composed by Śambhu, the soul of all:
"Within the principle of *nāda*, however, there is Dhvanipati, Indhikā, Dīpikā, or Recikā."

Śiva, known as the Lord of the worlds such as Nivṛtti, exists within the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) as the most eminent possessor of power (*śaktimat*), the Supreme Lord who is the ultimate cause of the entire universe, as well as Kuṇḍalinī, the Lords of Speech (*vāgīśāḥ*), and the Lords of the worlds above them;
beyond that is the absolute, supreme Śiva. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra* (13.162):
"In Sound is the Lord of Resonance; in Power is the best among all possessors of power.
The Mistress of Speech is the source of the universe; beyond her are the Lords, and beyond them is Śiva.
Thus it is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*.
In that regard, O Dear One, the Kuṇḍalinī power follows karma and is the cause of the lords of the worlds as well as of those who dwell therein.
"O fair-limbed one, that which has transcended it is the supreme reality, free from all affliction.
And in the *Suprabheda*:
"Above that is the principle of the Bindu (Point), and above that is indeed the Nāda (Sound)."
Above that is indeed the Śakti-tattva; above that [tattva] is the Tattva-tattva.
Above that, there should be the Śiva-tattva, which stands above all other principles (tattvas).

Pervading from Śiva down to the earth by means of that splendor, this very reality of Sound (nādatattva) is the eternal, supreme cause. Some teachers declare that it alone is Mahāmāyā. In their view, there are only four effects that are pure principles (śuddhatattvas).
Just as they remember the five pure principles at the beginning and end— namely the principle of Śiva,
the principles of Śakti and Sadāśiva, and the principles known as Īśvara and Vidyā.

The explanation of this is as follows: among those [sixteen categories], the ancient masters maintain that the Śiva-tattva, consisting of the *bindu*, is the first, the primary material cause (*upādāna*). And because it is the supreme material cause, its eternity is established, just like that of *māyā*. Therefore, the implication is that the other four categories are its effects.

Thus it is said. However, in the *Śrīmat Pauṣkara*, it is stated that although the Śiva-tattva called Nāda is indeed an effect (*kārya*), there are only four pure effects because [Nāda] is included within the Śakti-tattva. As it says:
"And its fourth state, consisting of the principles (*tattva*), is established as its function (*vṛtti*)."
The Śiva-tattva, known as Sadeśa, as well as Īśa and that which is called Vidyā;
"These principles (tattvas) are pure for the high-souled individual souls of Rudra.
However, in the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is stated that the principle of the Bindu alone, designated as Śakti, is the supreme cause. As it says:
Above this is the Bindu-tattva, which is stainless, facing in all directions,
the supreme among all principles, and consisting of infinite light.
Now, by means of another scriptural passage, he points toward the creation of sound— that all four modes of speech are the effects of Mahāmāyā:
"Her four modes of speech, consisting of voice, are Vaikharī and the others."
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, another called Paśyantī, and that known as Sūkṣmā. || 25 ||

Speech (*vāk*) consists of the four modes beginning with *vaikharī*, which are the functional manifestations (*vṛtti*) or effects of that Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*). He states the names of these four in sequence, beginning with *vaikharī*:
one manifestation is called by the name *vaikharī*; another manifestation is called by the name *madhyamā*; the next is called by the name...

The Paśyantī [speech] is another, known as the subtle (sūkṣma). The author of the Saṃgraha will himself explain the nature of these later on. By this, it is stated that the creation of sound also has the Bindu as its material cause.
Herein is the sequence of creation: first, by the will of Śiva, the Mahāmāyā becomes agitated.
From the *sakāśa* (the source) the *nāda* (sound) arises; from the *nāda*, the *bindu*; from the *bindu*, the *akṣara*; and from the *akṣara*, the *mātṛkā*.
Thus it is said in the *Parākhya*: "Then, the *bindu* being agitated by His will, the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) came into being."
"In the *Mṛgendra*, it is said: 'From power (*śakti*) arises sound (*nāda*); from that, the point (*bindu*); from that, the imperishable (*akṣara*); and from that, the mother-letters (*mātṛkā*).
Sound, originating from space and wind, emerging from the body, reaches the mouth."
"That which, being divided into various positions, attains the state of phonemes (varṇa), is sound (śabda). Thus it is said in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"The Supreme [Self], the source of the self, whose essence consists of nine hundred chapters, is of the nature of the seed."
The seed-syllable beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga consists of sixteen syllables.
"The remaining thirty-four *yoni*s are indeed imperishable and consist of the nature of the syllable (*akṣara*).

She is the power (*śakti*) of the God of gods; by her this entire world is pervaded. Thus [it is said]. The *kalā*s, beginning with *nivṛtti*, are the substrata for these four modes of functioning (*vṛtti*s).
And there are five effects of the *bindu* alone. Thus it is said in the *Ratnatraya* (85):
"This fourfold activity, based on the *kalās* such as *nivṛtti* and the rest, is further divided into five; those *kalās* are the activities of the *bindu*."
In the *Mūlatantra* as well, it is said: "The five digits (*kalā*) arising from the center of the previously mentioned point (*bindu*).
This Mahāmāyā consists of both sound and substance; [she is the source] of the subtle and so forth.
This is because it brings about both sounds—consisting of phonemes, words, and mantras—and objective entities. Thus, it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"The Bindu consists of both sound and object; it is not composed of either one alone."
"The path of mantra, the path of word, and the path of phoneme are [the paths] according to sound;
