the path of world, the path of principle, and the path of energy are [the paths] according to meaning, in their respective order. Thus it is said.

In this regard, the proponents of Śabdabrahman (the doctrine of the Word-Brahman) maintain that the Self itself exists through a sequence beginning with *nāda* (sound). This is incorrect, because it is impossible for that which is changeless to undergo transformation into the form of *nāda* and so forth.

Nor can it be the case that it is the power (*śakti*) of the Self [that transforms], since that too cannot logically undergo transformation. For if both were admitted to be subject to modification, [the doctrine of the Self's immutability would be abandoned].
Because it would follow that [the bindu] is insentient. Therefore, it must be accepted that the bindu alone is the material cause of sound.
Likewise, in the *Nādakārikās* (verse 16): "The Self is said to be unchanging, and its power likewise; therefore, those two are not suitable [as the material cause]."
Or rather, because it would be subject to modification if it were to exist in many ways or if it were devoid of consciousness. Thus [ends verse 25].
Having thus defined the characteristic of pure *māyā* as a bond (*pāśa*), he defines the characteristic of impure *māyā* by means of the *Svāyambhuvasūtra*:
"The *māyā*-principle is the seed of the universe, indestructible, and of the nature of Śiva."
The Lord is free from parts, subtle, beginningless, imperishable, and sovereign.
It is called *māyā* because the entire world is dissolved (*māti*) within it during the dissolution, or because the world is measured out (*mayati*) by means of it as food.
Thus, it is said in the *Pauṣkara*: "Because the entire world is measured out (*mayati*) from this, it is therefore proclaimed as *māyā*."

The reality that is the form of *māyā* is the *māyātattva*. This very reality is celebrated by many names, such as "the knot" (*granthi*) and so forth. It is the seed of the world, the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the entire universe, beginning with the *kalās*. By this qualification, it is shown that this world possesses a material cause.

The proof of *māyā* has been stated on the grounds that it possesses the property of arising, just like a cloth or similar objects. As it is said in the *Mṛgendra* (9.3): "By whatever causal characteristic of the world a creator is inferred, by that same [characteristic] there must also be a material cause (*upādāna*); for a cloth does not exist without threads."

It is indestructible and eternal. If, at the time of the dissolution of the universe, even its material cause called Māyā were to perish, then from what material cause would the universe arise again at the beginning of a new creation? Therefore, it is not impermanent.

Now, it might be argued that at the beginning of creation, the Lord will also create the material cause (*upādāna*). This is not tenable; for if this were the case, then just like his effect, this [material cause] too would not arise without its own material cause, and thus another material cause would have to be postulated for that one as well, and yet another for that one, and so on.

There would be an infinite regress. However, there is no fault whatsoever in its remaining in the form of a latent power (*śakti*) through its reabsorption into the individual manifestation (*vyakti*).
This is what was stated in the *Mṛgendra* (9.5): "If this effect is impermanent, why does it arise again?"

"Non-auspicious in nature" means impure; it is "non-auspicious in nature" because it does not possess the conscious nature of Śiva. That is to say, it is insentient (*acetana*), since its effects, such as *kalā* and the rest, are observed to be insentient. Even though its effects are observed to be insentient, if one were to assert that its cause is sentient, there would be a violation of the principle of causal regularity (*kāraṇāniyama*).

The total abolition of all inference and the loss of all worldly transaction would also be a fault. As it has been said in the *Mṛgendra*: "That [cause] would indeed be insentient, since its effect is seen to be insentient; otherwise, the fault of the non-restriction of causes would result, which destroys everything."

"Vibhu" means all-pervasive. It is so called because, for the sake of the experience (*bhoga*) of the *puruṣa*, it produces all effects in every direction through its streams situated horizontally, upwards, downwards, and in the middle. As it has been said:
"If it were not all-pervasive, how could it be present for all [beings] with its faces turned in every direction? (Mṛgendra-tantra 9.5).

Thus, just as the various distinctions such as wings and beaks are the locus of experience (*bhoga*), so too the various effects such as *kalā* and the rest are the locus of experience; therefore, [the Self] is devoid of distinction. For if it were distinct—that is, manifold—it would follow that, being insentient, it would possess the quality of being produced (*utpattimat*), like a jar or a cloth. But this [Self] is not produced.
It is produced by a cause, because it possesses the nature of being the ultimate cause; for there cannot be many ultimate causes. As stated in the *Mṛgendra* (9.7–):
"That which is manifold and non-conscious is observed to have the property of origination."
"Therefore, let it be accepted that [the cause] is one, for it does not possess [multiple] origins.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the production of the world, let there be a multiplicity of material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), as in the case of the atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth imagined by others;
for we observe the production of a single cloth from many threads, and the world is likewise [produced].

If it is argued that "let everything arise from multiple causes; what is the use of postulating a supreme cause consisting of a knot?", we say: no. That which is stated to be the cause of a cloth—consisting of multiple threads—is indeed multiple, yet it is considered one because it has arisen from a single substance such as silk or cotton. And just as [from a single substance],...

From substances such as *dukūla* silk and cotton, there arises cloth and other products in manifold forms; likewise, from the supreme cause—the substratum of creation, maintenance, and dissolution—there is the emergence of the world from the principle of *māyā* at the beginning of creation. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
As it has been said:
"A cloth is seen to arise from a multitude of threads; thus, the one arises from the many. Yet even that multiplicity is produced from a single seed. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra* (9.7).
In this way, if there were multiplicity, it would follow that non-conscious things are impermanent.

It is to be disregarded even those, such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that atoms are the cause [of the world], whose sharpness of intellect is revealed by their description of the knowledge of either the six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha) beginning with substance or the sixteen categories as the cause of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), for they do not understand the refutation of the status of being the ultimate cause.
[You] said: "It has been stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
'For those for whom atoms are the cause of the world up to the limit of the elements, the subtlety of their knowledge is known precisely from the reason previously mentioned.'"

"Without parts" (*akalam*) means devoid of parts (*kalā*). "Parts" refers to specific features such as the arrangement of cities and so forth, which are associated with the *hāva* and *āvṛta* [manifestations] and are enjoyed by multiple Rudras; it is devoid of those. Here, no eternal cities are seen anywhere, nor their arrangements, nor the state of being an object of enjoyment.

If it is objected that, since there is no distinction there, the scriptural statement—"the eight Lords of the Mandala are situated in order within the Māyā which establishes the location of the Lords of the Mandala"—is untenable, we reply:
No. Because Māyā is of the nature of power (*śakti*), worlds (*bhuvana*) cannot exist therein; thus, their residence there is impossible.

This is because the scriptural statements regarding their residence there are justified through metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to those who reside at the summit located in the same space and time as that [Māyā].
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra* (13.3):
"Even within Māyā, the presiding lords such as Gahaneśa and others are recited."
"And the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi) occurs in initiation; all that is at the head of its [the initiation's] performance.
Thus, his lordship consists in presiding over the womb of Māyā, but it is not a lordship over fixed worlds as is the case with the lords of the five or eight [worlds]. This is the point.
The intention here is that the term "metaphorical designation" (*upacāra*) is employed in order to make this known.

It is subtle (*sūkṣma*); it is not gross (*sthūla*). The meaning is that, unlike the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, it is not gross. Furthermore, it is precisely this [reality] that is subtle because it is the ground where the gradations of subtlety come to rest. Likewise, in the *Pauṣkara*:

The subtle elements (tanmātras) belong to earth and the other gross elements; from these arises the ego (ahaṅkāra). Subtler than that is the intellect (buddhi), and subtler still is primordial nature (prakṛti) itself.
"And the group beginning with *kalā* belongs to that [Māyā]; Māyā is subtler than that.
That wherein the ultimate limit of subtlety is reached is designated as 'Māyā'.
The subtlety of this [Māyā] is intended to be like that of the inner lining of a hidden cloth or the interior of a pot; it is not, however—
It is the state of being entirely free from modification. As stated in the *Mṛgendra* (9.21):

"Just as a cloth or similar object hidden by a mat or other covering is not manifested by the removal of that [covering]—since it was not previously non-existent—so too is the knot [of karma] removed by the *kalās*. Thus.

Because it is the ultimate cause, it is beginningless; and that which is beginningless does not undergo transformation in its entirety. Rather, from that which exists in the form of power (*śakti*), manifestation arises and attains visibility through a single part consisting of *māyā*.

For those for whom the seed of the universe transforms in its entirety, that [seed] would be impermanent; thus, by the term "beginningless" (anādi), the proof of partial transformation is established. This being so, in this system, the state of being an effect is not through a mode of existence (*vṛttitayā*) like that of a cloth or a hut, because it is impossible for the nature of a hut to exist when it is in the state of a cloth. Nor is it like curd, as held by the Sāṃkhyas.

It is not by way of transformation (*pariṇāma*) according to the analogy of milk, because if that were the case, it would follow that the material cause (*upādāna*) is destroyed in its entirety, just as the milk is destroyed. For this very reason, it is not like the Buddhist analogy of the seed and the sprout, since even there the seed is destroyed in its entirety. Nor is it by way of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) according to the analogy of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, as held by the proponents of *māyā*.

Otherwise, it would follow that the effect is unreal. Therefore, in this system, the status of being an effect is established solely through partial transformation, according to the analogy of the ghee-worm. As it has been said:
"The modification of the Bindu, Māyā, and Pradhāna is like that of the ghee-worm."
In the *Siddhāntadīpikā*:
"Impelled by the will of Śiva and further agitated by Nandanātha,
it undergoes transformation through a portion [of its essence], according to the analogy of the ghee-worm."
"The kalās and other principles, whose essence is power (śakti), attain a gross form.
There is no existence for the non-existent, nor is there non-existence for the existent.
Herein, the effects such as the body and the senses [dissolve] into their material causes, such as the *bindu*, during the process of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*).

Abiding in the form of power (*śakti*), they become manifest again for the purpose of bondage during creation. Thus, it is said in the *Mṛgendra* (9.13): "At the time of withdrawal, the effects, which have that [power] as their support, exist in the form of power."

"In the transformation, the forms of manifestation function for the accomplishment of the purpose. Thus, it is "indestructible" (*avyaya*); that is, its powers of transformation do not go to destruction or ruin, meaning it is devoid of the exhaustion of its powers. By the word "indestructible," its distinction from those who maintain the theory of non-existent effects (*asatkāryavāda*) is established here.

This has been indicated; for it is stated in the *Mokṣakārikās* that because it is possible for them to produce specific effects, [the primordial matter] possesses "lordship" (*īśvaratva*)—just like Īśvara—by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of all transformations, filling [them], and accomplishing the goals of the person (*puruṣārtha*). || 26 ||
Although this principle of Māyā is one, its capacity to produce effects of manifold forms and its dependence upon auxiliary factors are established by the *Mṛgendrasūtra* (9.2):
"That single, non-auspicious seed of the universe possesses variegated powers."
It is co-existent with its auxiliaries, persists until the end of its term of office, is all-pervading, and is imperishable. || 27 ||
That principle of Māyā is one; it is non-auspicious (aśiva) and impure because it causes delusion. It is the seed of the world.

"Possessing manifold powers" means that its powers are manifold—that is, variegated and diverse. Thus, although it is one, there is no contradiction in its producing diverse effects due to the multiplicity of its powers. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, what is obstructed by the section concerning the auxiliary (sahakāryadhikāra)? The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). By this, it is stated that karma is the auxiliary, because in the absence of karma, the principle of the knot (*granthitattva*) does not function. "Pervasive" (*vyāpi*) and "imperishable" (*anaśvara*)—these two words have already been explained previously. Here, regarding the qualifiers such as "oneness" (*ekatva*) and so forth:

Furthermore, there is no tautology, because [the term] is used specifically to indicate that it coexists with two qualifying forms: possessing diverse powers (*vicitraśaktimat*) and obstructing the final stage of the auxiliary factors (*sahakāryadhikārāntasaṃrodhi*). The nature of this *māyātattva* has also been stated by the Teachers:
That which is called Māyā is encompassed by manifold powers, partless, the sole seed of the path of darkness (kṛṣṇavartman),
eternally obstructing other actions, residing within its own effects, pervading those effects,
[unmanifest] due to its nature as an effect, producing the tenfold [world], and delusive during the time of sleep.
And that very self of sentient beings is thus the supreme, pure, awakening cause. Thus [it is said]. (27)
Now, by means of half a verse from the *Kiraṇatantra*, he demonstrates the distinction between the presiding efficient cause—the two Māyās, which are the pure and impure material causes—[as follows]:
"Śiva is declared to be the agent in the pure path; the Lord Ananta is the agent in the dark [impure] path. (28)

Śiva, the pure Supreme Lord, is declared to be the agent and the efficient cause within the pure path—which is devoid of impurity and consists of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and mantras such as *vidyā* and the lords of mantras (*mantreśa*). The meaning is that He is the creator of all that is produced by Him, including the principles, worlds, and so forth. Ananta [is the first of these].
The group beginning with Ananta is said to be the Lord—the agent of creation and so forth—within the dark [path] consisting of impure *māyā*;
this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*). Here, the agency of Ananta and the others is intended to exist solely through the impulsion of Īśvara.
As it has been stated in this very same work:
"The Lord impels the individual souls (aṇu) who are the lords of the lower sciences;
as soon as they are impelled by Him, they create the lower world. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the Kailāsasaṃhitā:
"Ananta is the agitator of Māyā through his union with Maheśvara.
If it is argued that, in this way, Śiva’s status as the creator of all would not be tenable, we say: no; [it is like the case of] an intimate minister—

For a king who performs the duties of the priest and other constituent elements himself, his ministers and others act as his external self; similarly, there is no contradiction in Śiva’s being the universal agent, for while he performs Ananta and the others himself, they act as his external agents through his impulsion. As it has been said in this very work:

It is called *sahakāryadhikārāntasaṃrodhi* because its nature is to obstruct the auxiliary karmas until the end of their period of authority (*adhikāra*), thereby binding the individual souls (*aṇu*). The meaning is that in the absence of such karmas, the principle of *māyā* does not function.
"Just as one appointed by the Lord of the Earth becomes a sovereign over all,
so too does he perform everything, awakened by His power.
Here, [the text refers] specifically to the principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *pradhāna*, belonging to Ananta who is impelled by Śiva.

The agency [belongs to Śrīkaṇṭha]. The agency over the principles (tattvas) beginning with Guṇa and ending with Earth belongs exclusively to Śrīkaṇṭha, who is impelled by Ananta. However, the distinction is that the agency for the material creation belongs to Brahmā, who is impelled by Śrīkaṇṭha.
As it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"The agitator here is the one of great splendor, Śrīkaṇṭha, of infinite prowess;

O Supreme Lord, he becomes fully developed merely through contact with Power, from whom arises the entire collection of principles beginning with the Guṇas and ending with the Earth. (Pauṣkara 6.30, 6.31, 6.18)
In the Śrīmataṅga it is said:
"In the beginning, the Lord of Beings created bodies for the stability of all beings; he then fashioned gross bodies distinguished by those [subtle elements]. (Mataṅgapārameśvara 19.2–4)
Likewise, in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"Those Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), beginning with Ananteśa, whose power was thus kindled and who were capable of exercising sovereignty over all, came into being through the will of the Cause."
Other than them are those of immeasurable power, and other than them are the appointed officials;
they are pure-souled beings who bestow both white and black fruits.
"From them also, others possessing *añjana* were born who followed the will of their lords, from whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings was produced. (28)
Thus, by means of the *Mṛgendra-sūtra* (10.1), he demonstrates the impure forms that are the effects of the infinite *māyā-tattva*:
"The knot, *kalā*, time, *vidyā*, passion, the individual soul (*nṛ*), and the *mātṛ*s."
The qualities, intellect, ego, mind, and the senses arise in succession from the unmanifest. || 29 ||

The effects produced—both directly and indirectly—from the *granthi* of *māyā*, which is eternally agitated, follow a sequence according to their respective fitness. As stated in the *Śrīmataṅga* (Kalātattvapaṭala, verse 2):
"When the knot consisting of *māyā* is agitated by Anantanātha..."
Then, by means of its own transformation, it makes the vast world manifest.

Herein is the sequence of origination: first, from the principle of Māyā, there arise four principles—the two principles named Kalā and Niyati, which constitute the referents of the word "Kalā"; the principle of Kāla; and that specific principle which is the cause of the masculine suffix for the person (pums) denoted by the word "nṛ."

There is the direct manifestation of the *tattvas*. From the *kalā-tattva*, however, there is the manifestation of three *tattvas*: the *vidyā-tattva* and the *rāga-tattva*, as well as the *pradhāna-tattva*, which constitutes the referent of the word "mother" (*mātṛ*).
From the *pradhāna-tattva*, agitated by Śrīkaṇṭha, [there arises] the referents of the word "qualities" (*guṇa*).

There is the manifestation of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. From these, there is the manifestation of the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), which is the referent of the term "intellect. And from the principle of intellect, there is the manifestation of the principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva)—denoted by the term "pride"—which is threefold, consisting of the forms known as taijasa, vaikārika, and bhūtādi.

From the *taijasa* ego arises the mind—designated by the term "citta"—as well as the organs of cognition, which are designated by the term "akṣara. From the *vaikārika* ego arises the production of the organs of action. And from the ego designated by the term "bhūtādi" [arises the subtle elements].

The emergence of the principles (tattvas) known as the *tanmātras* designated by the word "measure" (*mātrā*) occurs; from those *tanmātras*, the production of the five elemental principles (*bhūta-tattva*) follows. In this sequential order, these thirty-one principles [arise] directly and indirectly from the principle of the knot (*granthi-tattva*) through Ananteśa and the others.
"Manifested" means that because there are many traditional views (*saṃmatayaḥ*) on this point, they have not been written down here.

Of this impure path (*adhvan*), the pure fivefold aggregate (*pañcaskandha*)—consisting of Paraśakti, Nāda, Bindu, Sadāśiva, and Vidyā—is established as all-pervasive. Among these, the supreme cause is...

The subtle *nāda*, whose form is the Great Illusion (*mahāmāyā*), pervades the *kalā*. The gross *nāda*, endowed with the five *kalās* beginning with *indhikā*, pervades the principles (*tattvas*) consisting of Time (*kāla*), Necessity (*niyati*), Knowledge (*vidyā*), Attachment (*rāga*), and the Person (*puruṣa*).
The *bindu*, accompanied by the four *kalās* beginning with *nivṛtti*, [pervades] the four knots, primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and the qualities (*guṇas*).

It pervades the principles of intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Within this, the principle of ego, together with the mind, pervades the ten instruments consisting of the organs of perception and the organs of action. The principle of intellect, situated within that *bindu*, [pervades] the states such as merit and demerit, their material causes, and the cognitive factors.

Sadāśivanātha pervades [the gross elements]. Having assumed the body of the five mantras, beginning with Sadyojāta, as the presiding deities over the pentad of subtle elements starting from earth, he pervades that pentad of subtle elements. The Mantreśvaras, however, pervade the specific elements that constitute the subtle body. As for the Mantras:

They pervade the gross earth and the other elements. Thus, there are five aggregates (*skandhas*): first, the aggregate of knowledge (*vidyā-skandha*), which consists of both knowledge and ignorance; second, the aggregate of Sadāśiva; third, the aggregate of Bindu; fourth, the aggregate of Nāda; and fifth, the aggregate of Kāraṇa. This is the fivefold aggregate.
It should be understood as "the pure path" (*śuddhādhvan*). Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra* (13.196–198, 195):
"O Sage! Sound (*nāda*) is subtle within the pair consisting of *kalā*, *kāla*, and *rāga*, together with *puruṣa*. The gross sound consists of five *kalās* and rests upon the five *tattvas*."

The treasure of the four knots, beginning with Pradhāna, consists of the Bindu and the four Kalās; within the Ego (garva) reside the gods headed by Manas, and within the Intellect (buddhi) reside Bhāva and the others.
The Lord, whose body consists of the five mantras, resides in the pentad of the subtle elements (tanmātras);
the Lords of Mantra reside in the subtle elements, while the Mantras are established in the gross elements.
"Vidyā, the body of five atoms, the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and then the cause;
the supreme path consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Thus, because this constitutes the "impelling section," its pervasion over the "enjoyed" and "enjoyer" sections is logical.
In the Acintya [Kalpa], there is the impure section of objects (*bhogyakāṇḍaka*) consisting of twenty-four principles;
following that is the mixed reality (*miśratattva*), which is the sevenfold section of subjects (*bhoktṛkāṇḍa*).
The pure principle (śuddhatattva) is the impeller, and it is independent of Śiva.

The section concerning the impellers is pure; because it consists of the five principles beginning with Nāda and because it impels Vaikharī and the others, those who dwell in its worlds possess omniscience.

Because it is the cause for uprooting the state of being a universal agent, and because its nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) as well as its activity is that of consciousness (*cid-rūpa-kāritā*), [it is so described].

Herein, the mode of impulsion is the subtle function called *nāda* (sound); the *paśyantī* function is *bindu* (the point); the *madhyamā* function is *akṣara* (the syllable); and the *vaikharī* function is called *mātṛkā* (the mother-letters). And that *vaikharī* is of two kinds:

[These are] those perceivable by one's own hearing and those perceivable by another's hearing. These *vṛttis* are connected, respectively, to the five principles beginning with Śiva. Their locations, in order, are the five: the bladder, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the mouth. As it is said in the *Siddhāntarahasyasāra*:

During the time of experience for human beings, there occurs the accompaniment of the organ of speech by the five principles beginning with *vidyā*, as well as the distinctions such as *vaikharī* and the others.
The subtle sound (nāda) becomes the point (bindu); Paśyantī is the intermediate (madhyamā) syllable;
Mātṛkā is to be known as Vaikharī; and Nāda and the others are Śiva and the rest.
Vaikharī resides in the *īśvarī-tattva* at the throat and lips;
Sūkṣmā and the others are situated in the bladder, the navel, the heart, the neck, and the mouth.
Vaikharī reaches the ears of others; Madhyamā, which resides in the throat and lips, possesses conceptual thought (savikalpa); and Paśyantī is endowed with non-conceptuality (nirvikalpa).
The subtle [form] among these is the cause; that is called the *brahmaghoṣa*.

It is the *bhoktṛkāṇḍa* (the section of the enjoyer), which is both pure and impure. It is pure because it serves as the cause for strengthening the limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) and other qualities of those residing therein who are veiled by *puruṣamala*. It is impure because its activity consists of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
The category of the object of enjoyment (*bhogyakāṇḍa*); from that indeed [proceeds] the mixed reality (*miśratattva*), while the category of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛkāṇḍa*) consists of seven [levels].
The impelling pure reality (*śuddhatattva*) is, however, the independent sovereignty of Śiva.
"Likewise, there are the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller; these three are to be contemplated.

Herein, the section concerning the Impeller (preraka-kāṇḍa) is pure, because it is the impeller of Vākvarī and the others through the five [powers] beginning with Nāda, and because those who dwell in its world possess omniscience and omnipotence.

And because it is free from suffering and the like. The *bhoktṛkāṇḍa* (the section concerning the enjoyer) is both pure and impure; for those dwelling therein, there is purity due to being partially omniscient, and impurity due to the connection with suffering and the like.

The *bhogyakāṇḍa* (the section concerning the object of enjoyment) is entirely impure, because those dwelling therein are always only partially knowledgeable [of reality] and [subject to] suffering and the like.
And because it is logical: "The impure consists of twenty-four, the pure-impure sevenfold, and the eternally pure; these five constitute the nature of the thirty-six principles. (29)
Thus, immediately after the characteristics of the noose of *māyā*, he defines the fifth noose, which is the form of *karman* (action), by means of the *Viśvasārottara-sūtra*:
"Action consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and it is threefold in its essential nature."
By which [karma] birth, lifespan, and experience are bestowed, and which never ripens in isolation. (30)

Action (*karman*) consists of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); "merit and demerit" (*dharmādharmau*) refers to those two, and that which has them as its essence or nature is "consisting of merit and demerit. Furthermore, that action is threefold—that is, of three types—in terms of its actual result (*phala*). He states this very point: "it bestows birth, lifespan, and experience. Birth (*jāti*) refers to [rebirth as] a deity and so forth; lifespan (*āyuḥ*)...

"Living for even a hundred years," and so forth. "Experience" (*bhoga*) refers to the experiencing of pleasure and pain. That which gives these is called "that which bestows birth, lifespan, and experience" (*jātyāyurbhogadam*). For that reason—meaning, by virtue of that cause—it yields a threefold fruit: namely, that which bestows birth, that which bestows lifespan, and that which bestows experience. Likewise, in the *Yoga-sūtra* of Patañjali:

"When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. These factors—birth and the rest—are also threefold, according to the sequence of superior and so forth. Thus, it is stated in the venerable *Maṭaṅga* (Chapter on the Determination of Dharma and Adharma, verses 6–8):
"Due to the distinction of caste, the distinction of form, and the distinction of valor and knowledge..."
And it is also characterized by the distinction between good fortune and misfortune.
Thus, according to the distinction between middling-superior enjoyment and even the lowest,
there are those that are inferior and most inferior, as well as those that are excellent and most excellent.
"Regarding the divisions among animals, it is now stated:

'And that threefold karma, unmixed and devoid of mutual connection, is not ripened—that is, it is not made ripe—at any place whatsoever. The meaning of the word *pāka* (ripening) is the granting of results."

Because it bestows birth, lifespan, and experience, it is stated that the accomplishment of the quality of vision (*dṛk-guṇa*) and karma occurs by way of being the cause of those various, perishable, and individually determined factors— pertaining even to those residing in that [particular] place— as well as the respective classes, bodies, senses, and objects existing in other states of existence.
Because qualities that are impossible in the cause are not perceived in the effects. As stated in the *Mṛgendra* (8.2):

"Because it resides in specific locations, because of its diversity, because of its momentariness, because it is restricted to each individual soul, and because it is continuous, it possesses those qualities."
The diversity of species is well known. As for the diversity of sense organs:
for example, elephants and others have tongues that can be turned back; serpents have eyes on their ears;
owls do not see in the light; and among humans, some possess large eyes.
Non-perception [is seen] even among those who are like the blind, yet they possess the capacity to perceive subtle objects. As for the diversity of objects:
for example, the cātakas and peacocks subsist on drops of water fallen from the clouds;
whereas chickens and other such birds feed on refuse. "Refuse" (avakara) is the same as "scattered waste" (saṃkara), and "scattered waste" is likewise "refuse."
Thus says Amara. The tasting of the nectar of lotus filaments by bees and cranes, and so forth, is to be understood.
Now, with two and a half verses beginning with the "Lion-King" aphorism (8.3–4), he also states the specific distinctions of action:
Because it is produced by the activity of karma and exists in a subtle state, the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) is the generator,
the sustainer, and the object of experience, possessing the three internal means beginning with the self (adhyātma).

Because it is produced by an operation—that which is produced by an operation is "operation-produced" (vyāpāra-janya); the state of being such is "the fact of being operation-produced" (tattvam), and for that reason [it is called *adṛṣṭa*]. An action (*karma*) is that which is performed; it is "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*) because it is not seen due to its subtlety—the state of being subtle is "subtlety" (*saukṣmyam*), and from that subtlety it is not perceived.

The meaning is that it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Likewise, in the *Mataṅga* (Vidyātattvapaṭala, verses 61–62): "In the world as well, it is well known that the karma of those who perform actions is of two kinds:
that which culminates in action (*kriyāvasānika*) and that which is unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), [the latter] being destroyed therein."

It is the cause (*janaka*) by way of being the instrumental condition (*nimitta*) for the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth; for it is from this [cause] that the production of the respective connection with bodies, organs, and the like occurs solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma. It is the sustainer (*dhāraka*) by virtue of bestowing that very [experience] at its specific time. And it is the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) by means of those fruits. Furthermore, it is the threefold instrument consisting of the internal self (*adhyātma*) and so forth.
That which possesses the three means of accomplishment, beginning with the internal (adhyātma), is described as such.

Therein, by the term "internal" (adhyātma), that which operates with reference to the self (ātman) through the contact of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is called "cognition" (mati). By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), speech and bodily actions are also included. And thus, the mind...

That whose means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are speech and bodily action consists, respectively, of activities of a virtuous nature (*dharmātmaka*), such as meditating upon the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), prostration, reciting hymns of praise, and performing sacrifices; [as well as] the desire to seize the property of others.

That which has as its means the actions of mind, speech, and body—namely, false speech regarding that [object], its destruction, and so forth, respectively—is unrighteous action (*adharmātmaka-karma*). As it is said in the *Acintya*:
"Merit and demerit arise from those actions of mind, speech, and body."
They say that the action of the mind belongs to the person due to the dependence of the mind upon him.
The teaching of truth and knowledge, as well as what is pleasant, unpleasant, or otherwise;
that which is impermanent, delighting in ignorance—this is called the action of speech.
Furthermore, one who is devoted to giving and non-violence, yet practices violence and is under the sway of liquor [is likewise described].
"Attachment to, delight in, and so forth regarding sense objects is declared to be physical.

Alternatively, with reference to the three—namely the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva)—as causes, there arises pleasure and pain; of that [pleasure and pain]...

The means for all three types [of suffering] are as follows: internal (ādhyātmika) pleasure and pain arise through the power of karma, manifesting as mental clarity, agitation, and so forth; external (ādhibhautika) suffering takes the form of the enjoyment of women or being oppressed by elephants, lions, and the like; and superhuman (ādhidaivika) suffering consists of [the encounter with] desired and undesired [divine forces].
[It is] caused by rain, heat, and so forth. Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*:

"One encounters three kinds of suffering—namely, that pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*), that pertaining to external objects (*adhibhautika*), and that pertaining to the divine (*ādhidaivika*). Listen now to [the description of] the internal among them."
Internal [disease] is said to be twofold: physical and likewise mental;
it manifests in many ways, such as abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids (arśas), dysentery (atisāra), fever, and various types of colic (śūla).
O observer of noble vows! The bodily suffering has been described by humans, deer, piśācas, cattle, yakṣas, thieves, and rākṣasas; now hear about the mental suffering.
Furthermore, by means of grief, envy, contempt, jealousy, avarice, and so forth,
that which is thus described as mental is called the affliction caused by other beings (ādhibhautika).

The suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning, thunderbolts, and storms—by these elemental forces—is called *ādhibhautika* (suffering caused by beings). *Ādhidaivika* (suffering caused by divine or supernatural factors) is that which arises from these [natural] elements.
"Thus, the threefold suffering arising from conception, birth, old age, ignorance, death, and hell has been described; indeed, it is experienced in these very states. (31)

Because it originates from both truth and falsehood, that [subtle body], which consists of the nature of dharma and adharma, undergoes its fruition during sleep; it is then employed in the process of creation.
And it persists within illusion until the end; moreover, that which has not been experienced does not go to destruction.

That action, because it has truth and untruth as its source (*satyānṛta-yonitvāt*), consists of truth and untruth (*satyānṛte*). The state of having those two as its source—that is, its material cause—is its essential nature; therefore, it has the form of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). The meaning is that action whose material cause is truth is of the nature of merit, while action whose material cause is untruth is of the nature of demerit. Such [action]...

At the time of the dissolution of all beings during the sleep of karma, that karma—which has reached its maturation and transformation—attains its full development on all sides. Such karma, having ripened in accordance with its own fruition, becomes operative at the time of creation; immediately after creation, it functions according to its appropriate nature.
The meaning is that experience proceeds from *kalā* down to the earth (*kṣiti*). This has been stated in this very [text]:
"Thus, beginning with *māyā* and ending with *kāla*, it is without beginning and is the impeller" (Mṛgendra-tantra 8.6).
And at the end, at the time of dissolution, it abides within *māyā*, that is, within the *māyā*-principle; it burns away that which produces birth.
(§14) Action performed through mind, speech, and body is called "gross action. By this, the threefold nature of action is stated.
Likewise, in the *Siddhāntasārāvalī*:
"Action, which is accomplished by means of speech, intellect, and body, and which produces results to be experienced as merit (*dharma*) and so forth [or demerit], is [the subject]."
And during sleep, it reaches maturation together with the state of persistence; until the end of the *kalā*, it bestows experience. Thus [it is said].
In the Śivadharmottara it is said: "The divisions of dharma and adharma are to be understood through the various modifications of the mind;
they are gross, subtle, and extremely subtle, manifold in their many millions of divisions."
"Unexperienced" means that which has not been experienced; such unexperienced karma does not undergo exhaustion or destruction.
This is likewise stated in the Pauṣkara:
"Karma that has not been experienced is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas."
"By the word 'and' (ca), it should be understood that [the bondage] is perishable even when there is no destroyer such as initiation (dīkṣā) or knowledge (jñāna),
or when there is expiation (prāyaścitta), or through experience (bhoga), either simultaneously or sequentially.
Thus [it is said].
Thus, these five—impurity (*mala*), the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*), great illusion (*mahāmāyā*), illusion (*māyā*), and karma—have been described in sequence;
all five are well known in this scripture as the "fivefold bond" (*pāśapañcaka*) because they bind the person (*puruṣa*).
As it is heard:
"Impurity, action, the entire universe arising from Great Māyā and Māyā, and the power that effects concealment—these five categories constitute the fetter. (32–33)

Having thus described the nature of the fetters (pāśas) through fourteen verses, he now demonstrates, by means of a *Svāyambhuva-sūtra*, the nature of the three states of the bound soul (*paśu*) which are dependent upon them: "Now, the self is impure, bound, and again liberated through initiation."
He is to be known as existing in three states: the solitary (kevala), the manifest (sakala), and the stainless (amala).

Here, by the word *ātman*—derived from the verbal root *at*, meaning "to go continuously"—the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is denoted. That self exists in three states, being endowed with three conditions: as *kevala* (isolated), *sakala* (with parts), and *vimala* (pure). "Impure" (*avimala*) means not being pure; that is to say, it is extremely defiled. This [self], however, is in the state of isolation (*kevalāvastha*).
Bound—meaning bound by the fetters of *kalā* and so forth, being attached to karma—this [state] is the condition of the *sakala* (the embodied).

Furthermore, liberated by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*), that is, by the practice known as initiation, he is freed from the bondage of *kalā* and the rest. This should be understood and known as "stainless" (*amala*), the pure state. Thus it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
"The person is said to exist in three states: the pure (śuddha), the conditioned (sakala), and the isolated (kevala).
The state of the self as pure is traditionally known as the form of Śiva. (34)

In the preceding [verse], it was stated that [the Lord] is "purely absolute" (*kevala*), "with parts" (*sakala*), and "immaculate" (*amala*). Since the purely absolute was mentioned first therein, the author now demonstrates the nature of the purely absolute first, by means of another aphorism:

The individual soul (paśu) is insentient, all-pervading, eternal, devoid of qualities, inactive, powerless, subject to obstruction, incapable [of independent action], to be purified, to be awakened, and partless. || 35 ||

Here, "insentient" (acetana) means devoid of consciousness; its insentiency implies that the pure primordial nature (prakṛti) lacks the consciousness of the Self, which consists of knowledge and action. However, in this context, only knowledge is intended, because action will be negated later. And that consciousness, being completely obstructed by impurity (mala), does not function toward objects for the sake of another.

Thus, the meaning is that [the soul] is insentient (*acetana*). However, it is not insentient like a clod of earth, because scripture declares the manifestation of its sentience during the state of experience; for there can be no manifestation of what is non-existent, since manifestation belongs only to that which already exists.
Here, sentience manifests precisely as having the nature of the appearance of the objects of enjoyment; but it is not...

It is also of the nature of self-existence (*svabhāva*), because for it there is no possibility of obstruction by impurity (*mala*); this is due to its being eternal, all-pervasive, and having the nature of self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotis*). This has been explained in detail in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-bṛhaṭṭīkā*.
If this is so, why does it not manifest even prior to the manifestation of objects? Why?

Does he say this? However, because its nature consists of being illuminated by another, in the absence of that external illumination—as in the state of deep sleep—it is like something non-existent, for it is impossible to function while remaining fixed merely in its own inactive essence. But upon the manifestation of omniscience and other qualities, [it attains... its full realization.
The expansion of the activity of consciousness (*cit-kriyā*) indeed shines forth because it illuminates all objects.
If this is so, since its own nature—which is self-luminous—is unobscured, what could obstruct its cognition regarding objects? [If you argue: "It is like a person whose eyes are in thick darkness."
True. That cognition of an object is indeed its very own nature (*svarūpa*); and because that [nature] is veiled, there is no fault.

It is all-pervading (*vibhu*), meaning it is omnipresent. It is omnipresent because wherever there is a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*) such as the body or the senses, there this consciousness is manifested. It is eternal (*nitya*), meaning it is devoid of origination.

Although that which is distinguished by its states is impermanent, this [Self] is eternal because it lacks that impermanence consisting in being produced by its own causes. "Devoid of qualities" (guṇahīna): for the sake of accomplishing experience, its limbs—such as the *kalās* and other qualities—are its attributes; devoid of those, it is "devoid of qualities. It is inactive (*akriya*).

It is devoid of action (*kriyā*). Action is the operation of an instrument (*karaṇa-vyāpāra*); this is not possible for the Self (*ātman*), because action is non-self (*anātma*) by nature and is a property of insentient objects (*jaḍa-vastu-dharma*). Therefore, since its capacity for action has been obstructed, it lacks agency (*kartṛtva*), which is the power to perform that action; thus, it is "actionless" (*akriya*). It is "not a lord" (*aprabhu*), [lacking] lordship (*prabhutva*).

Sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is the mastery over all causal factors (*kāraka*); since that [mastery] is blocked by impurity (*mala*), he is "without lordship" (*aprabhu*). Nor is there redundancy with [the term] "inactive" (*akriya*); for there is a distinction possible between the negation of independent agency (*svatantra-kartṛtva*) in that case (a), and the negation of instrumental agency (*hetu-kartṛtva*) here (b). [The phrase] "possessing contradiction" refers to Śiva’s power (*śiva-śakti*).

*Vyāghāta* means obstruction or concealment; that which possesses this is *vyāghātabhāk*. "Incapable" (*aśakta*) means that, because it is itself blocked by impurity (*mala*), it is unable to direct the senses toward their objects. "To be purified" (*śodhya*) means that even in this state, [the soul] is to be purified from impurity by Śiva. "To be awakened" (*bodhya*) means [to be awakened] from impurity.

Having had the network of powers (śakti-jāla) folded into a bud, one must cause that network of powers to blossom. To the question "Who is explained in this way?", he says: "The Akala. He is called Akala because he is not overcome by the kalās and so forth. He is called Paśu because of his connection with the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) and because of possessing bonds (pāśavatva).

If it is asked, "How can contradictory attributes such as being subject to contradiction (*vyāghātabhāktva*) and being an object of purification (*śodhyatva*) coexist in a single Self?", we say: no, because there is no contradiction even between being subject to future development (*bhāvitva*) and being an object of purification. In this context, attributes such as omnipresence (*vibhutva*) are not intended to be described in reference to the state of absolute isolation (*kevalāvasthā*); [for] omnipresence—

Because both permanence and [the state of being] liberated are possible even for the *mukta* (liberated one), and because both the state of being purified (*śodhyatva*) and the state of being to be known (*bodhyatva*) are possible even for one in the *sakala* (embodied) stage; therefore, pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) and other qualities are mentioned here as qualifiers. And in the *Suprabheda*, the nature of the state of the *kevala* (isolated/individual soul) is stated as follows: [The text continues with the specific description of the *kevala* state.]
That soul is formless, eternal, devoid of qualities, inactive, and powerless;
though all-pervading, it has entered the belly of Māyā and is incapable of the means for enjoyment.
He is called "the solitary" (kevala), yet he possesses sleep due to the bondage of impurity.

One might object that this alternative state of the self must be said to depend on impurity (*mala*), yet that is not possible because impurity is as non-existent as a hare’s horn; anticipating this doubt, he establishes [the point] by means of another aphorism:
"If impurity does not belong to the person (*pums*), then by what is attachment to enjoyments produced?"
O wise one, for a pure person, that experience of [suffering] is not logically possible. || 36 ||
If there is no impurity or stain in the person— the Puruṣa— then, in the absence of impurity,
by what cause is that attachment produced even in a pure person toward objects of enjoyment which are by nature impermanent, impure, and painful? For it cannot belong to one who is pure.

Attachment occurs in the impure for one who is stainless. If it is argued that since even the proponent of impurity admits passion (*rāga*), attachment should be attributed to passion alone and not to impurity, [the reply is: True. However, because passion, only when accompanied by impurity, produces the effect of attachment to the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth—and because a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) alone produces an effect—[impurity is necessary].
Because passion alone lacks the status of being a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). If that is so, let the mere habituation to enjoyment itself be the cause of attachment;
what is the use of "impurity" (*aśuddhi*)? As it has been said:
"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects."
"Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more.

(Manusmṛti 2.94). Therefore, he says: "When the person is pure. When the person (*pums*) is pure, the enjoyment of that [object] does not even occur; it is not logically tenable, so how much less its repeated practice? And why would there be attachment?

"O wise ones," "O learned ones"—this is an address to the sages (*ṛṣis*). The intended meaning is as follows: experience (*bhoga*) is indeed a manifestation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) in the form of cognition, produced by the senses; yet, because it is colored by impure objects, this [power], though essentially pure, lacks the manifestation of its purity due to its impurity. Therefore, its connection is with that which is truly pure alone.

It must be said: for the manifestation of power (*śaktivyakti*) in one who is pure and stainless is never seen to be impure, because of its absolute identity with Śiva. Therefore, since an eternal impurity (*anādyaśuddhi*) is necessary as the cause of attachment to enjoyment and as the constituent of impure experience, the determination of the self's states depends upon that [impurity].
It is not untenable. || 36 ||
Now, one might object: "The Self does not even possess consciousness, such that its cessation could account for the establishment of its different states.
Anticipating this doubt, he establishes that consciousness does indeed exist in the Self by means of two *Mṛgendra* sūtras (2.5):
That consciousness, which consists of the nature of seeing and acting, exists at all times and in every respect within this Self;
for it is heard that in liberation it is "all-facing" (omnipresent).
Even though it exists, because it does not manifest, it is perceived as ceased;
for one whose vigor is unobstructed, there is no liberation from the stream [of existence]. (38)
He says that [the soul] exists even without [the body], its range being revealed by knowledge:
"Is it not joined with the instruments such as the intellect, even when colored by passion? (39)
One whose field of experience (*gocara*) has been revealed as its fruit by knowledge (*vidyā*) is "one for whom the field is revealed by knowledge" (*vidyā-darśita-gocara*),
which is to say, one for whom it is the field through traditional succession (*paramparā*). In this context, because there is no direct intervention,
the objects of experience that are the fruits of the person— consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and colored by sound and so forth— are the "direct fields of experience" (*sākṣād-gocara*).

Sound and the other [objects] are the spheres of perception through a traditional succession. By this, it is shown that the assistance of *vidyā* pertains to the aspect of the Self's manifestation of objects. As stated in the *Mṛgendra* (10.10):
"By that [power], which is of the nature of light and which causes the power of knowledge to shine forth..."
"It understands the supreme object as something to be accomplished by all causal agents.
Now, one might object: "Even when the object is thus perceived, one does not proceed to grasp it without passion (*rāga*).
To this he says: "Even for one colored by passion. That is, colored by passion—that is, by the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*).

The meaning is that even that which consists of suffering and delusion is experienced as pleasure. Furthermore, the capacity to generate attachment belongs exclusively to the principle of *rāga* (passion), because for one who is free from passion, experience (*bhoga*) is impossible even with respect to an extremely attractive object. As it has been stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
"That which produces attachment toward an object of enjoyment is *rāga* (passion) in this system.

By this, the assistance provided by the principle of *rāga* (*rāgatattva*) regarding the aspect of the self's possession of attachment is shown. Thus, the person whose activity has been generated by these three principles [māyā, kalā, and rāga] once again [engages with] the object of enjoyment through the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*).

He says that [the Self] "accomplishes" by stating, "endowed with the instruments such as the intellect. This means it is endowed with, or accompanied by, the instruments beginning with the intellect; the word "becomes" is to be supplied. The meaning is this: through the act of filling, the primary matter (pradhāna) and its qualities (guṇas) provide assistance to the intellect and the other instruments; likewise do the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the gross elements (bhūtas).

Furthermore, time (*kāla*) and necessity (*niyati*) function as the causal factors for the activity [of the intellect] by way of being its substratum. For time indeed measures (*kalayati*) the person who has already entered into activity with units such as *tryuṭi* and so forth. Necessity likewise, producing attachment toward that very object where the fruit of karma resides, restricts the person who has already entered into activity to that specific result. As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
But because they lack omnipresence, the instruments (karaṇas) operate by presiding over their respective effects. Thus [ends the discussion of verses 37–39].

Thus, by means of another aphorism, he describes the locus of experience for the Self who has acquired objects of enjoyment: "In the path consisting of the principles (tattvas) and elements (bhūtas), beginning with Māyā and ending with the Earth. (19)
The commentary on the two previously mentioned *Mṛgendra* sūtras is not found in the manuscript;

furthermore, two quarters (*pāda*) of this particular sūtra are not seen at all. However, judging from the commentary, it may be inferred that these two quarters have been lost due to the negligence of a scribe. Therefore, here...
The two marked feet are established as the thread;
there, a man who is solely intent on enjoyment partakes of the enjoyments situated therein. (40)
"From Māyā down to the earth" (*māyādyavaniparyantam*) refers to that which begins with Māyā and ends with the earth;

this is an adjective qualifying "the path" (*vartmanaḥ*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality is not attributed to the object (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*), meaning "that of which Māyā is the first.
Thus, only [the principles] beginning with Kalā are included, but not Māyā itself; for there are no worlds (*bhuvana*) within it.

Because of the impossibility of enjoyment [in that state]. On the path of the principles (tattva), the elements (bhūta), and the selves (ātman)—that is, on the path consisting of the fivefold group of principles, elements, and selves.
Here, by the word "principle" (tattva), the worlds (bhuvana) of the principle are indicated through secondary figurative usage (lakṣaṇā). [The phrase] "arisen from time" (kaloccalita)...

Since "consciousness" (*caitanya*) has already been mentioned as the path to reality (*tattvavartman*), here the word "elements" (*bhūta*) refers— by means of a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) based on their connection with gross qualities—

to the worlds-born entities from *kalā* down to earth, which are the instruments of experience and constitute the gross bodies of the *bhuvana*-beings. The word "self" (*ātman*) is used because these [bodies] directly assist the self.

Just as in the expression "a hamlet on the Ganges," the suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used here by way of a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on extreme proximity; thus, the "series of states" (*bhāvapratyayasantāna*) is spoken of.
The "states" (*bhāva*) are the eight [perfections] beginning with *dharma*; the "conditions" (*pratyaya*) are the four beginning with *siddhi*.
The meaning is: "in the threefold path consisting of worlds (*bhuvana*), celestial abodes (*bhauvana*), bodies (*deha*), states (*bhāva*), and conditions (*pratyaya*)."
The meaning of the term *bhāva* (mental states) has been stated:

"Because they cause the *liṅga* (the subtle body) to become manifest (*bhāvayanti*), they are proclaimed as *bhāvas*; because they cause the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) to perceive [objects], they are remembered as *pratyayas* (cognitions). Thus it is said.

In this regard, although the person (*puruṣa*) stands upon all three paths as the enjoyer of that which is to be enjoyed, he experiences—that is, attains—objects of enjoyment. For this very reason, being forcibly impelled by the Lord toward experience, he sometimes experiences the enjoyment of a bound soul (*paśu*), even though he does not desire it. Likewise—
"Wherever and by whatever means one must experience the fruit of the good or evil karma one has performed, there one is led by force by destiny, as if bound with a rope.
Furthermore, he states that this person lacks even the desire for enjoyment: "one whose sole delight is in enjoyment," meaning in certain types of enjoyments.

"Rasa" refers to one whose desire is fixed upon that [object]. The meaning is that even while enjoying an impure object of enjoyment, he neither becomes dispassionate nor is he satisfied. By this, it is indicated that passion (*rāga*) has an operation even at the time of enjoyment.
Furthermore, since *vidyā* (knowledge) functions as an instrument, its operation in the accomplishment of enjoyment is already established for the agent.

Because activity toward an object is impossible without an instrument (*karaṇa*), and because activity toward an object is impossible for that which is distinct from knowledge (*vidyā*). This state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) has been stated in the *Matanga* [Tantra], even in the *Puṃpradhāneśvarasādhanapaṭala* (verse 104), with respect to all three paths: [The text continues: "In the *Matanga*, it is also said: 'Even though the Lord is omnipresent and possesses the power of action, he does not act without an instrument; therefore, he is endowed with instruments. "By means of the power [of consciousness] awakened by that [nature], it experiences the qualities born of nature.
And in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* as well:
"And this [self] wanders, by the force of karma, through all the bodies born of the world. (40)
Now, he provides the answer to the two questions—"What is experience? and "From what does experience arise?"—by means of another verse:
"Experience for this person consists of sensation characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth;
endowed with consciousness as established [by the self], the person undergoes that [sensation] through karma. (41)

The "experience" (bhoga) of this person—meaning this Puruṣa—is what is called sensation, consciousness, or apprehension. And that experience is characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), delusion is included. That which has pleasure and the rest as its characteristics is "characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth."

Because it is colored by objects such as pleasure and pain; the meaning is that enjoyment (*bhoga*) is of three kinds: the feeling of pleasure, the feeling of pain, and the feeling of delusion. Having stated the answer to the question regarding the essential nature of enjoyment, he provides the answer to the question regarding its cause with the word "that" (*tām*): "that," namely, the feeling which consists of enjoyment and is of these three kinds.

The person (pumān), the self (ātman), whose consciousness has been established and whose consciousness is manifested through its powers (kalā), attains—by means of action (karman), that is, under the influence of karma—that very karma which has ripened into the states of pleasure, pain, and delusion; the meaning is that this [ripened] karma alone becomes the objective support for the experience of the person. || 41 ||

The existence and non-existence of the body and so forth are also caused by karma; for, since it is impossible for karma to serve as a means of experience without a body and so forth, karma is logically established as their cause by virtue of projecting them. This he states in another sūtra:
And by virtue of karma, bodies, objects,
and organs come into being or cease to be for the enjoyer, in order to accomplish experience.
The bodies are the gross forms, the objects are sound and so forth, and the instruments are the intellect and so on—

all these arise and come into being for the sake of accomplishing the experience of the experiencer, the Puruṣa, as a means of enjoyment resulting from karma, that is, caused by karma; and they do not exist in the absence of that karma.

They neither exist nor are they born. Here, by the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that whatever object serves as a cause for any kind of experience whatsoever, all of that is *karman*. An illustration of this is as follows: the absence of snakes, thorns, and so forth is a cause for the experience of pleasure; the absence of sons, food, and so forth is a cause for the experience of suffering. [Suffering...]

The absence of garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, is the cause for the experience of delusion (*moha*); the presence of snakes, thorns, and so forth, is the cause for the experience of suffering (*duḥkha*); the presence of sons, food, and so forth, is the cause for the experience of pleasure (*sukha*); and the presence of garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, is the cause for the experience of both pleasure and delusion. In this regard, just as [the manifestation of] the body and so forth [occurs] through karma—

Likewise, since the body and other factors are also generators [of action]— because they generate karma— it should be understood that the continuum of karma and the body is beginningless in its flow, just like the continuum of the seed and the sprout. As it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Through action, however, bodies [are acquired]; from the existence [of latent dispositions], the emergence of action occurs.
The existence of previously accumulated actions is the cause of conjunction.
Thus it is said elsewhere.
"Constantly joined in pairs, mutually [dependent] like the seed of a banyan tree. Thus [it is said]. (42)

Thus, by means of another aphorism, he describes the supreme state of the bound soul (*baddhātman*), which is characterized merely by the perception of [limited] objects (*paśu*) and devoid of the vision of Śiva and the rest:
"In this way, the individual soul (*aṇu*), situated in the collyrium of *māyā*, is obscured by its own defects."
Delighted by those enjoyments born of illusion, he becomes absorbed in them. || 43 ||

In the sequence thus described, [the soul] is set in motion by *kalā*; "having been discerned by *vidyā* and refined by the intellect (*buddhi*) and the other faculties" is the meaning. "Situated in the collyrium of *māyā*"—by the term "collyrium of *māyā*," those principles (*tattva*s) which exist within *māyā* are intended; and these are *kalā* and the rest. (ga)

Due to its association with the self (*ātman*), although it resembles pure crystal, the subtle atom (*aṇu*) causes the self to appear as its own reflection—just like the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a hibiscus flower—and thus colors the self; these are called "colours" (*añjana*).
Because he abides among them and functions with an exceedingly charming intellect, he is "situated in the colour of *māyā*" (*māyāñjanastha*); such is the subtle atom.
The self (ātman) is obscured by its own inherent defect—that is, it is veiled by its innate impurity (mala).

The meaning is that, being constrained below and not looking upward toward Śiva and the other [levels], it remains in such a state. Being colored—meaning, being enamored—by those objects of enjoyment consisting of Māyā, it becomes attached to those enjoyments of Māyā.
It attains identity with that; it considers itself non-distinct from and inseparable from that.
The meaning is that it considers itself favored by the favor of that [object] and afflicted by its affliction.
Thus, these are the names appropriate for the bound self (*bandhātman*) in all its states.

He states this by means of another scripture: "The transmigrator, the subject of objects, the enjoyer, the knower of the field, and indeed the embodied one—this bound self is called 'sakala' (the differentiated) by the wise. (44)

"Bound by nature" (*bandhātmā*) means that whose very essence (*svarūpa*) consists of bondage. "With parts" (*sakala*) means existing together with the *kalās* and other [categories]. Such a one who is "with parts" is indeed the self (*ātman*); he is a "transmigrator" (*saṃsārī*) because he transmigrates through the taking up and casting off of bodies and so forth. He is an "object-possessor" (*viṣayī*) because the object (*viṣaya*) exists for him as something to be experienced.

One who possesses an object is a "possessor" (*viṣayin*). One who experiences enjoyment is an "enjoyer" (*bhoktā*). One who has a field (*kṣetra*)—that is, a locus for the manifestation of his own power—is a "field-possessor" (*kṣetrī*). One who knows the field—the net of bonds presented as an object of experience—is a "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*). His body serves as the abode for experience.

The meaning is that these designations— such as "it exists" and "the embodied one"— are spoken by the wise solely for the sake of scriptural convention, based upon their respective underlying causes. In the *Suprabheda*, however:
The self, when complete and enveloped, is bound by the three impurities;
thus, the "complete" one is the bound self, the transmigrator, and likewise the enjoyer of sense-objects.

"The field, the knower of the field, the enjoyer, the bound soul (paśu), likewise the wise one (jñānī), the experiencer (bhogī), and the embodied one (śarīrī)—these are synonyms for the self (ātman). Thus [ends verse 44].

Having thus described the Self in all its states, he now demonstrates, by means of two and a half verses of the *Mṛgendra-sūtra* (5.1), the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which is the primary cause for the pure state, in order to describe that pure state itself:
Upon the cessation of the dominion of the power of darkness (tamas) and its subsequent withdrawal, Śiva reveals the infinity of vision and action within the soul, who is the beloved of the world. 45.
*Tamaḥ-śakty-adhikāra* refers to the domain (*adhikāra*) of both *tamas* and *śakti*.

Of these two, *tamas* is the impurity (*mala*), and *śakti* is the power belonging to the Lord, namely the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*). Their *adhikāra* is their state of being occupied with the act of subduing [the soul].

This is the meaning of "tasya" (of that). From "nivṛtteḥ" (from cessation)—cessation being *virāma* (withdrawal)—due to that cause, upon its disappearance (*paricyutau*), there occurs the withdrawal of the power of vision (*darśana-śakteḥ*) due to its concealment; this withdrawal is the state of being oriented toward liberation (*kaivalya*).
When that [state] exists, Śiva is the kinsman of the world (*jagad-bandhuḥ*), the friend of the world, and one intent upon the upliftment of the world.

The Supreme Lord manifests—that is, makes evident—the infinity of vision and action (*dṛk-kriyānantya*) belonging to the atomic self; that is, He reveals the fullness of both vision and action. This occurs because, although vision and action are indeed eternal and infinite, their infinity is obscured by being delimited by impurity (*mala*); thus, through the maturation of that impurity, the obscuration is removed.

The meaning is that manifestation is brought about, not production as something previously non-existent. By this, it is stated that when karma is destroyed and the impurity has matured, the Lord’s grace-bestowing power descends upon the bound souls (paśus).
This is stated in the Pauṣkara:

"Upon the destruction of karma, even when the impurity (*mala*) is ready for its fruition, the power that brings about liberation (*unmīlanī-śakti*), which consists of grace (*anugraha*), descends. (Pauṣkarāgama 4.37).
Because the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is difficult to discern, [the author] shows the signs that indicate it (Mṛgendrāgama 5.4):
For those embodied beings whose power descends so as not to turn back,
their indicative mark is a longing for liberation and an aversion to existence.
Devotion toward the devotees of Śiva, and faith in the ritual prescribed by him. (47)
One who possesses a body is a "possessor of a body" (*śarīrin*); the power of those possessors of bodies is the supreme power of the Lord. "Non-return" (*avinivṛtti*) means not manifesting again;
[the soul] falls for the sake of non-return, that is, for the sake of not manifesting again. (Note: *ka* indicates a citation from the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, 2.14.30.)

In this context, since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is difficult to perceive in those who are bodiless, it is stated [by the teachers] that it pertains to "those who possess bodies. For those embodied beings, there is a longing (*autsukya*) for liberation (*mukti*), and a distaste (*dveṣa*)—that is, detachment (*vairāgya*)—for remaining in existence (*bhavasthiti*), which is to say, for abiding in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Śiva—

And devotion toward those devotees who are intent on devotion to Śiva; and [devotion] toward His teacher—that is, toward that teacher whose ruler is Śiva—meaning toward the *vidhi* (prescription), the scripture, namely the Śiva-āgamas. In that regard, faith is the sign (*liṅga*), the mark of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). By these signs, even those of dull intellect among embodied beings [can recognize it].
The intended meaning is that they infer the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). As it is stated in the *Śrīmatsvāyambhuva*:
"When that [impurity] has been exhausted, she [the power] may, through the intellect, lead toward supreme liberation."
He states this purpose of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) in the four verses of the *Matanga-sūtra* (4.45–49):
"And by that descent, even for such an ignorant person who possesses a longing [for liberation], an intellect arises spontaneously through discernment residing within the self. (48)

In this very manner, for the ignorant person— who possesses the conceit of self in what is not-self and is full of desire, that is, one whose nature is characterized by longing— even for such a person, through the falling away of that [power],
meaning due to the descent or removal of that power, there arises a discernment residing within the self, directed toward the self.

The meaning is: by means of such discrimination as "I am a conscious *puruṣa*, distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self, and who, while self-luminous, is dependent upon the Supreme Lord. The ellipsis is that [the intellect] is joined with that. The intellect—that is, the cognitive faculty—arises or is born without cause, i.e., spontaneously. In that regard:
The meaning is that there is no other cause apart from the descent of power (śaktipāta).
Thus, he describes the effect that arises immediately after discernment:
"In one who possesses discernment and is dispassionate, a desire to know arises;
and this consciousness, endowed with the desire to know, [delivers] the bound soul from the ocean of transmigratory existence. (49)
The Lord joins him with the desire to grasp [the object], and once joined, He impels him.

For the discerning one—endowed with the aforementioned discriminative intellect (*viveka-buddhi*) and possessing detachment (*virakta*), meaning one who has renunciation toward *saṃsāra*—there arises a desire to know (*jijñāsā*). This means that the desire for knowledge regarding the Lord (*Īśvara*) and the individual soul (*puruṣa*) is the primary cause for the cessation of *saṃsāra*. That [desire] comes into being.

He joins— that is, yokes— the individual soul (paśu), whose consciousness (caitanya) is endowed with the desire to know (jijñāsopeta), to the ocean of worldly existence (saṃsāra-sāgara)— for worldly existence itself is an ocean— from which He desires to rescue it, that is, from the wish to lift it out; [the subject is] the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān), as is understood from the context.
Furthermore, what does He do? To this he says: "The Lord impels this one who is joined. The meaning is that the Lord, the Supreme God, impels this bound soul (paśu) toward the Teacher (ācārya).
He states that it is indeed Īśvara who brings about the relationship between both the teacher and the disciple:
"The glorious King of Mantras is the impeller in the act of impelling both;
likewise, he is the one to be favored in the discipline of the recipient of grace, and the favorer of the one who bestows grace. (51)
However, because compassion is so rare in these two, their union is extremely difficult to find. (52)

— Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.48–49: The illustrious one, endowed with sovereignty such as omniscience and other qualities, the king of mantras, the leader of mantras, that Lord, regarding the act of impelling— that is, in the matter of instigation— is [the authority] for both of them, namely, for both the disciple and the teacher.

The Prompter says: He states the distinction regarding the aspect of prompting for those two with the words beginning "anvi" and so forth. Between these two—the disciple and the teacher—*anugrāhyasya* means of the one worthy of favor;
*vinaye* means in discipline, specifically the practice of service to the guru (*guru-śuśrūṣātmaka*). In that regard, the word "the prompter" is to be supplied by ellipsis. Likewise...

Regarding the compassion of the benefactor—that is, the teacher who performs the act of grace—the term *kāruṇya* is derived from *karuṇā* itself by means of the suffix *ṣyan* according to the rule beginning with *cāturvarṇya*. By the word *tu*, the connection is made that he is the impeller even toward the desire for grace; thus, Śiva alone is the impeller of both the one to be graced and the one who bestows grace.
The meaning is that he establishes a connection. He states the reason for this with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).

Because the union—that is, the connection—between those two, the disciple and the teacher, is very difficult to obtain and is impossible to accomplish without Īśvara, therefore Īśvara alone is the generator of that connection. Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
Detachment quickly arises from this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra,
and a longing to behold the lotus feet of Śambhu also arises.
"When shall I behold the Lord of Gods? When shall I be liberated from bondage? Who will show me Śambhu?"—such thoughts arise within him.
"Thus, if the Lord bestows grace upon one who is afraid of *saṃsāra*," so it is said (*Vijñānabhairava*, chapter 4, verses 39–41).

Now, how can there be a "falling down" (*nipāta*) of *śakti*, given that she is all-pervasive? For it is impossible for an all-pervasive reality to undergo a "falling down" characterized by movement; [it would be like] the heat of fire. Śiva—

Furthermore, because it is inherent [in Śiva], its falling away from Śiva is impossible. Moreover, since that eternal and all-pervading power resides in the souls of bound beings (paśus) at all times and in every way, there would follow the undesirable consequence of simultaneous liberation for all.
Nor can it be argued that this power bestows grace only at a specific particular time; for if that were so, [then...]

If it is asked, "In that case, since time itself would become the agent of liberation, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that Śiva has no purpose [in bestowing grace]; therefore, how can there be a 'descent of power' (śaktipāta)?", do not say so. The application of words is twofold: figurative (gauṇī) and primary (mukhyā). Here, the application of the word "pāta" (falling/descent) is figurative. As in common worldly usage:
When it is said, "His gaze has fallen upon this beloved woman," it is not observed that the gaze has actually departed from the man and fallen upon the woman;

rather, because of the mere relationship between the seer and the seen, it is figuratively expressed that "the gaze has fallen. Similarly, here too, in this [Supreme] Person, there exists the characteristic of being the benefactor and the beneficiary (*anugrāhyānugrāhakatva*).

Because of the connection [of the power] with that which is connected, it is said metaphorically that "the power has fallen," but not in a primary sense; thus there is no fault. This very point is clearly established in the *Kiraṇāgama* by way of a question and answer. As follows: Garuḍa said:
Initiation occurs through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); it is not due to [Śiva’s] omnipresence, for Śiva is present everywhere, even within the bound soul (*paśu*).
Since power is always present, why would there not be the cessation of worldly existence? Or, if time is said to be its assistant, what is the use of Śiva if it is time [that acts]?
The Lord said: It is observed that the application of words occurs through figurative usage (*upacāra*), as for example:
"The Person is all-pervading, eternal, yet destroyed and has attained the state of Śiva."
In this way, even the "falling of the power" (śakti-nipāta) is spoken of figuratively (upacārataḥ).
Also, in the Siddhānta:
"Just as the rays of the sun are instantly obstructed by a mass of clouds..."
In the same way, the power whose nature is knowledge is completely enveloped by the nets of bonds.
