"In the snares that have been ripened, she is said to be clearly fallen" (ṅa).
Thus, a disciple who fears saṃsāra like one terrified of falling from a mountain peak seeks out a teacher through the realization of Śakti-consciousness. As stated in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Just as, out of fear of a falling object, one might suddenly move away from it to another place, so too does the self [move] toward the teacher. And so forth.

Having thus explained the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), [the author] states, by means of the *Svāyambhuvasūtra*, the attainment of the nature of the state of purity obtained through the initiation (*dīkṣā*) that follows it:
"Having approached a teacher, his bonds severed by initiation..."
Being stainless and free from affliction, he attains union with Śiva. || 53 ||
That person who desires the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and possesses the descent of power (*śaktipāta*),
having approached and attained a Guru who has been received by the will of Śiva, becomes one whose bonds are severed by initiation (*dīkṣā-vicchinna-bandhana*);
that is, one for whom the bonds have been severed by means of initiation.
The meaning is that for one who has received initiation from a guru, the bonds of the three impurities (*mala*) are severed. Likewise, in the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
"That initiation is considered to be complete in every respect, whether by means of ritual action (*kriyā*) or by means of power (*śakti*)."
"By initiation, the embodied soul is liberated from the threefold bondage of existence.

Being thus, and for that very reason being stainless—that is, free from impurity—one who has become such attains *śivasāyujya*, which is liberation consisting in equality with Śiva. Thus [it is said] in the *Cintya-viśve*—

"Having initiated [the disciple] according to the rule upon the thirty-six principles (tattvas), he certainly unites him with the partless (niṣkala) and stainless (nirmala) reality; this is the certainty.
Here, by the word "stainless," the distinction of the pure state from the non-exclusive (akevala) state is shown.

By the term "unperturbed" (*nirupaplava*), he indicates the distinction from the state of bondage. He demonstrates through the *Sarvajñānottara-sūtra* that it is precisely this kind of initiation (*dīkṣā*) that is the cause of liberation, and not knowledge (*jñāna*) and the like: "The wise one who has been initiated by the Guru, Even if he is ignorant, attains liberation. But even one who knows all the scriptures, If he is not initiated, does not attain liberation. Thus, the *Sarvajñānottara* shows that initiation alone is the cause of liberation, and not knowledge and so forth. Furthermore, the *Mālinīvijaya-tantra* states: "O Goddess, initiation alone is the cause of liberation; Knowledge and the rest are merely its auxiliaries. The *Svacchanda-bhairava* also says: "O Goddess, initiation alone is the cause of liberation; Knowledge and the rest are merely its auxiliaries. And the *Vijñānabhairava* states: "O Goddess, initiation alone is the cause of liberation; Knowledge and the rest are merely its auxiliaries. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "knowledge alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra (*mantramārga*), initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of knowledge, knowledge alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Hence, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the practice of yoga is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of yoga (*yogamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of yoga, yoga alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "devotion alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of devotion (*bhaktimārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of devotion, devotion alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "merit alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of merit (*puṇyamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of merit, merit alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "grace alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of grace (*prasādamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of grace, grace alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the guru alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the guru (*gurumārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the guru, the guru alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the self alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the self (*ātmamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the self, the self alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the supreme reality alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the supreme reality (*paramārthamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the supreme reality, the supreme reality alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the sixfold path alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the sixfold yoga (*ṣaḍadhvamārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the sixfold [yoga], the sixfold [path] alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the fourfold initiation alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the fourfold initiation (*caturvidhadīkṣāmārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the fourfold initiation, the fourfold initiation alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the fivefold initiation alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the fivefold initiation (*pañcavidhadīkṣāmārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the fivefold initiation, the fivefold initiation alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the sevenfold initiation alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the sevenfold initiation (*saptavidhadīkṣāmārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the sevenfold initiation, the sevenfold initiation alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the ninefold initiation alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the ninefold initiation (*navavidhadīkṣāmārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the ninefold initiation, the ninefold initiation alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the twelvefold initiation alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the twelvefold initiation (*dvādaśavidhadīkṣāmārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *Trika-sadbhāva* says: "In the path of the twelvefold initiation, the twelvefold initiation alone is the cause of liberation; In the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Therefore, it is established that initiation alone is the cause of liberation. As for the statement that "the sixteenfold initiation alone is the cause of liberation," that refers to the context of the path of the sixteenfold initiation (*ṣoḍaśavidhadīkṣāmārga*). However, in the context of the path of mantra, initiation alone is the cause of liberation. Thus, the *
One whose self is bound by these principles and who is joined with all dharmas cannot be liberated by this [knowledge] alone, except through initiation whose essence is Śiva.

Joined with these principles beginning with *kalā*— that is, endowed with all dharmas and all the specific qualities of those respective principles such as the worlds (*bhuvana*) and so forth— the bound self (*nibaddhātmā*) is that very self which is thoroughly fettered by beginningless impurity (*anādi-mala*) and by action (*karman*) in the form of a continuous stream.

The bound soul— the soul that is fettered— is not able to be liberated, nor can it be caused to be liberated, by this means of knowledge and so forth, if one excludes initiation (dīkṣā), which consists of the activity of the Guru and has the nature of Śiva, whose essence is Śiva. Likewise—
Liberation does not exist through knowledge and the like; therefore, initiation alone is the liberator.
By his very nature, the divine Śiva is the bestower of grace upon all.
Through initiation (dīkṣā), liberation shall occur here for all living beings;
therefore, by the power of Śiva, liberation is accomplished everywhere.
Likewise, in the Niśvāsa:
"Through bathing one becomes pure; through the recitation of mantras, success is attained without a doubt.
Through worship there is presence, but without oblation (*homa*), it does not bestow fruit."

"Through meditation one attains the omnipresent God; through yogic practices, one attains the state of a yogi; through vows, there is purification of the body; and through initiation, liberation is sought.
Thus it is stated in the *Saurasaṃhitā* of the Purāṇas.
"Having performed the lifelong initiation (*naiṣṭhikī dīkṣā*), those who dwell as liberated ones—
to them [the teacher] should impart that supreme knowledge at the end, which is the highest state.
Thus it is said in the *Skanda Purāṇa* regarding the curse of Bhṛgu.
No superiority whatsoever based on the stages of life (āśramas) exists for men here,
except for the supreme initiation of Śiva which releases one from the three bonds.
Therefore, liberation occurs through initiation alone, not through the stages of life nor by other ritual acts.
Likewise, in the Jñānatilaka:
"The supreme state is not attained through gifts, nor through austerities, sacrifices, observances, or auspicious vows; nor is it reached by the multitude of ritual baths at sacred fords."
This [individual] does not attain liberation through various multitudes of austerities or through accumulations of merit;
rather, they bind themselves in every way, just as a silkworm binds itself with its cocoon.
Through the process of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) resulting from the ripening of impurities, one attains liberation by means of initiation (*dīkṣā*), and not otherwise.

By means of knowledge and other such methods; for these are heard of as being constituent parts of initiation (*dīkṣā*), since yoga and the like directed toward Śiva are impossible without initiation, and because impurity (*mala*), being a substance, cannot be removed by mere knowledge— just as a cataract on the eye cannot be removed by knowledge alone— but only by the activity of the Lord known as initiation, just as the activity of an oculist removes it.
And because the accomplishment of cessation occurs through the very act [of initiation] itself. It is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
"Initiation alone shall liberate one from bonds and bestow the state of Śiva upon the individual soul" (*Pauṣkarajñāna* 174).
Also, in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"Initiation alone bestows liberation upon men and effects the manifestation of consciousness. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the nature of the individual consciousness (*ātman*) as manifested through the process of initiation (*dīkṣā*),
the *Mṛgendra* Sūtra (10.3) states:
"The power of agency belonging to the individual soul is eternal and all-pervasive, just like the power of the Lord."
Because it is shrouded by darkness, [consciousness] does not shine forth with respect to objects, being devoid of assistance.

The atomic self possesses an agentive power consisting of knowledge and action; this power is like the power of the Lord—just as the power of the Lord is eternal, devoid of beginning or end, all-pervasive, and omnipresent. If this is so, then because of its eternity and omnipresence, there would follow the undesirable consequence that [the self] must always be perceived.
Likewise:
"Wherever this [soul] has a body, there indeed is the manifestation of the qualities for the sake of experience; therefore, its all-pervasiveness is understood."

Therefore he says: because she is covered by darkness—that is, concealed by *tamas*, the primordial impurity—within objects, which are the very nature of the sense-fields, she does not shine; being devoid of favor (*anugraha*), that is, lacking the manifestor, she does not appear.
As it is said in the *Ratnatraya* (252): "When the bond has dissolved in every way and the individual impurity (*āṇava-mala*) is liberated,
the power that illuminates all objects unfolds like that of Śiva."

Even though the power of the Self is all-pervasive, because the manifestation of that [power] depends upon a manifestor, even omniscience does not exist; this is shown by the Parākhyasūtra: "Though it is all-pervasive and of the nature of knowledge, it knows only in a particular location."
Therefore, he is called "one who knows only a little," because of the lack of demonstration of any intervening [obscuration]. || 56 ||

He whose very nature, his essential form, is knowledge is "knowledge-formed" (*jñāna-rūpa*). Although he is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), by virtue of being in a particular location—the location that manifests the *kalās* and so forth—he knows that object of knowledge; for that reason, that Self is called "limited in knowledge" (*kiñcijjña*), meaning it knows only a little.
He is declared and established as one who knows only a little. He states the reason for this: "because of the non-perception [of objects] due to obstruction.
This means that in a place devoid of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), there is no perception—that is, an absence of perception—due to the absence of cognition because of the intervening obstruction.

If the soul's state of limited knowledge were due to the influence of a manifesting agent (*vyañjaka*), then even when the manifesting agent in the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is present, the soul would not possess omniscience; for there would be no difference in the nature of the manifesting agent. To dispel this doubt, he provides another aphorism that establishes the gradation of manifesting agents by means of an illustrative example:
Even when the manifestor is small, that [manifested form] is small; when it is large, it is large. It becomes exactly as [the manifestor], just as a lamp [is affected] by darkness. (57)

That consciousness, obstructed by impurity, manifests itself as small when the manifesting agent is small; it manifests as great when the manifesting agent is great. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: just as a lamp—the lamp that manifests objects—is such [in its intensity] within the darkness of gloom.

It may be a minor manifestor (*svalpa-vyañjaka*) or a great manifestor (*mahā-vyañjaka*). Likewise, the word "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*) is to be supplied [to the subject] *caitanya* (consciousness). Such [a manifestor], whether small or large, exists as a manifestor. And thus, from a minor manifestor in the form of *kalā* and so forth, [arises] initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Form possesses the capacity for great manifestation; thus, the meaning is that there is no impossibility of the Self’s omniscience.

Furthermore, the fact that the Self is conscious due to its connection with its own power, and unconscious in the absence thereof, is demonstrated by means of an illustration in the *Niśvāsakārikā-sūtra*:
When that conscious living being is joined with power, it is called "jīva";
otherwise, the self is indeed partless and appears as if in a deep, poison-induced sleep.

When, at whatever time, the *jīva* (the individual self) is joined with—that is, connected to—its own power through its manifestation, then that *jīva* is known as "conscious" (*cetana*), meaning endowed with consciousness (*caitanya*). The phrase "by those who know the scriptures" is to be understood as the ellipsis. For otherwise, in the absence of the manifested power, the self as *jīva* would be "partless" (*niṣkala*), since *kalā* is consciousness.

Devoid of that [consciousness], it is partless and insentient. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "as if by poison-induced sleep"—that is, as if joined with a stupor (mūrcchā) caused by poison, it is thus characterized and perceived. Just as in the state of being stunned by poison, the soul's insentience arises solely from the absence of the manifestation of consciousness, and not otherwise.

The meaning is: because of the absence of sentience; likewise, this [body] also possesses insentience precisely due to the non-manifestation of sentience, and not because of a total absence of sentience like that of a clod of earth.
Now, by means of an illustration in the *Kiraṇasūtra*, he refutes the notion that the awakening of the self in its past state occurs through the power of knowledge:
"Just as a teacher might awaken sleeping students with a staff standing before them."
Śiva, too, shall awaken with his power those who are asleep in the slumber of delusion. || 59 ||

As for the term *guru* or *ācārya*: here, the meaning of the word *guru* is as follows—the syllable *gu* signifies darkness (*andhakāra*), and the syllable *ru* signifies that which obstructs it. Because he obstructs darkness, he is called *guru*.

One should awaken—that is, cause to wake up—by means of a rod such as a cane, those disciples who are lying down before one, in front of one, under the sway of sleep, and who are worthy of instruction. Although there is no difference in their being situated in front, the meaning is that the Guru awakens with a rod only those who are worthy of instruction because they are fit for the ripening of their impurities (*mala*), and not those who are not disciples. Likewise...

Even Śiva, the Supreme Lord, [awakens] the bound souls (paśus)—who, though remaining asleep even while that [state] exists, are devoid of the consciousness of the means for its cessation—by means of His power (śakti) acting as the instrument, namely Jyeṣṭhā. "Mohanidrā" refers to the sleep of delusion; "moha" is impurity (mala), and its "sleep" is the incapacity regarding effects, which is a specific state of maturation. Even when that [sleep] is present, He awakens those who are slumbering.
One should awaken [the disciple] according to one's capacity.
He explains the manner in which one's own power is manifested through another aphorism by means of an illustration:
"Just as the supreme strength of those who are powerless arises from the efficacy of medicine, so too, through the application of that power, immeasurable capacity comes to be. (60)

For those who are incapable and deprived of strength by disease, through the efficacy— the power or potency— of medicine, that is, of the medicinal drug, there may arise, in whatever manner, a supreme and most excellent strength, meaning a capacity that was previously present; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Likewise, by that connection with His power— that is, through the union (*yoga*) or contact with the power of that Śiva, namely Raudrī, who is the power of grace— there arises an immeasurable capacity, devoid of limitation by space and time,
which is of a primordially established nature and consists of the essence of knowledge and action.
It would become manifest. || 60 ||
By means of the Sārdha-sūtra, which is called *Parā*, he states that this self requires Śiva and Śakti not only for liberation alone, but also for bodily enjoyment and yoga:
"Because of its nature as Śiva, it is joined [to Śakti] in liberation; because of its nature as a bound soul (*paśu*), it is joined [to Śakti] in the body."
And even regarding enjoyments, O best of sages, it is through the power of karma. || 61 ||
Since his self is presided over by Īśvara, he is therefore not independent.

Because, for the reason that he is not independent— that is, devoid of autonomy regarding the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired— for that reason, his self is presided over by the Lord; that is, his self,
which is his essential nature consisting of knowledge and action, is presided over (adhiṣṭhita) by the Lord (īśvara), the Supreme Lord.

Because the self is Śiva, its state of being Śiva is the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśu), which is the ripening of impurity (mala); for that reason, it is joined to or connected with liberation. Because of the state of being a bound soul—the absence of the ripening of impurity—it is joined to the body, the physical frame. Furthermore, by the power of karmas, it is also joined to enjoyments consisting of pleasure and pain.
This is appropriate; "O Best of Sages" is an address to the listener. (61–62)
Now, [the author] demonstrates with the *Mṛgendrasūtra* (7.5) that for the self, distinct causes are required for enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*):
"Even though he is a treasury of eternal, all-pervading consciousness-power, for the sake of accomplishing his purpose..."
One seeks power either through the animal way (pāśava) or the way of Śambhu (śāmbhava), and not otherwise. || 63 ||

The treasury of the eternal and all-pervading power of consciousness (*nitya-vyāpaka-cicchakti-nidhiḥ*): this power of consciousness is both eternal and all-pervading; it is the "treasury" (the repository) of that [power], which serves as its abode for the sake of accomplishing the two goals—namely, *artha*, which refers to enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).
For the accomplishment of those two.
In the *Mudritamṛgendra*, however, the reading here is: "He does not seek power otherwise" (*mṛ0* 7.5).

In the state of worldly existence (*bhavāvasthā*), for the sake of accomplishing the object characterized by enjoyment, there is the "animal power"—that is, this animal power belonging to the bound soul (*paśu*), the capacity related to the bound soul, which consists of the stimulation of the *kalās* and so forth appropriate for the bound soul.

He seeks; he requires. And for the sake of liberation, he seeks the power pertaining to Śambhu—that is, related to Śambhu—in the form of initiation (*dīkṣā*); this is to be supplied to the sentence. In both states—of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*)—this Self requires either the bondage-related (*pāśava*) or the supreme-lord-related (*pārameśvara*) stimulation of its own capacity.

This is the meaning. Otherwise, there would be no accomplishment of the goal in the absence of the stimulation of power; thus, the ellipsis [is supplied]: "enjoyment and liberation are not accomplished. || 63 ||
Now, he shows the nature of that knowledge which is required for both worldly enjoyment and liberation by means of a *kālottara* sūtra:
"The knowledge of the universe, which possesses manifold forms, is one and has Śiva as its essence."
By which that [state] is all-pervading, stainless, and peaceful, consisting of both enjoyment and liberation. || 64 ||

That knowledge by which *bhukti* (enjoyment) and *mukti* (liberation)— both enjoyment and liberation— arise for the manifold universe (*viśva*) consisting of the fourteen kinds of elemental forms (*bhūtarūpa*), is of the nature of Śiva; it is the form of Śiva, the supreme knowledge (*parajñāna*), unique (*eka*), non-dual (*advitīya*), all-pervasive (*vyāpaka*), and omnipresent (*sarvagata*).
It is stainless, peaceful, and free from passion and hatred. || 64 ||

He demonstrates that this very power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) is inherent in Śiva and acts as the uniter of the self with Śiva by means of the Niśvāsa Sārdha-sūtra: "In reality, there is only one, the supreme, stainless power of Śiva."
It is inseparable from Śambhu, just as heat is inseparable from the lordly fire. || 65 ||
By that [power], the union of the self and Śiva is the supreme-non-supreme awakening of Śiva. 66.

The power belonging to Śiva (śaivī), which is stainless—meaning free from impurity—and supreme—meaning most excellent—is in reality, from the perspective of the ultimate truth, one and indeed devoid of differentiation. As stated in the Niśvāsottara: "Śiva alone is the power, and likewise the effects [appear] through differentiation."
"Therefore, Śakti, whose essence is Śiva, [bestows] enjoyment and liberation by the will of Śiva.
Furthermore, of what nature is she? To this he says: "Like heat, which is the quality of warmth, belonging to fire (śuci), so [is she] of the Lord (prabhu) who is characterized by creative power;
[he is called] Śambhu because from him (asmāt) auspiciousness (śam) arises. Of him.

"Inseparable" (*avinābhāvinī*) means that which possesses inseparability (*avinābhāva*), namely inherence (*samavāya*); thus, it is "inherent" (*samavāyinī*). Accordingly, in the *Pauṣkara* (Vi. 1.8):
"That stainless power consisting of knowledge which is inherent in Śiva..."
"That very [consciousness] is declared to be knowledge (*jñāna*), and the scripture is that which leads to its inference.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? To this he says: "Supreme and non-supreme with respect to the awakening of Śiva" (*śivabodha-parāparā*).
The awakening of Śiva is the knowledge of Śiva; regarding that, it is both supreme (*parā*) and non-supreme (*aparā*), meaning it is distinguished as both supreme and non-supreme. And so:

It was stated at the very beginning that "knowledge is said to be twofold. By means of such a power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), there occurs a union (*sandhi*)—that is, a conjunction (*sandhāna*)—between the Self and Śiva; that is, between the Self and Śiva (*ātma-śivau*). The remainder [of the sense] is that this constitutes a relationship characterized by the state of the one being graced and the other being the gracer. (65–66)
This Śāmbhava knowledge is distinct from perception and the other means of cognition; it is immediate and has all things as its object. This is shown by the *Mṛgendra-sūtra* (5.16):
"It is neither perceptual, nor inferential, nor even verbal, but belongs to Śaṅkara."
Pure knowledge shines eternally with respect to all things.
That knowledge pertaining to Śaṅkara, which relates to Śaṅkara, is not *adhyakṣa*, that is, it is not *pratyakṣa* (perceptual).
For knowledge dependent upon the senses (*akṣa*) is indeed *pratyakṣa*.
Since there is no operation of the senses for the Lord (*īśvara*), it is therefore not *pratyakṣa*. Nor is it *laiṅga*, meaning produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*).

It is not even inferential, because inference functions in dependence upon perception. Nor is it verbal, for even knowledge produced by words does not have it as its object, since such knowledge concerns objects that are entirely beyond the senses. And nothing whatsoever is beyond the perception of the Blessed One. Therefore, it is pure, free from beginningless obscuration, and ever-present.
It shines forth and manifests at all times, in all things, and across all objects.

But surely, even in the Āgamas, the Lord’s connection with a body and sense organs is heard of through such passages as "five-faced" and "fifteen-eyed. Even if that [connection] exists, why is the Lord’s knowledge not dependent upon it?

If it is argued that [the Lord] acts, we say no; because the Lord lacks connection with a body and sense organs required for knowledge and action, but rather perceives all objects by His very nature and possesses the power of action, being capable of effecting creation, maintenance, and so forth by mere will alone. He assumes a body only to show favor to His devotees; otherwise, He remains formless.
For meditation and worship would otherwise be impossible. Indeed, it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"This form is taught for the sake of protecting the practitioner;
it has hands and feet everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces on all sides."

In this context, however, by the statement "pure" (*vimala*), it is asserted that the knowledge of Śiva does not depend upon a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), nor is it characterized by doubt, error, or indecision, as is the case with the knowledge of transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*). Indeed, those knowledges which are veiled by the power of impurity (*malaśakti*) for the sake of experience—
For the sake of production, they depend on manifesting factors such as the *kalās*;

however, because those manifesting factors like the *kalās* possess only limited illumination, they are subject to such limitations in their manifestation regarding the objects of knowledge—even though [the Lord] may encounter obstacles. But the Lord’s knowledge is not of this nature.
Because He is devoid of beginningless obscuration.
As it is said in the *Kiraṇa*: "Because He is free from beginningless impurity, He is therefore the omniscient Śiva.
And in the *Mṛgendra* (5.14–15): "And because He is devoid of such obscuration, He does not depend upon a manifestor."
Therefore, that [cognition] is never doubtful, nor is it ever erroneous.
"Those [powers] which perceive the manifestor because they are enveloped by the powers of impurity may, in accordance with that manifestor, appear even as if they were obstructed. (67)

Now, having referred to the threefold bondage and its nature as bondage, [the author] states, by means of the *Svāyambhuvasūtra*, the means that has proceeded from Śiva for the liberation of this individual soul (*aṇu*) and for the manifestation of its state as Śiva:
"From this extensive bondage, which obstructs the supreme state..."
Initiation alone liberates and leads one even to the supreme abode of Śiva.
"From the destroyer of the state of others" means from that which destroys the state of others; "the isolation (*kaivalya*) of that [state]" refers to its cessation, its obstruction, its destruction.

"From the extensive" means from that which is extensively spread out, expanded—that is, from the threefold [impurity] in the form of *mala*, *karman*, and *māyā*. As it has been said in that very same place:
O young man, this illusion is a bond of such subtle attachment;
all of this, born from the section concerning the nature of saṃsāra, has been explained by me.

Initiation alone liberates one from this bondage. Here, the restrictive particle *eva* (alone) is used for the purpose of excluding other means such as "awakening" (*bodha*) mentioned in other systems. For instance, those means such as awakening taught by the Paśupatas do not lead to the goal of human life, because they merely manifest the fetters and are themselves of the nature of fetters.
They become practitioners. As it is said in that very same [text]:
"Liberation does not come from the knowledge of the fetter (pāśa), nor likewise from the knowledge of the bound soul (paśu);
since liberation comes from everything, it is attained through the knowledge of the Lord (pati)."
The nature of the fetter (pāśa) and knowledge (jñāna), and so forth, has been explained in the *Cintya*:
"O fair-faced one, the entire web of scriptures up to the end of Nāda constitutes the knowledge of the fetter;
it is called the 'knowledge of the bound soul' (paśujñāna) because of the conceit that 'I am Brahmā'."
"Beyond that is the supreme Śivavastu, which transcends mantras, is stainless, omniscient, omnipresent, tranquil, the self of all, and facing in all directions. Thus,
those [practices] such as *vijñāna* and *yoga* taught in this scripture are ancillary to initiation (*dīkṣā*).
It is established by this much alone that these [means] are taught for the sake of accomplishing that [liberation]. Likewise, in the venerable *Parākhyatantra*:
"Initiation is held to be the cause of the means, such as knowledge and the rest;
the status of these four as ancillaries is declared according to their essential nature and divisions."
The meaning is that "cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers to the purpose (*prayojana*).
As long as that state has not been attained, there can be no sequence of ritual action;
therefore, even ritual action—characterized by worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth—is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of that [state].
Even now, practices such as the observance of living amidst ashes have come to be regarded as ancillaries to spiritual conduct.
Even the yoga of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and the rest, when conjoined with concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna),
occurs only after the material body has been utterly consumed.

Ritual action, enjoyment, and disposition toward Śiva—augmented by the state of being Śiva—constitute initiation (dīkṣā), because they are its constituent parts; thus, that initiation is the possessor of those parts.
The meaning is that this initiation (*dīkṣā*) manifests that which exists as the supreme excellence above all.

"Śaiva" means pertaining to Śiva; "dhāma" refers to power (*prabhāva*). According to the *Viśva* lexicon, "dhāma" is used for a place, a beautiful location, birth, and also power. It is equivalent to being equal to Śiva—that is to say, having the form of equality with Śiva. That too...

It leads, that is, it causes one to attain. The meaning here is that if one desires enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), one attains the state of Śiva; if one desires liberation (*mumukṣu*), one attains the state beyond the bound soul (*paśv-atīta*) and union with Śiva (*śiva-sāyujya*) at the end of the body. In this regard, those who have reached the four worlds beginning with Nivṛtti—which reside within the principles of bondage—either by the power of yoga or by being appointed through initiation, [attain these] in succession.

There are those who possess the state of embodied isolation (mūrti-kevalin), those with isolated yoga (yoga-kevalin), those with isolated knowledge (jñāna-kevalin), and those with isolated power (śakti-kevalin). Thus it is stated in the Mataṅga: "Endowed with the vigor and strength of yoga, or else appointed by initiation, they are all equal to Sadāśiva; yet they are not the single Lord of Causes."
They have not yet attained the state of Śiva; their karma is now described.
They are considered to be those who reside in proximity [to liberation], abodes of peace, and possessors of pure knowledge (jñāna-kevalins).
Those who have attained *sālokya* through knowledge, as well as those who are grouped below them,
and even the *yogakevalins*— all these are defined in this Tantra.
Due to their presence during the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), they are considered Śaktikevalins;
those established in renunciation (nivṛtti) are remembered as Mūrtikevalins, who are indeed subject to desire.
For example:
those atoms that are established in the principle called Nāda,
as well as the Mūrtikevalins, are proclaimed to be the remaining Rudras.
The meaning of the word *kevala* is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Because it is the abode (*nilaya*) of the *kalās*, it is therefore remembered as *kevala*.
Here, a specific distinction is shown in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
O Putraka! The ritual service (saparyā), as well as the roles of the practitioner (sādhaka) and the teacher (ācārya), must all be applied within the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva).
O son! One should know that in the principle of Māyā he is a meditator (samādhi), in the principle of Vidyā he is a seeker (putraka);
in Īśvara he is a practitioner (sādhaka) for the sake of enjoyment; and in the Sakala state he is established as a teacher (ācārya).
Having understood this, one should diligently effect dissolution (laya) and enjoyment (bhoga).
But that guru who performs initiation without knowing dissolution and enjoyment—
"The teacher, together with his disciples, shall be cooked in the Raurava hell;
therefore, the instructor, having understood [the disciple's fitness], should perform initiation with great care.
Beyond that, is the supreme Śiva-tattva indeed the ultimate?
There shall be a single place of liberation, stainless and facing in all directions.
"Immovable, all-pervasive, peaceful, and free from gender and stages of life"—thus [it is described].
Beyond these is the One, who is the subtle object of both cause and effect;
He is transcendent, perfectly complete, independent, and facing in every direction.
One [system] is considered to be without a Lord (nirīśvara) and self-abiding; the other six are held to be with a Lord (seśvara).
Now, by means of two verses from the Mataṅga-sūtra, he defines the meaning of the word *dīkṣā*: "In these two teachings, *dīkṣā* consists of *kṣapaṇa* and *dāna*.
*Kṣapaṇa* and *dāna* are 'the two [acts of] destruction and bestowal. By the word *kṣapaṇa*..."

It is the destruction of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva). By the word "giving" (dāna), the bestowing of the state of Śiva is expressed. When these two purposes are accomplished, that which has arisen within this teaching, the Śaiva scripture, is called "initiation" (dīkṣā). The meaning is that initiation is indeed the power of Śiva (śivaśakti) itself, which effects the destruction of the bound souls' state of bondage and bestows the state of Śiva. Thus—
"The true nature of knowledge is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
because it is said 'it is bestowed' and 'it is destroyed,' the word *dīkṣā* is explained in two ways."
But would it not follow that by giving away His own power (*śakti*), Śiva would fall into a state of poverty regarding power? To this, [the *Mātaṅgapārameśvara*, Vidyāpāda 4.59–60] says:
"That which is called 'giving' is one's own very existence, which consists of knowledge and action. (59)
That power, having become manifest through contact with Him, is perfectly pure;
that alone is called the "gift" (dāna) from the Lord, for it does not manifest by itself in the bound soul (paśu).

The very existence of one's own self—which consists of knowledge and action, whose nature is knowledge and action, and which is the capacity (sāmarthya) that is the form of reality—is itself renowned by the name "the gift" (dāna), meaning the object to be given. Thus, since it is one's own existing existence alone that is to be given, there is no expenditure of power; therefore, there is no loss of power.
The sense is that Śiva is poverty-stricken. To the objection that, in that case, the meaning of the word "giving" (dāna) would be untenable, he says:

"That power," and so forth. That power, which consists of His own existence, becomes perfectly pure through contact with—that is, by being touched by—the grace-bestowing power of that Supreme Lord, like a lotus ripened by contact with the rays of the sun.
And likewise in that very same [text]:
"Just as a lotus becomes fully blossomed through contact with the rays of the sun, so too is that manifestation itself the manifestation of the Lord, the Supreme God."

It has been stated that this is "giving" (*dāna*). It is the manifestation of one's own existence—whose nature is omniscience and so forth—through the removal of all veils. The manifestation of the state of Śiva for persons from the Supreme Lord is called "giving" by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), not in its primary sense; such is the meaning. [Objection: But surely, nothing is desired without a purpose?

Regarding the phrase "transgressing the primary meaning of the word," he says "no" and so forth. The existence (*sattā*) of the individual soul (*paśu*) is not manifested by itself—that is, it does not become manifest through its own self. The underlying intention is this: existence is not always manifested by itself in its entirety, because it is obscured, like copper covered by a stain; however, the *puruṣa* (the Supreme Spirit) is not [so].

It is established that it is not merely knowledge that brings about cessation [of bondage], but rather knowledge that is accompanied by excellence—just as in the case of an eye-physician. Here too, God alone is the agent of liberation, and not the person himself. Likewise, in the Pauṣkara (Viṣṇudharmottara 1.94):
"A person never attains liberation through his own power."
"Except by the grace of the Lord Śiva, the remover of all inauspiciousness. (69–70)
He shows the manner of perceiving the Self in its state of purity through Śiva-initiation by means of the Devyāmata-sūtra:
"When one perceives the bodiless Self with the eye of knowledge..."
Then one becomes tranquil in soul, with longing departed from everything. || 71 ||
When— at which time— by means of the eye of knowledge (*jñāna-cakṣus*), that is, by the eye or organ of consciousness itself as manifested through the power of opening [the eyes of wisdom];
one perceives the Self (*ātman*) as bodiless (*aśarīram*), meaning other than the body, distinct from the body, and different from both the gross and subtle bodies.

He perceives— that is, makes directly manifest— that which is self-luminous, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, and which illuminates others. At that time, he is one whose longing has departed— that is, whose desire has ceased— with respect to all objects of abandonment, consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) from Earth up to Śiva.
"Tranquil-souled" means that his soul becomes tranquil, free from impurities such as downward-facing tendencies;
the meaning is that he is devoid of passion, hatred, and the like. || 71 ||
The Śrīmataṅgasūtra states that for one who is devoted to the unity of the Self, there is no return, just as there is none for those liberated through other systems of philosophy:
"For a person whose impurities have been burnt away by the fire of initiation, his own innate power attains manifestation through yoga."
Kissed on the region of the heart by the power of the Lord, it does not turn back from its course through any other means. || 72 ||

For one whose impurity (*mala*) has been scorched by the fire of initiation (*dīkṣānala*): "the fire of initiation" (*dīkṣānala*) refers to the fire in the form of initiation; "one whose impurity has been scorched" (*pluṣṭamala*) means one whose impurity—which veils consciousness—has been scorched, burnt, and brought to absolute cessation. For such a person, for the self (*ātman*), there is its own power (*svakyaṃ balaṃ*).
The capacity for vision and action arises from *yoga*, that is, from contact with the power of Śiva. As it is stated in the *Mataṅga* (4.5):
"His yoga consists of his own powers, which flash forth in every direction.
Furthermore, manifestation attains a state of being manifested that is devoid of any other manifestation, belonging to the all-pervading Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

The region of the heart of the person (puruṣa), having been kissed— that is, touched— by the grace-bestowing power, attains a state of released consciousness; it does not undergo further manifestation or return through another specific bondage, just as copper, once transmuted by mercury, attains the state of gold.

Furthermore, it does not return to its state as copper; likewise, this Self, having attained the state of Śiva, does not again fall into the state of a bound soul (paśu). As it is said in the Svacchanda-tantra:
"Copper, when joined with mercury and fire, is united with blackness [and thus loses its original nature]."
But when purified by those who know reality, it attains the state of gold.
The self never again returns to its state of being copper-colored,
for it has been rendered stainless by a Guru who is learned in the Tantras;
once stainless, it never again becomes stained, but attains the state of Śiva.

In other philosophical systems (*darśana*), there is indeed a return for those who have attained liberation, because that which is to be attained in those systems does not transcend the categories of reality (*tattva*). As it is said in the *Vātulottara*:
"He who consists of consciousness, both within and without, is joined with liberation from the thirty-six principles."
For in reality, that deity is indeed the supreme Śiva, who transcends all categories of existence.

Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: "That which is isolation (*kaivalya*) resulting from the discrimination between the Spirit (*puruṣa*) and Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), or that cessation [of worldly activity] which comes from considering everything as Brahman,
or whatever other liberations are born of the fetters (*pāśa*)."
All those various powers undergo differentiation during creation.
When Śiva is realized, the other [powers] shine at his head; liberated, the foremost of men does not descend into creation, having supported all worldly evils with his own abiding light.
"They are always impelled by all the Īśvaras. — Mṛgendra-tantra 2.29. 72.
In this treatise, having first defined liberation as being free from rebirth, [the author] subsequently establishes— preceded by a summary of the stages leading to it—

the non-recurrence of the liberated self as preceded by its causal origin, according to the *Svāyambhuva Sūtra*. Alternatively, [he establishes] the non-recurrence of the liberated one, preceded by a summary of the sequence of liberation.
He demonstrates the preceding cause by means of the *Svāyambhuvasūtra*:
"By this sequential yoga, having attained supreme isolation (*kevalatā*), one reaches no further state of existence because of being devoid of beginningless impurity. (73)

By this sequential method, there is a gradual union (*yoga*): first, the union with the power (*śakti*) of Śiva; then, the union with the fruit consisting of the destruction of impurity (*mala*); then, the union with the attainment of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) and so forth; then, the union with the *dīkṣā*; again, the union through *dīkṣā*; and finally, the union with the fruit consisting of the severance of bondage.

Regarding "yoga": by such a sequential yoga (*kramayoga*), one attains the supreme, most excellent state of *kevalatā*—solitude characterized by union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*). Previously, one was established in mere isolation; for *kevalatā* is indeed solitude, yet that is not the supreme [state], because even in that condition, the self possesses a second element: impurity (*mala*). [This is the state of] union with Śiva.
But the supreme state is absolute oneness (*kevalatā*), because in that state there is not even the slightest second thing.

Having gone to—that is, having attained—that state, one does not undergo another existence or another birth, because of being devoid of beginningless impurity; "beginningless impurity" refers to the *āṇavamala*, and because of being empty of that, one is free from it. Indeed, not...

The meaning is that an effect does not arise without a cause; even when karma exists, impurity (*aśuddhi*) is the seed of rebirth, and because of its emptiness, how could there be the attainment of another existence?
Even if the primordial stain of illusion (*māyīya-mala*) were destroyed at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), it would still function as the cause for another future birth.

The term "beginningless" (*anādi*) was employed in order to negate the notion that [the world] is something "seen. As stated in the *Raurava*: "Just as a heap of cotton thrown into a blazing fire is consumed and extinguished therein, it would never again attain grossness."
Thus, having entered the maṇḍala arising from initiation and mantra, the initiated best of men does not undergo birth again. (73)
Now, by means of the *Niśvāsakārikā-sūtra*, he shows the state of the person whose essential nature has become manifest, wherein knowledge is fully perfected:
"He for whom all states of being dissolve in the waking state as if in deep sleep..."
His consciousness was sufficient; by it, the three steps were leaped over.
For that person whose entire (ka) states—meaning all mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*)—dissolve completely, as if in deep sleep (*suṣuptavat*);

*suṣupta* being derived from *suṣupti* with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the state itself; [that is,] just as in the state of deep sleep, they go to dissolution (*pralīyante*), reaching a state of profound absorption even while in the waking state (*jāgrat*). For such a person...

The meaning is that when consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is conceptual knowledge, has reached its full extent and completion, non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) arises. By that person endowed with non-conceptual knowledge, even the three stages—known as *adhikāra* (sovereignty), *bhoga* (enjoyment), and *laya* (dissolution)—are transcended and surpassed. Thus:
In the *Sarvajñānottara*: "He who, having restrained all the senses while in the waking state,
is endowed with the qualities of the fourth state (*turya*), should then meditate upon that [state] even without it."
"He is called liberated while living; at the end of the body, he is said to be liberated.
Likewise:
"He does not rejoice because of a favor, nor is he distressed by an injury."
He who is equal toward all beings is said to be liberated while living.

Now, according to another scripture, he says that this pure self meditates upon and perceives Śiva through a vision consisting of his own power, which has been empowered by the rays of Śiva’s solar power:
"By the vision of consciousness empowered by the rays of the power of the sun that is Śiva..."
The self, its veils having been removed, beholds Śiva together with Śakti and the other [deities]. (75)
The veil has been removed; that Self whose obscuration of ignorance has vanished is [revealed] by the ray of the power of Śiva, who is the Sun.

Śiva himself is the Sun; his power is the ray of power, the cognitive power (*saṃvit-śakti*) which dispels the darkness of ignorance. By that very ray, the vision of consciousness (*ciddṛś*) is empowered—that is, it is made capable of perceiving Śiva.

The consciousness (*cit*) that has been produced through its capacity (*samarthatayā*) is itself the "vision" (*dṛk*); the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).

Together with those beginning with "power"—that is, along with Śiva’s inherent power (*samavāyi-śakti*), which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi-rūpiṇī*) of various powers such as will (*icchā*) and the rest—one beholds Śiva, the Supreme Lord; one makes him directly manifest (*aparokṣīkaroti*).
Likewise, [it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (verse 29)]:
"He perceives Śiva through his own power and meditates upon that Śiva with a vision sharpened by [that] power.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [is meant] the collection of sentient and insentient forms presided over by the power of Śiva, each of which—

The fivefold duties (*kṛtyapañcaka*), the enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) to be accomplished by them, and so forth, are included here. For this very reason, it is not possible for Śiva to be an object of the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties as asserted by the Pātañjalas and others, because He is beyond the sphere of the fetters (*pāśa*). As it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*:
That modification of the internal organ known as cognition is not capable of illuminating the Great Lord, because it is a fetter, like a shackle or similar restraints.

In that regard, Śiva, whose essential nature is non-different from consciousness, cannot be an object of perception like a jar or other such things; for since both the seer (the Self) and the object seen (Śiva) possess the nature of pure consciousness and are all-pervasive, such [objective] perception is impossible. This has also been stated thus in the commentary on the *Mokṣakārikā*. 75.

Now, by means of another scriptural passage (sūtrāntara), he states— with an illustrative example— that after the direct knowledge (aparokṣa-jñāna) of Śiva, there is no need to depend upon the knowledge of Śiva contained in the Kāmika and other tantras, which serves as the cause for the indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) that acts as a means [to liberation].
Just as someone with a torch in hand might discard it after seeing an object by its light, so too,
having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should subsequently relinquish that knowledge.
An *ulkā* is a specific kind of wood with its tip set ablaze; according to Amara, "an *ulkā* is that which has emitted flames.

A certain person who holds such an *ulkā* in his hand would, upon perceiving—that is, seeing—an object or substance required by himself, cast that *ulkā* aside. In the same way, through *jñāna*—that by which something is known, such as the *Kāmika* and other [Tantras]—[one casts aside ignorance].

By that [means], the knowledge of Śiva is to be known; having perceived—that is, having made directly manifest—the nature of supreme Śiva, which is self-luminous consciousness, one should thereafter abandon the scripture, which is the means for indirect knowledge. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility. (76)
Now, by means of two verses from the Niśvāsa-sūtra, he describes the state of being immersed in the true nature of the object of knowledge:
"When the mind, having attained its mark in the supreme reality, becomes absorbed therein, then all objective cognition indeed comes to destruction. (77)
This verse is not found in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* as edited by Mudrita, nor is its presence there even conceivable;
however, it is found in the *Mokṣakārikā* as the one hundred and sixth verse.

When, at which time, the mind has "attained its target"—meaning that its target, the reality of Supreme Śiva (paraśivatattva) devoid of beginningless limiting adjuncts (upādhi), has been made manifest through repeated contemplation—and thus becomes such [a state], it [merges] into the Supreme, which is beyond all principles; the meaning is that it transcends dissolution (layātīta). Thus, in the Niśvāsa:
"The supreme deity transcends all states of existence, is indefinable, and is free from affliction;
knowing this, one is called a man of knowledge even while enjoying sense objects. Thus it is said.

In that [state], it merges; it goes to dissolution. At that time, "entire knowledge"—meaning all knowledge, including conceptual cognition—attains destruction, that is, dissolution. Here, by the word *manas*, the mind in its state of self-dissolution (*svalīnāvasthā*) among the four types of mind is denoted. Likewise...

In the Niśvāsa [Tattvasaṃhitā], the mind is said to be of four kinds: fused (saṃsṛṣṭa), absorbed (svalīna), distracted (vikṣipta), and moving to and fro (gatirāgati). Listen now to this classification of it.
Neither the mind, nor that which is to be thought, nor the thinker is perceived;
perfectly withdrawn and liberated from sense objects, one becomes unified like one in deep sleep.

Even while being grasped as objects, they attain the status of being objects of knowledge; yet they do not become joined with that cognition, for it is said that [the object] is merely "conjoined" with it.
From ignorance one goes to knowledge, and from knowledge one goes to ignorance;
he who wavers due to weakness undergoes this coming and going.
Because one who is devoted to the objects of the senses is bound by knowledge,
being perpetually agitated throughout the three periods of time, he is called "distracted."
Among them, the one who is completely absorbed and has transcended the qualities (guṇas) is the supreme and free from affliction;
that which is closely attached is to be known as the middling, and is remembered as being characterized by sattva.
The lowest is the restless and base *rājasa* state, characterized by coming and going;
the *tāmasa* state is the distracted one, which is indeed the fourth and the lowest of the low.
It is taught that for embodied beings, [the world] consists of qualities and is largely composed of impurities;
however, it is beyond qualities (nirguṇa) in its preeminence, wherein one shall become absorbed.
The bliss experienced by the mind when it is fully absorbed and witnessed by the Self—
this, indeed, those who know yoga declare to be the supreme state of yoga.
This subject has been explained in detail in the *Niśvāsakārikā*; let it be understood from that. || 77 ||

By means of another aphorism, he states that one attains union with Śiva: "But when one is joined to the reality that is inexpressible, supportless, ungraspable, devoid of measurement, and beyond the principles (tattvas), one is liberated; such is the certainty of the scripture. (78)

In that which is inexpressible, names such as "powerful" (śakta) or "exerted" (udyukta) are applied; yet it is devoid of those, being without support, devoid of the foundations of sound (nāda), the point (bindu), space (vyoman), mantras, and so forth, and ungraspable by the instruments of cognition such as the intellect.
The forms *nirālambe* and *agrāhye* are Vedic archaisms for *nirālambaḥ* and *agrāhyaḥ*. It is free from all measure.

He is joined to the Supreme Reality—which is devoid of conjunction and the like, which does not consist of the three qualities (*guṇa*), which is beyond all principles (*tattva*), and which transcends all categories of existence.

Here, the root *yuj* is taken in the sense of "joining" (*yoga*), and not in the sense of "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*) as in *yuj samādhau*. Thus, the meaning is that he has been brought to the well-known state of union (*sāyujya*), which consists in the attainment of the Self's true nature. As it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
The form united with Śiva is called *sāyujya*. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the scripture, the Śiva-āgama, is that one who has attained such *sāyujya* is liberated.
In this context, by the term *sāyujya* (union), similarity to Śiva is meant, and not a relationship such as identity (*tādātmya*) and so forth. As it has been stated in the *Cintya*:
"Otherwise, O fair-faced one, there would be the teaching of many liberations in the scripture."
"Liberation, which is easily attained through the state of Śiva, is now being described by me.
Thus it has been stated by those who are well-versed [in our tradition]:
"Liberation is not the annihilation of the self, nor is liberation here the identity of the bound soul (paśu) and Śiva."
There is neither the abandonment of the devouring of ignorance, nor the dissolution of the qualities (*guṇas*), nor even liberation from the stone; rather,
that nature of the Self which is of the form of consciousness and bliss, manifested upon the departure of the three impurities (*malas*),
is called "union" (*sāyujya*) with the all-pervading Lord who resembles Śiva— this is liberation according to the *Tantra*.
In the Devīkālottara it is said:
"One should awaken the consciousness that is asleep, and again pacify it when it is distracted;
when both sides have been abandoned, one should not move it at all."
The mind is always without support and devoid of all objects of perception;
consciousness, being free from the states of the mental faculty (manas), is characterized by liberation. Thus [it is said]. (78)
Now, he shows the persistence of this [Self], which has attained the form of self-acquisition, by means of a Sūtra of Svāyambhuva:
"Transcending the state of worldly existence, it remains like an unflinching flame."
Because he has manifested his Śiva-nature in liberation, he is one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 79 ||
[Since, for which reason, he has accomplished his purpose and attained union with Śiva, therefore] for that reason,
being one who has transcended the state of "bhava" (existence), "bhava" refers to saṃsāra; within that, "udbhavapadāni" refers to births—

The "places" (sthānāni) are as follows: the "place of existence" (bhavapada), so called because it is the state of becoming; the "place of the self" (ahampada), which is the station of the Sakala, Pralayākala, and Vijñānākala classes of souls; and the "place of emergence" (udbhavapada), so called because it exists above that [self-place], being the station of Ananta and the other deities. Being one who exists having transcended—that is, having passed beyond—that [place of emergence].

He stands like a flickerless flame—unwavering, free from trembling, like a steady blaze. Alternatively, there are six stages of the supreme liberation: the stage of the arising of existence (*bhavodbhava*), the stage beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*), the principle of peace (*śāntitattva*), that called *nāda*, that called *aiśa*, and that called *vidyā*. Among these, the sixth, the stage of the arising of existence, is the highest of all.
The meaning is that he who exists having transcended [the previous levels] remains like the flame of a lamp. As it is said in the *Śivatattvavilāsa*:
"The state of Bhavodbhava is one; beyond that is the Śāntyatīta."
And the reality of peace (śāntitattva) is that which is called Nāda, belonging to Īśvara, as well as that which is called Vidyā.
Thus, six steps of the liberated ones have been cited in sequence.
All of this has been explained in detail in Sadyojyoti’s commentary; let it be understood from that. 79.
Now, by means of the *Devīkālottarasūtra*, he establishes that for one who has accomplished all that was to be done, there is no further duty such as daily rites and so forth:
"In this [state], there is no worship, no prostration, no recitation, nor even meditation."
It is said that the object of knowledge is absolute; nothing whatsoever is to be known.

In this state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*), there is no worship (*pūjā*) or adoration (*arcanā*), no prostration (*namaskāra*) or honoring (*satkāra*), no recitation (*japa*), and no meditation (*dhyāna*) or reflection (*cintana*). Therefore, what remains of the obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rites? To this he says:

"It is said to be the Knowable alone" (*kevalaṃ jñeyam iti uktam*). By the term "the Knowable," it is indicated that there is no longer even the mere state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyabhāva-mātra*).

It should be understood and known that there is nothing whatsoever, not even the slightest thing; likewise, the meaning is that he does not bind his affection to external activities. Similarly—neither is there any restrictive rule for him, nor is fasting prescribed.
Engagement and withdrawal, as well as the vows of celibacy.
In that very section on conduct (Ācāraprakaraṇa), it is said:
"O Maheśvara! For him there is no meditation, no recitation, no worship, no fire-oblation, nor any means of accomplishment; he has no entitlement even to the ritual service of the sacred fire. (80)

Thus, even though one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) remains joined with the cognition of objects due to the force of latent impressions (vāsanā), he remains established solely in the knowledge of his own true nature by virtue of Śiva’s power; as stated in the Niśvāsakārikā Sūtra:
"Just as the wind, however swift it may be, does not go anywhere once it has left the ether."
But one whose mind is fixed upon the object of knowledge does not let go, even while remaining amidst sense objects. || 81 ||

Just as the wind, though extremely swift and moving with great speed, does not go beyond or traverse the sky— that is, it does not pass through or move across the all-pervading void— so too is the person whose mind (caitanya) has been cast into Śiva, the object of knowledge; that is, one by whom the mind has been cast, meaning firmly established therein.

"Abiding in the object"—that is, one who stands within the sense-object (*viṣaya-sthaḥ*). Even being such, he does not release; he does not abandon the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). In that very same [text]:
"But he enjoys all objects, yet he is a non-smearer of the smearable."* *Note: This refers to the state of one who experiences sensory objects without being stained by them.*

"Whose being is all-pervading, established in Śambhu, and uninterrupted. This means that, by virtue of having directly realized the nature of Śiva, he constantly experiences the nectar consisting of that very knowledge. Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having drunk the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, wander according to your pleasure. Thus [it is said]. 81.
Now, by means of another scriptural passage (*sūtrāntara*), he states—preceded by an illustration—that its very nature is the manifestation of the temporal paths (*adhvan*):
"Just as the mind of embodied beings always moves toward the objects of the senses, so too does it move toward that formless state which transcends the senses. (82)

Just as the mind (*citta*) of embodied beings (*dehinām śarīriṇām*) constantly and perpetually moves toward and engages with the objects of the senses (*indriyārthe*), even so, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of that one liberated while living (*jīvanmuktasya*) moves toward and remains fixed in the very state (*pade*) that transcends the senses, is beyond the range of the senses, and is formless (*nairākṛte*). This is the intended meaning:
Just as a person's mind functions every moment without obstruction regarding sense-objects and their domains,
yet the steadiness of the mind does not occur during the practice of all objects of knowledge— likewise,
the meaning is that even the mind of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) always attains the state that is beyond the senses, stainless, and absolute. || 82 ||
Just as a calf turns away from its mother’s udder when the milk is exhausted, so too does the mind of men quickly turn away when passion is exhausted. 83.
Just as a calf takes in its mother’s milk as long as that milk exists, and ceases [to do so] when it is exhausted, in the same way the mind also ceases. Thus, in that very same [text],
following the phrase "here he states by way of an illustration," it says "the object of the senses" and so forth, [and concludes that the mind] does not exist internally.

Then follows the reading beginning with "mātuḥ stanyam" (the mother's milk) and ending with "kiṃ kariṣyati" (what will he do?). Then follows the reading beginning with "kṣīrakṣayāt" (due to the exhaustion of milk) and ending with "nairākṛte pade" (in the state of formlessness). Then the reading "dehināṃ virāgiṇām" (of embodied beings who are dispassionate) is observed. According to the commentary and for the sake of relevance to the present subject, [this is adopted here].
It should be understood that a transformation has been accomplished.
Though the body and its attachments move, he does not move; he is immovable.
He for whom all this is known as the object of knowledge—his mind is perfectly steady.
Thus, what will he do to you, who has already been conquered by the wise? || 83 ||

He describes the power of time and the majesty for a person established in such a state. Alternatively, by means of another aphorism, he demonstrates the time and the majesty of one who stands in the station of all stations beyond [this world].
Whether for the duration of milking a cow, the flight of an arrow, or merely the blink of an eye,
one who is united with the supreme state even once shall not undergo rebirth again.

*Godohaḥ* refers to the time it takes for a cow (*gaurī*) to be milked; this duration is *godoha*, or that which is merely equal to it. *Nayanonmīlanamātrakam* means merely the time of the opening of the eyes—that is, the duration of the opening of the eye or the visual organ. The accusative case ending (*dvitīyā vibhaktiḥ*) is used here according to the rule: "The second case is used after words denoting time or distance when there is uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). *Sakṛt* means once, at some time.
One who is joined—meaning united or having achieved meditative absorption—in the supreme state, which transcends all paths and is the unconditioned state of Śiva, shall not undergo rebirth;
that is, he shall not go forth again into birth. || 84 ||

Now, by means of another scriptural passage (sūtrāntara), he demonstrates that his attainment consists precisely in the acquisition of his own Śiva-nature, which is similar to [the nature of] Śiva; and that this is neither identity with Him as in the Advaita doctrine, nor traveling to His location, as in the case of attaining the status of Indra and others: [The text continues: "The attainment [of Śiva] is the acquisition of one's own Śiva-nature, which is similar to His Śiva-nature. It is not identity with Him, as in the Advaita view, nor is it going to His region, like the attainment of Indra and others."
When, having transcended the state of a bound soul (paśu), one abides in the state of a Lord (pati), that indeed is his "going. For how could there be going for one who is all-pervading?
When—at which time—one has transcended, having passed beyond, the state of a bound soul, the condition of being a beast...
He abides and exists in the state of Śiva. Then, for that liberated one, his "existence" or "movement" as His consort (tat-patitva) is well known. As it is said in the *Svāyambhuva*:
"For the person whose seed of transmigratory existence has been burnt, that which follows from the ultimate goal..."
That should be understood as his "going," not as remaining in another location.
"Just as in the world, when a previous state has been superseded by another manifestation,
a substance such as the color of a cloth is said to have 'gone' [there], so too is the person [said to go]. Regarding this,
he states that the primary meaning of the word "going" (gamana) is not applicable [to the self], because it is "all-going" (sarvaga), that is, all-pervading.

How can there be movement toward an object? Since both the Self (ātman) and Śiva are all-pervading, the relationship between these two as "that which is to be attained" and "the attainer" is not possible; this is the meaning. The underlying point is this: the attainment of Śiva-nature by the Self must be either union with Śiva or identity with Him. || 85 ||
Now, by means of the *Svāyambhuvasūtra*, it is stated that even the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and so forth does not belong to him:

"For one who has offered himself to the abode of Śiva and is no longer an enjoyer of worldly experience, there is never again the state of being an enjoyer, nor the state of office, nor the imitation of the duties of a Lord (*pati*). (86)

The term *śivadhāmārpita* refers to one for whom the abode of Śiva—that is, equality with Śiva—has been offered and manifested; such a person, an enjoyer of [liberated] experience, never at any time possesses the state of being an enjoyer, which is to say, the agency of the act of enjoyment that is observed in the case of the *sakala* (the embodied soul). This [agency] does not exist in him.

The state of being an *adhikārī*—that is, the state of being an *adhikārī* within the womb of *māyā* which was observed in the case of the *pralayākala*—does not exist [in this case] either. "Imitating the activity of the Lord" (*patikṛtyānukāritā*) means having the capacity to act subsequently (*anu-paścāt-kāritvam*) after the activity of the Lord. Those who proceed when the Lord’s mere will has set them in motion by saying, "Do this," are the imitators of the Lord's activity; of such [agents].
"Bhāva" means the imitation of the husband's duties; that is to say, the state of conducting oneself according to the husband's desires and intentions.
This imitation of the husband's duties is observed even among all three types—sakala, pralayākala, and vijñānākala—but he [the Supreme Lord] does not possess it.
The meaning is that because he is independent, he lacks the state of being impelled by another. Thus, it is said in the Sarvajñānottara:
Like Śiva, he is eternal, pure, and devoid of the nature of creation.
Truth, truth, and again truth—this triple truth has been established as my vow.
O Guha, there is nothing further than this to be known anywhere! 86.
Now, by means of the *Kiraṇasūtra*, he states with an illustration that even in that state, the persistence of impurity (*mala*) is inferable:
"Just as the potency associated with poison is suppressed by mantras..."
Just as that poison is not destroyed then, so too is the destruction of a person's impurity [not achieved]. || 87 ||

The power associated with poison—that is, the power belonging to poison which produces effects such as delusion and death—is restrained by mantras, such as those of the Gāruḍa tradition; it is brought to a state of restraint, meaning its activity toward producing those effects is obstructed. And at that time, that poison [does not produce its effect].

"Exhausted" means that its essential nature—consisting of color, form, and so forth—has not reached a state of total cessation (*kṣaya*). In this manner, for the person whose self (*ātman*) has been purified by initiation, there is the "destruction of impurity" (*malakṣaya*), which is the destruction of the impurity co-existent with itself; at that time, "destruction" is simply the obstruction of the activity toward effects of the power of agency. It is not [total extinction].

The meaning is the destruction of impurity (*mala*) in its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Here, this is investigated: by means of methods such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), is a separation of the impurity effected?
Or is it its destruction? Or is it its concealment? Not the first, because [it would imply] those two [impurity and the soul] are distinct from one another.

Because the relationship is beginningless, its disjunction is impossible. Furthermore, disjunction is preceded by conjunction; however, there is no conjunction between the impurity and the self, as such a connection is impossible given that both are all-pervasive.
Indeed, nothing that is all-pervasive is ever seen to be separated, nor is disjunction [possible] for it.

Birth occurs due to causes such as the action of one or another; and that action, when arising, occurs in a substance possessing limited dimensions. Since that [action] is absent in an all-pervading substance, there is no disjunction between those two.

Now, what of destruction? That too is untenable, because if the innate impurity (*mala*) were destroyed, it would follow that the self (*ātman*), which is its substratum (*dharmin*), would also be destroyed, since the attribute and its substratum are non-different. Furthermore, this impurity is accepted as being capable of obstructing the power of all individual souls (*pudgala*); if it were to be annihilated, [the soul's power would be unimpeded].

In that case, because it would be common to all *pudgalas*, upon the favoring of a single person (*puruṣa*), the entire multitude of living beings would become pure. Therefore, even destruction is not tenable.
Now, what of concealment (*tirobhāva*)? That too is not tenable; for there must be some object whose concealment occurs.

Furthermore, its re-manifestation must necessarily be admitted at some other time; otherwise, it could not even be said that it was concealed. If it is asked, "What is the fault in that? [the answer is: because it would follow that the worldly transmigrator (saṃsārī) is absolutely liberated, which contradicts established usage. Therefore, concealment (tirobhāva) is also not tenable, and there is no other alternative.
Therefore, since multiple faults would arise, how can there be the removal (*apāya*) of this impurity (*mala*)?

To this it is replied: True; in this scripture, through means such as initiation (*dīkṣā*), neither the division, nor the destruction, nor the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of the all-pervading impurity is admitted. Rather, just as...

The burning power of fire’s hot touch is restrained by a mantra; likewise, the operative power of impurity (*mala*) is restrained by spiritual means (*upāya*). Just as in the world fire whose power has been paralyzed is said to be "paralyzed," so too, due to the separation from the power of impurity, that impurity is designated as "separated" by way of metaphorical usage.

It has been stated in this very context: "Just as fire, though all-pervading and common to all *pudgalas* in its function of burning, nevertheless possesses infinite powers (*śakti*). And so, for that person with whom the Guru is pleased, [the Guru] restrains the burning power of that fire and makes the fire cool like snow; and for others...

That fire, being unobstructed, certainly performs its effect characterized by burning. Likewise, impurity (*mala*) also [does not expand] for one whose power is obstructed; for others, however, worldly existence (*bhava*) certainly occurs due to the absence of obstruction. Therefore, this is not a fault.

As for the objection that was stated—that upon the destruction of the innate (*sahaja*) impurity, there would be the destruction of the self—that too is not [correct]. For even when a property (*dharma*) is destroyed, there is no destruction of the substratum (*dharmī*). If it is asked, "Where has this been seen?
it is said: Just as the blackness (*kālikā*) coexisting with copper perishes through contact with acid, but [the copper itself does not].
