Copper is diminished; however, for that very substance which remains, another quality manifests. There is a change in the attributes of the persisting entity, but not of one that has perished. Therefore, just as there is the removal of tarnish from copper, so too is there the removal of impurity for this person.

Thus, here too there is no inconsistency. It has been stated in this very context: "The innate [impurity] is simultaneous with the copper; yet when that [copper] is destroyed, there is no destruction of that [innate impurity].
In the same way, the destruction of the impurity of this Person (puruṣa) occurs. (87)
Having explained the destruction of innate impurity (*sahaja-mala*), he demonstrates the destruction of karma through another scriptural passage:
"Karma pertaining to many births is burnt like a seed by the [atomic] powers (*aṇu*);
and that which is yet to come is blocked by this [power], namely through experience. (88)

That accumulated karma (*saṃcitakarma*) acquired and amassed over many existences and births—that accumulated karma is burnt by subtle mantras like a seed. Just as a seed burnt by fire, its potency being destroyed, is no longer capable of producing a sprout; as it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Seeds burnt by fire do not sprout upon the earth.

Likewise, the meaning is that action whose power has been destroyed by a mantra does not lead to the yielding of fruit. Furthermore, future action—that which is yet to come—is also "completely restrained," meaning it is thoroughly blocked by the power of the mantra.
It is obstructed. But surely, since it has not yet arisen, how can there be an obstruction? This is not true;

its very non-arising is the obstruction. It has been said that whatever other auxiliary karma is its producer is like a burnt seed (ga). Therefore, because it is obstructed, future karma does not arise.
This is the meaning. The remainder [of the sentence] is: "by which karma this body was produced.
That *prārabdha*-karma (projected karma) comes to an end only through experience—that is, through actual enjoyment—and not otherwise. As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"The karmas that have initiated the body are experienced by oneself alone."
Likewise, the meaning is that by means of initiation (dīkṣā), only those karmas other than prārabdha-karma are obstructed.
And this prārabdha is of three kinds: prārabdha by desire (icchā-prārabdha), prārabdha without desire (anicchā-prārabdha), and prārabdha by the desire of another (parēcchā-prārabdha). Thus—
Desire, aversion, and the desire of another—these are known as the three types of *prārabdha* (commenced karma).

Even thieves who consume unwholesome things and those who take pleasure in the wives of kings, though fully aware of their own impending ruin, still desire it due to the force of their commenced karma. (Pañcadaśī 7.152–153)

This is undertaken out of desire. Bound by one's own action born of nature, O son of Kuntī, that which you do not wish to do because of delusion, you shall do even against your will. (Bhagavad Gītā 18.60)
This is what is called "commenced by no desire":
"Neither unwilling nor willing, yet joined with the courtesy of others, they experience pleasure and pain; for this is indeed karma preceded by the desire of another. (Pañcadaśī 7.162)
This is that which has been undertaken through the desire of another. || 88 ||

But surely, initiation has been accepted as the destroyer of all fetters; and once one's own true nature has been manifested by it, does it not follow that at that very moment the body must fall away?
As it has been said in this very same work:
If the complete severance of all bonds occurs through the initiation of the Lord,
once it has taken place, what purpose would there be for the continued existence of the body?
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with another verse:
"Just as when the production of a jar is complete, the wheel continues to spin due to the force of prior momentum, so too is this body said to persist. (89)

The completion of a jar is its manifestation; even when that has occurred—that is, once it has been produced—the wheel continues to spin, maintaining its rotation. In the same way, this visible body, the physical form of the self, remains established by prior impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*). By means of those prior impressions...
It remains standing, having been fully accomplished and supported by a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by causes characterized as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
This is the meaning: first, for the sake of manifesting a jar or a fruit, the potter would cause the wheel to revolve.
Just as that wheel continues to spin even after the production of the jar has occurred,
so too this body— pervaded by prior latent impressions (saṃskāra)— remains as if it were the self even after the accomplishment of its purpose has occurred.

[Objection: But surely, in that case, the act of rotation occurs in the wheel due to momentum (*vega*), and that is applicable even when the fruit has been accomplished. However, in the case of the body, no other cause exists by which its continued existence might be maintained. [Reply: Not so. I do not admit here the total exhaustion of all karma, as follows: ... [The text continues with the refutation of the opponent's view regarding the persistence of the body after liberation. ... Just as...

From the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as "abiding momentum," the effect of whirling continues to occur. Likewise, from the cause characterized by merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*), a specific latent impression characterized as common [to all] arises.
From that specific latent impression, this body remains stable. As it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
"Even when the asafoetida is removed from that vessel, its fragrance does not perish; just as the potter's wheel continues to spin even after the work is finished. Thus [it is said]. (89)
Now, by means of the *Matasūtra*, the Goddess shows the state of the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) at the time of the body’s end:
"Just as a lamp shines forth everywhere when a jar is broken, so too, upon the fall of the body, the Self shines everywhere and at all times. (90)

Just as a lamp, when the jar is broken—that is, when it has been shattered—shines forth everywhere, in all directions, shining perfectly; the meaning is that, having abandoned its contraction, it becomes a self-luminous light everywhere. In the same way, the Self and the liberated soul, upon the fall of the body—at the end of the body—[the consciousness of] the body...

When the body that causes contraction is destroyed, it shines—that is, it manifests—everywhere, in all places, and at all times, in every moment. The meaning is that its light becomes undivided by space and time. As it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
Just as a lamp hidden within a jar shines forth when the jar is destroyed,
so too does the sun hidden by the jar shine forth upon liberation.
"Liberation arises from the knowledge of the true nature [of reality]; he is indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Upon the destruction of the body, there is supreme pervasion, like a lamp when its vessel is destroyed. || 90 ||

Having thus established the three states of absolute purity of the Self by means of defining the nature of the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the fetter (*pāśa*), [the author] provides a discernment of those who are qualified and unqualified for this science of knowledge (*jñānaśāstra*) according to the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
She reveals it: "O fair-faced one, manifest this knowledge to my devotees;
it must be guarded with great effort, like wealth from thieves. (91)

Thus ends the *Śataratnasaṃgraha* compiled by Umāpati Śivācārya. "O fair-faced one!"—this is an address to the Goddess. This "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the scripture (*śāstra*), for it is called knowledge because by means of it the Lord (*pati*) and the other [principles] are known. And so it is said in the *Vāyavīya*:
"Knowledge is the discernment of reality, and reality is known to be threefold.

Thus [it is said]. Reveal—that is, manifest—this to my devotees, those who practice devotion to me. The meaning is that those endowed with compassion and tranquility, who are devoted to the gods, the sacred fire, and the guru, possess the qualification for this scripture of knowledge.
And so it is stated in the Tantra:
"It should be given to one who is peaceful, self-controlled, and devoted to the worship of Śiva;
and to one who regards the teacher—who has reached the further shore of reality—as equal to Śiva himself."
This knowledge should be given to one whose devotion to the Guru is always greater than that toward Śiva; otherwise, it should never be given.
In the Kālottara:
"To one who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the Guru as for the Lord,
and who has no attachment to other scriptures— to him one should impart knowledge."
Likewise, in the Sarvajñānottara:
"This scripture should be given to one who is devoted to the Guru, the deity, and the sacrificial fire, and who is constantly endowed with devotion; one should not bestow it upon others."

He states the characteristics of those who are ineligible for this knowledge in the passage beginning with "rakṣaṇīyam" (it must be protected). Just as in the world people protect wealth, deposits, and so forth from thieves and robbers with great effort and exertion, so too [one must protect] the means of knowledge from "thieves," that is, from those who lack devotion and the like.
The meaning is that it must be guarded with great effort. Thus it is said in the Tantra:
"O Goddess! This supreme essence of knowledge must not be given to one who is poorly purified, to a rogue, to a cruel person, or to one who walks the path of injustice."
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"This true essence of Śiva has emerged from the mouth of Śiva;
it is the secret of secrets, most secret, and should be understood with great effort."
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has no son.
Thus ends the *Śataratnollekhanī* compiled by Umāpati Śivācārya. Om.
Homage to Vināyaka.
Salutations to Śiva, the Lord of Cidambaram, and to Kāmasundarī.
